us-scotus-607-492.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-607-492.summary: The Court held that parents asserting due-process claims were likely to succeed because California’s school policies concealed information about a child’s gender transition and thereby excluded parents from significant decisions concerning the child’s mental health. Applying established parental-rights precedent, the Court recognized parents’ right to direct their children’s upbringing and education, including participation in significant mental-health decisions.
excerpts: The same is true for the subclass of parents who object to those policies on due process grounds. Under longestablished precedent, parents—not the State—have primary authority with respect to “the upbringing and education of children.” Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 534–535 (1925); accord, Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390, 399–400 (1923). The right protected by these precedents includes the right not to be shut out of participation in decisions regarding their children's mental health. Parham v. J. R., 442 U. S. 584, 602 (1979).

us-scotus-606-522.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-606-522.summary: The Court held that parents’ protected right to direct the religious upbringing of their children extends to public-school instruction. Requiring children to attend instruction that poses a substantial threat of undermining their parents’ religious beliefs can burden that parental right and religious exercise.
excerpts: Today, we hold that the parents have shown that they are entitled to a preliminary injunction. A government burdens the religious exercise of parents when it requires them to submit their children to instruction that poses “a very real threat of undermining” the religious beliefs and practices that the parents wish to instill. Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, 218 (1972). And a government cannot condition the beneft of free public education on parents' acceptance of such instruction. Based on these principles, we conclude that the parents are likely to succeed in their challenge to the Board's policies.

The practice of educating one's children in one's religious beliefs, like all religious acts and practices, receives a generous measure of protection from our Constitution. “Drawing on `enduring American tradition,' we have long recognized the rights of parents to direct `the religious upbringing' of their children.” Espinoza, 591 U. S., at 486 (quoting Yoder, 406 U. S., at 213–214, 232). And this is not merely a right to teach religion in the confnes of one's own home. Rather, it extends to the choices that parents wish to make for their children outside the home. It protects, for example, a parent's decision to send his or her child to a private religious school instead of a public school. Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 532–535 (1925).

us-ca8-12-f4th-834.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-12-f4th-834.citation: Hal Stanley v. Asa Hutchinson, 12 F.4th 834 (8th Cir. 2021)
us-ca8-12-f4th-834.summary: The court applied the parental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children, balancing it against the State’s compelling interest in protecting children. It held that officials removing children during an abuse investigation are protected by qualified immunity when the removal is founded on reasonable suspicion of child abuse, evaluated under the totality of the circumstances at the time of removal.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children,” but this interest is “limited by the state’s compelling interest in protecting a child . . . .” Swipies v. Kofka, 348 F.3d 701, 703 (8th Cir. 2003). To balance these competing interests, we have adopted the rule that, “when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.

Reasonable suspicion “must be determined by analyzing the totality of the circumstances at the time of the removal.” Stanley I, 899 F.3d at 629. “The liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling government interest in protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828 (1987).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-591-464.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-591-464.citation: Espinoza v. Montana Dept. of Revenue, 591 U.S. 464 (2020)
us-scotus-591-464.summary: The Court recognized that parents have a constitutionally protected right to direct the religious upbringing and education of their children. It held that Montana’s categorical exclusion of religious schools from a generally available scholarship program burdened that parental choice and violated the Free Exercise Clause as applied through the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: And the prohibition before us today burdens not only religious schools but also the families whose children attend or hope to attend them. Drawing on “enduring American tradition,” we have long recognized the rights of parents to direct “the religious upbringing” of their children. Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, 213–214, 232 (1972). Many parents exercise that right by sending their children to religious schools, a choice protected by the Constitution. See Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 534–535 (1925).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (incorporating the First Amendment Free Exercise Clause against the States)

us-ca8-959-f3d-887.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-959-f3d-887.citation: Dwight Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services, 959 F.3d 887 (8th Cir. 2020)
us-ca8-959-f3d-887.summary: The court applied the substantive due process protections for parent-child care, custody, companionship, and familial integrity in reviewing the children’s removal and prolonged separation from Mitchell. It also applied the rule that interference with marriage violates substantive due process only when it has more than a collateral effect on the marriage, and held that Mitchell alleged no sufficient nexus.
excerpts: Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. Webb ex rel. K.S. v. Smith, 936 F.3d 808, 815 (8th Cir. 2019). Children and parents also share a liberty interest in their mutual care and companionship. Id.; see also Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258 (1983).

The children also claim a violation of their substantive due process rights based on their prolonged separation from their father. While parents and children have a liberty interest in each other’s companionship, Webb, 936 F.3d at 815, “[l]aw enforcement and social workers face difficult decisions in deciding whether the risks facing a child justify intruding into the highly protected rights of familial integrity.

Mitchell also claims that the defendants violated his substantive due process rights by interfering in his marriage to Litvinenko. The right to marriage is a substantive due process right, but actions that only collaterally effect family decisions do not violate the right to marry. Muir v. Decatur Cty., 917 F.3d 1050, 1053–54 (8th Cir. 2019).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-929-f3d-1024.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-929-f3d-1024.summary: The court held that 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b) governs transfers from state court to tribal court and does not require a state-court hearing when no state-court proceeding exists. Applying the parental right to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of children, the court concluded that due process was satisfied because the parents had notice of and were heard in the tribal proceedings.
excerpts: To the contrary, § 1911(b) does not require a state court hearing. Section 1911(b) addresses the transfer of proceedings from state court to tribal court. Here, there were no state court proceedings.

Lastly, Watso and Dietrich allege that the absence of a state court proceeding violated their due process rights, based on parents' fundamental right "to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children." Troxel v. Granville , 530 U.S. 57, 66, 120 S.Ct. 2054, 147 L.Ed.2d 49 (2000) (invalidating state law that allowed any third party to petition state courts for child visitation rights over parental objections). They allege due process rights "to object and to stop the transfer, a right to notice and a right to a meaningful court hearing." Watso and Dietrich had sufficient notice of the tribal court proceedings. They were heard in tribal court. They have presented no evidence of a due process violation.

us-ca8-919-f3d-1054.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-919-f3d-1054.citation: Calgaro v. St. Louis Cnty., 919 F.3d 1054 (8th Cir. 2019)
us-ca8-919-f3d-1054.summary: The court applied the Fourteenth Amendment substantive-due-process principle protecting a parent's interest in the care, custody, and control of children. It held that a medical provider's recognition of a minor's statutory consent did not terminate the parent's rights; only a Minnesota court could terminate parental rights.
excerpts: Anmarie Calgaro sued several parties alleging violations of her parental rights over one of her minor children under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The district court granted the defendants' dispositive motions and dismissed the complaint with prejudice. Calgaro appeals, and we affirm.

Calgaro contends that the providers exercised a "public function" by terminating her parental rights concerning health care decisions, but this claim mischaracterizes what happened. Section 144.341 states that certain minors may give effective consent to medical services, but a provider does not terminate parental rights by recognizing a minor's consent, even if the provider is mistaken. Only a Minnesota court can terminate parental rights. See Minn. Stat. § 260C.301.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-899-f3d-623.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-899-f3d-623.summary: The court applied the rule that parents have a protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, balanced against the state's compelling interest in child protection. It held that removing children during an abuse investigation is constitutionally permissible for qualified-immunity purposes only when supported by a reasonable suspicion of abuse, and that the complaint plausibly alleged that such suspicion was lacking.
excerpts: As the district court recognized, it is clearly established that the removal of children from their parents' custody violates a constitutional right if the removal occurs without reasonable suspicion of child abuse. See Heartland Acad. Cmty. Church v. Waddle, 427 F.3d 525, 534 (8th Cir. 2005) ; Abdouch v. Burger, 426 F.3d 982, 987 (8th Cir. 2005). "Parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children," but this interest is "limited by the state's compelling interest in protecting a child

To balance these competing interests, we have adopted the rule that, "when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-577-404.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-577-404.summary: Per curiam, the Court held that the Alabama Supreme Court erred in refusing full faith and credit to a Georgia adoption judgment making V. L. a second parent; a State may not disregard a sister-State judgment because it disagrees with its reasoning, and the Georgia court's subject-matter jurisdiction was not open to collateral attack on the ground asserted.
excerpts: The Full Faith and Credit Clause forbids a State to disregard the judgment of a sister State because it disagrees with the reasoning underlying the judgment or deems it to be wrong on the merits.

especially where the Full Faith and Credit Clause is concerned, a court must be “slow to read ambiguous words, as meaning to leave the judgment open to dispute, or as intended to do more than fx the rule by which the court should decide.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-ca8-800-f3d-955.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-800-f3d-955.citation: Stevenson v. Blytheville School District # 5, 800 F.3d 955 (8th Cir. 2015)
us-ca8-800-f3d-955.summary: The court recognized that parents have a fundamental but limited liberty interest under the Fourteenth Amendment to direct the education and upbringing of their children. It held that this right does not extend to controlling every aspect of a child’s public-school education or displacing the state’s educational authority.
excerpts: In [Washington v.] Glucksberg, the Supreme Court articulated the fundamental rights protected by the Due Process Clause.” Combs v. Homer-Ctr. Sch. Dist., 540 F.3d 231, 247 (3d Cir.2008) (per curiam) (citing Washington v. Glucksberg, 521 U.S. 702, 719-20, 117 S.Ct. 2258, 138 L.Ed.2d 772 (1997)). The Supreme Court “[ijneluded in the list ... the right ‘to direct the education and upbringing of one’s children.

Although [the appellants] assert the fundamental nature of their general right, it is a limited one.” Id. As the Third Circuit has recognized, “[t]he Supreme Court has never been called upon to define the precise boundaries of a parent’s right to control a child’s upbringing and education. It is clear, however, that the right is neither absolute nor unqualified.” C.N. v. Ridgewood Bd. of Educ., 430 F.3d 159, 182 (3d Cir.2005).

The case law in this area establishes that parents simply do not have a constitutional right to control each and every aspect of their children’s education and oust the state’s authority over that subject.” Swanson [v. Guthrie Indep. Sch. Dist. No. I-L,] 135 F.3d [694,] 699 [ (10th Cir.1998)

us-ca8-710-f3d-772.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-710-f3d-772.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process principles to a family-law dispute, holding that affected parties must receive notice reasonably calculated to apprise them of the action and a meaningful opportunity to be heard. It also recognized parents’ fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and control of their children, while explaining that the interest is limited by the government’s compelling interest in protecting children and does not include freedom from child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: only such procedural protections as the particular situation demands,” id. (quotations and citations omitted), “procedural due process has [a] clear [meaning]: Parties whose rights are to be affected are entitled to be heard; and in order that they may enjoy that right they must first be notified,” id. at 405-06 (quotations and citations omitted). “[T]he opportunity to be heard must come ‘at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.’ ” Id. at 406 (quoting Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 333, 96 S.Ct. 893, 47 L.Ed.2d 18 (1976)). A party “need not receive actual notice, but only notice that is reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action.

Additionally, “the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children.” Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57, 66, 120 S.Ct. 2054, 147 L.Ed.2d 49 (2000) (plurality opinion). “That liberty interest is limited by the compelling governmental interest in protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” Whisman Through Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303, 1309 (8th Cir.1997) (quotation and citation omitted); see also Dornheim v. Sholes, 430 F.3d 919, 925-26 (8th Cir.2005) (“However, the right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations, as the state has a strong interest in protecting the safety and welfare of minor children, particularly where protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” (quotation, alteration, and citation omitted)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-655-f3d-811.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-655-f3d-811.citation: Schmidt v. Des Moines Public Schools, 655 F.3d 811 (8th Cir. 2011)
us-ca8-655-f3d-811.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process principles to a noncustodial parent’s claim involving temporary interference with court-ordered visitation. It held that the brief interruption did not deprive the parent of a constitutionally protected liberty interest and that the officials’ conduct was not conscience-shocking.
excerpts: Parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 753, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982); see also Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57, 65-66, 120 S.Ct. 2054, 147 L.Ed.2d 49 (2000) (plurality opinion). But this right “is not absolute,” Manzano v. S.D. Dep’t of Soc. Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir.1995), as illustrated by our decision in Zakrzewski v. Fox, 87 F.3d 1011, 1014 (8th Cir.1996).

Even if Schmidt could show a deprivation of a fundamental liberty interest, moreover, the officers’ alleged conduct would not shock the conscience. The officers were asked to intercede in a contentious custody dispute involving a court-ordered visitation that the children apparently were unwilling to attend. That the officers may have misinterpreted their obligations under a court order while addressing this difficult situation does not rise to the level of arbitrary government action and egregious misconduct necessary to state a substantive due process claim. See Brittain, 451 F.3d at 996; Gordon v. Hansen, 168 F.3d 1109, 1113 (8th Cir. 1999).

us-ca8-595-f3d-798.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-595-f3d-798.citation: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle, 595 F.3d 798 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-595-f3d-798.summary: The court treated the alleged seizure and removal of students from Heartland as implicating constitutionally protected family and associational interests, including liberty interests in recognized family relationships. It also recognized that procedural due process generally requires a hearing before deprivation of a protected family-related interest, absent extraordinary circumstances justifying postponement.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has long recognized the constitutional rights the Officials allegedly infringed. See, e.g., Chandler v. Miller, 520 U.S. 305, 308, 117 S.Ct. 1295, 137 L.Ed.2d 513 (1997) (reiterating that warrantless seizures generally violate the Fourth Amendment absent an individualized reasonable suspicion determination); Roberts v. U.S. Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609, 622, 104 S.Ct. 3244, 82 L.Ed.2d 462 (1984) (recognizing a First Amendment “right to associate with others in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious, and cultural ends”); Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983) (stating “the relationship of love and duty in a recognized family unit is an interest in liberty entitled to constitutional protection” under the Fourteenth Amendment);

us-ca8-538-f3d-952.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-538-f3d-952.summary: The court applied Rooker-Feldman but held that it did not bar the § 1983 Fourth Amendment claim because the plaintiffs had not participated in the ex parte state proceeding and did not seek to overturn the state order. The court also recognized the parental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children, but rejected the familial-integrity claim because the detention did not violate the Fourth Amendment.
excerpts: We conclude that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine does not apply to David’s Fourth Amendment claim. First, the Riehms could not be considered parties to the ex parte petition. They had no opportunity to participate in the state court proceeding, either the CHIPS petition proceeding (prior to the February 28 hearing) or the ex parte petition proceeding in which the court issued the ex parte order. Second, the Riehms do not seek to overturn the ex parte order by this action. Rather, they seek redress under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for an alleged unconstitutional seizure of David.

Colleen also asserts a claim against Diercks regarding her Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in a familial relationship. "Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Manzano v. S.D. Dep’t of Soc. Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 509 (8th Cir.1995). In Manzano, we granted a social worker qualified immunity because he investigated "upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.” Id. at 511. This case does not concern child abuse, but, as discussed above, Diercks had a "reasonable suspicion” of a threat to David’s welfare that justified the ex parte order removing David from his home. Because there was no Fourth Amendment violation surrounding David's detention, we reject Colleen’s claim.

us-scotus-550-516.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-550-516.citation: Winkelman ex rel. Winkelman v. Parma City School District, 550 U.S. 516 (2007)
us-scotus-550-516.summary: The Court held that IDEA grants parents independent, enforceable rights concerning their disabled children's education, rather than merely recognizing parents as representatives of the child's rights. The decision characterized parents' interest in directing their children's upbringing and education as a recognized legal interest relevant to interpreting the statute.
excerpts: Even if we were inclined to ignore the plain text of the statute in considering this theory, we disagree that the sole purpose driving IDEA’S involvement of parents is to facilitate vindication of a child’s rights. It is not a novel proposition to say that parents have a recognized legal interest in the education and upbringing of their child. See, e. g., Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 534-535 (1925) (acknowledging “the liberty of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control”); Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390, 399-401 (1923).

us-ca8-434-f3d-1051.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-434-f3d-1051.citation: K.D. ex rel. Deason v. County of Crow Wing, 434 F.3d 1051 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-434-f3d-1051.summary: The court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s substantive due process protection for parental custody and familial integrity. It held that an emergency removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permissible when continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child’s health or welfare, and that the temporary removal here did not violate those rights.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest “in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Id. at 509. Parents and children have a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care and companionship of each other. Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303, 1309 (8th Cir.1997). However, “ ‘the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.’ ” Manzano, 60 F.3d at 510 (quoting Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.1987)).

The circumstances under which a child can be removed from his or her parents’ custody without a court order are extremely limited. Deputy Galles removed K.D. from Deason’s custody under Minnesota Statutes § 260C.175, which provides that a child may be taken into immediate custody by a peace officer “when a child is found in surroundings or conditions which endanger the child’s health or welfare or which such peace officer reasonably believes will endanger the child’s health or welfare.” MinmStat. § 260C.175, subd. 1. In light of the facts discussed below, we conclude that Defendants did not violate Plaintiffs’ constitutional rights when K.D. was temporarily removed from Deason’s custody under this statute.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children
Constitutionally protected familial integrity and parent-child companionship

us-ca8-431-f3d-325.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-431-f3d-325.citation: Johnson v. University of Iowa, 431 F.3d 325 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-431-f3d-325.summary: The court held that the parental liberty interest does not encompass a constitutional right to paid employer leave for bonding with a child. Because biological fathers are not a suspect class and paid parental leave is not a fundamental right, the University's distinction between adoptive and biological parents was subject to rational-basis review.
excerpts: Johnson contends that the policy should be reviewed with strict scrutiny because it interferes with his fundamental rights of child-rearing. Although the Supreme Court has recognized a number of fundamental rights concerning parents’ ability to raise their children, Johnson offers no precedent establishing that these rights include the ability to take time off from work to bond with a child. Furthermore, Johnson was allowed to take unpaid leave in accordance with the Family Medical Leave Act. He sued the University because he was unable to receive paid leave.

Because biological fathers are not a suspect class and because the right to paid leave is not fundamental, the appropriate standard of review is the rational basis test. Clayton v. White Hall Sch. Dist., 875 F.2d 676, 680 (8th Cir.1989) (upholding a school district’s policy of allowing the children of administrative employees, but not general employees, to open enroll into the district). A classification reviewed under this standard will be upheld “if it has some reasonable basis.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause and Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-430-f3d-919.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-430-f3d-919.summary: The court applied the substantive-due-process right of parents to control the care and custody of their children and balanced that interest against the State’s interest in protecting children. It held that officials conducting a child-abuse investigation are entitled to qualified immunity when their actions are reasonably founded on a suspicion of abuse, and that family integrity does not include a right to be free from child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: However, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations,” as the state has a strong interest in protecting the safety and welfare of minor children, particularly where protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves. Manzano v. S.D. Dep’t of Soc. Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir. 1995) (internal marks omitted).

These competing interests 'require us to balance the interests of the state and the children against the interests of the parent in determining whether a constitutional violation has occurred. “[W]hen a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.” Thomason v. SCAN Volunteer Servs., 85 F.3d 1365, 1371 (8th Cir.1996) (internal marks omitted).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Substantive Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-426-f3d-982.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-426-f3d-982.summary: The court recognized that Melissa alleged deprivation of a liberty interest in the care and custody of her children, but affirmed qualified immunity for the defendants on that claim. The court also affirmed absolute immunity for the social workers’ initiation or maintenance of judicial termination proceedings.
excerpts: Melissa brought her claims in the present action under § 1983. She concedes that it initially was appropriate for the defendants to remove the children from her home. She alleges, however, that the defendants continued to seek the termination of her parental rights after it became clear that the defendants could not make the showing necessary to terminate her rights. She characterizes this action as a violation of her right to be free from prosecution without probable cause. She also alleges that the defendants’ protracted placement of C.A. in foster care deprived her of her liberty interest in the care and custody of her children. As to the prosecution-related claim, the district court found that the social workers were analogous to prosecutors and therefore entitled to absolute immunity for their initiation of judicial proceedings against Melissa. As to the alleged violation of her liberty interest as a parent, the district court found that qualified immunity applied. We affirm.

us-ca8-427-f3d-525.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-427-f3d-525.citation: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle, 427 F.3d 525 (8th Cir. 2005)
us-ca8-427-f3d-525.summary: The court held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar federal jurisdiction because the requested prospective injunction would not interfere with a state-court judgment. It also applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process principles recognizing familial relations and held that Heartland had standing to assert a family-integrity claim based on its care and control of resident students.
excerpts: In the first appeal of this case, we rejected the challenge Waddle made to jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which prohibits federal-court review of a state-court judgment. We held that the injunctive relief Heartland was seeking would “not interfere with a state-court judgment”

We have recognized a right to familial relations, which includes the liberty interest of parents in the custody, care, and management of their children.” King v. Olmsted County, 117 F.3d 1065, 1067 (8th Cir.1997). And the Supreme Court held in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that a private school could assert such a claim on its own behalf.

us-ca8-420-f3d-823.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-420-f3d-823.summary: The court applied the judge-made parental-rights principle that parents possess a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children and may direct their upbringing and education. Because Blair’s parents knowingly consented to his enrollment and delegated parental authority to school administrators, the court held that he could not maintain a false-imprisonment claim against the schools.
excerpts: Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, Swipies v. Kofka, 348 F.3d 701, 703 (8th Cir.2003), and have the right to direct the upbringing and education of their children, Doe “A” v. Special School Dist. of St. Louis County, 637 F.Supp. 1138, 1146 (E.D.Mo.1986); Reece v. Reece, 890 S.W.2d 706, 710 (Mo.Ct.App.1995) (acknowledging that parent may arrange for another to provide care and education for minor child).

us-ca8-419-f3d-709.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-419-f3d-709.summary: The court held that a noncustodial parent with court-ordered visitation possesses a protected liberty interest in participating in the care, custody, and management of the child. It further held that the alleged deprivation was not de minimis because the parent was scheduled to have visitation for two weeks.
excerpts: The due process clause of the fourteenth amendment says, in relevant part, that no state shall “deprive any person of ... liberty ... without due process of law.” U.S. Const, amend. XIV, § 1. To establish a procedural due process violation under this provision, a plaintiff must first show that the state infringed on a cognizable liberty interest.

If a state court affords a non-custodial parent visitation rights, we believe that the parent possesses, at least in some form, the liberty interest recognized in Manzano. A parent with visitation rights takes part in raising the child by making decisions about care, custody, and management during the period of the visitation, and thus he or she has the sort of parental role that deserves to be protected as a liberty interest.

us-ca8-348-f3d-701.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-348-f3d-701.summary: The court held that parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, including a right not to be separated from a child based only on an officer’s suspicion that another person might abuse the child. It concluded that the alleged removal would violate that parental liberty interest and affirmed denial of qualified-immunity summary judgment because material facts were disputed.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. See Manzano, 60 F.3d at 509. This interest can be limited by the state’s compelling interest in protecting a child: “the parental liberty interest in keeping the family unit intact is not a clearly established right in the context of reasonable suspicion that parents may be abusing children.

Viewing the facts here in the light most favorable to Mr. Swipies, and noting the inconsistencies among Deputy Kofka’s statements in the summary judgment record, we conclude that Mr. Swipies retained the right not to be separated from his child in the face of Deputy Kofka’s suspicion that Mr. Stark might abuse Kendra. We further conclude that it would have been clear to a reasonable officer that removing Kendra in those circumstances would violate Mr. Swipies’s parental liberty interest.

us-ca8-253-f3d-1124.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-253-f3d-1124.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment due process principles to parents’ claims that a state social worker conditioned reunification with their children on sterilization. It treated the alleged interference with the Vaughns’ parental and familial interests as a constitutional deprivation relevant to qualified-immunity analysis.
excerpts: till in the hospital, Ruoff told Margaret that if she got her “tubes tied, that [she] would have [her] kids back in two to three weeks.” Ruoff also told both Margaret and Kevin Sr. that “if [he] or [Margaret] would get sterilized, [their] chances of getting the kids back would be really great.” Margaret then agreed to a tubal ligation, and Ruoff scheduled the procedure for October 8, 1994.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND APPLICATION TO FACTS Ruoff argues that she is entitled to qualified immunity on the Vaughns’ due process claims. Qualified immunity analysis initially asks the following two questions: (1) was there a deprivation of a constitutional right, and, if so, (2) was the right clearly established at the time of the deprivation? County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 841 n. 5, 118 S.Ct. 1708, 140 L.Ed.2d 1043 (1998). If either question is answered in the negative, the public official is entitled to qualified immunity.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-530-57.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-530-57.summary: The Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment protects a fit parent’s fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and control of the parent’s children. Washington’s statute, which allowed any person to obtain visitation whenever it served the child’s best interests, impermissibly authorized judicial interference with a parent’s visitation decision without adequate deference to that decision.
excerpts: The liberty interest at issue in this case — the interest of parents in the care, custody, and control of their children— is perhaps the oldest of the fundamental liberty interests recognized by this Court.

Section 26.10.160(B) of the Revised Code of Washington permits “[a]ny person” to petition a superior court for visitation rights “at any time,” and authorizes that court to grant such visitation rights whenever “visitation may serve the best interest of the child.” Petitioners Jenifer and Gary Troxel petitioned a Washington Superior Court for the right to visit their grandchildren, Isabelle and Natalie Troxel. Respondent Tommie Granville, the mother of Isabelle and Natalie, opposed the petition.

The Washington Supreme Court nevertheless agreed with the Court of Appeals’ ultimate conclusion that the Troxels could not obtain visitation of Isabelle and Natalie pursuant to §26.10.160(3). The court rested its decision on the Federal Constitution, holding that §26.10.160(3) unconstitutionally infringes on the fundamental right of parents to rear their children. In the court’s view, there were at least two problems with the nonparental visitation statute. First, according to the Washington Supreme Court, the Constitution permits a State to interfere with the right of parents to rear their children only to prevent harm or potential harm to a child.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-155-f3d-992.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-155-f3d-992.summary: The court recognized that parents have a constitutional liberty to choose the education their child receives, relying on Pierce and Yoder. It considered whether withholding special-education services from a child attending a private religious school impermissibly burdened or conditioned that parental choice.
excerpts: It is undisputed that Aaron has the right to receive special education services if he attends a public school. It is also clear that the Westendorps have the constitutional right to choose the education that Aaron shall receive. See Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 534-35, 45 S.Ct. 571, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925) (discussing “the liberty of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control,” which “excludes any general power of the State to standardize its children by forcing them to accept instruction from public teachers only”); see also Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205, 233-34, 92 S.Ct. 1526, 32 L.Ed.2d 15 (1972).

us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.citation: Whisman ex rel. Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303 (8th Cir. 1997)
us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.summary: The court held that parents possess a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, and that parents and children have a corresponding liberty interest in familial association. The alleged removal and continued retention of the child without reasonable suspicion of abuse or a prompt post-deprivation hearing stated a due-process claim.
excerpts: Michelle has alleged that defendants’ actions violated her constitutional right to not be deprived of the custody of her son without due process of law. Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.1987). Both parents and children have a liberty interest in the care and companionship of each other.

Even if defendants had a right to take temporary custody of Joel, defendants had a corresponding obligation to afford Michelle and Joel an adequate post-deprivation hearing. Doe v. Hennepin County, 858 F.2d 1325, 1329 (8th Cir.1988). The right to an adequate post-deprivation hearing was clearly established in February of 1995.

us-scotus-519-102.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-519-102.summary: The Court held that Mississippi could not condition an appeal from a parental-rights termination decree on an indigent parent’s prepayment of record-preparation fees. Because the State had authorized appellate review and the proceeding involved the permanent severance of a fundamental parent-child relationship, denying review solely because of poverty violated the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: By order of a Mississippi Chancery Court, petitioner M. L. B.’s parental rights to her two minor children were forever terminated. M. L. B. sought to appeal from the termination decree, but Mississippi required that she pay in advance record preparation fees estimated at $2,352.36. Because M. L. B. lacked funds to pay the fees, her appeal was dismissed. was Urging that the size of her pocketbook should not be dis-positive when “an interest far more precious than any property right” is at stake, Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U. S. 745, 758-759 (1982), M. L. B. tenders this question, which we agreed to hear and decide: May a State, consistent with the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, condition appeals from trial court decrees terminating parental rights on the affected parent’s ability to pay record preparation fees? We hold that, just as a State may not block an indigent petty offender’s access to an appeal afforded others, see Mayer v. Chicago, 404 U. S. 189, 195-196 (1971), so Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent.

Choices about marriage, family life, and the upbringing of children are among associational rights this Court has ranked as “of basic importance in our society,” Boddie, 401 U. S., at 376, rights sheltered by the Fourteenth Amendment against the State’s unwarranted usurpation, disregard, or disrespect. See, for example, Turner v. Safley, 482 U. S. 78 (1987), Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U. S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967) (marriage); Skinner v. Oklahoma ex rel. Williamson, 316 U. S. 535 (1942) (procreation); Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510 (1925), and Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923) (raising children). M. L. B.’s case, involving the State’s authority to sever permanently a parent-child bond, demands the close consideration the Court has long required when a family association so undeniably important is at stake.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses)

us-ca8-87-f3d-1011.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-87-f3d-1011.summary: The court recognized that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and that visitation rights may be subject to due-process scrutiny. It further held that a substantive due-process claim based on interference with visitation requires conduct that abuses official power and shocks the conscience; the court found no prior case establishing a constitutional violation at that level.
excerpts: It is beyond question that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1986) (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983), citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 753, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 1394, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)) (alteration in original). This right, however, is not absolute. Manzano v. South Dakota Dep’t of Social Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir.1995).

To the extent Zakrzewski claims a substantive due process violation of Ms parenting liberty interest, he must demonstrate that the defendants abused their official power in a manner that shocks the conscience, regardless of whether state-law remedies are available. New v. City of Minneapolis, 792 F.2d 724, 725-26 (8th Cir.1986). “[T]he theory of substantive due process is properly reserved for truly egregious and extraordinary cases,” Myers v. Scott County, 868 F.2d 1017, 1019 (8th Cir.1989),

us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.citation: Thomason v. SCAN Volunteer Services, Inc., 85 F.3d 1365 (8th Cir. 1996)
us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the government’s compelling interest in protecting children. In the context of a child-abuse investigation, officials are entitled to qualified immunity when an otherwise disruptive action is reasonably founded on suspicion of abuse.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991-92, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1988)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983).

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).

Clearly, our precedents provide that, when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (substantive due process)

us-ca8-70-f3d-1012.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-70-f3d-1012.summary: The court held that a child-welfare worker’s alleged failure to follow a state-court reunification plan or state agency policy did not, standing alone, establish a violation of the parent’s federal constitutional liberty interest. It affirmed qualified immunity because no clearly established constitutional right required strict adherence to the plan.
excerpts: Mr. Ebmeier claims the defendants “disregarded” both the Buffalo County Court’s order approving the reunification plan and NDSS policy, thereby violating his “constitutionally protected fundamental liberty interest in the care and custody of his children.” As the District Court put it, Mr. Ebmeier asserts a “clearly established right requiring the defendants to adhere strictly to the court order that directed them to devise a reunification plan.

It is established beyond peradventure that a state actor’s failure to observe a duty imposed by state law, standing alone, is not a sufficient foundation on which to erect a section 1983 claim. Although it is true that constitutional significance may attach to certain interests created by state law, not every transgression of state law does double duty as a constitutional violation.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-60-f3d-505.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-60-f3d-505.citation: Manzano v. South Dakota Department of Social Services, 60 F.3d 505 (8th Cir. 1995)
us-ca8-60-f3d-505.summary: The court recognized that parents have a Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children and in familial integrity. It held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the compelling governmental interest in protecting minor children, particularly during child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983). However, we have at the same time indicated that this right is not absolute.

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-ca8-59-f3d-92.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-59-f3d-92.citation: Amerson ex rel. M.H. v. Iowa, 59 F.3d 92 (8th Cir. 1995)
us-ca8-59-f3d-92.summary: The court held that the mother’s habeas petition primarily asserted her own parental right to custody, rather than the child’s liberty interests. Because a parental-rights claim cannot establish federal habeas jurisdiction under these circumstances, the district court properly dismissed the petition.
excerpts: Particularly when a habeas petition is brought by a parent seeking the release of a child from state custody, the action may really involve an assertion of the parent’s rights, not the liberty interests of the child. See Lehman, 458 U.S. at 511, 102 S.Ct. at 3237 (“Ms. Lehman simply seeks to relitigate, through federal habeas, not any liberty interest of her sons, but the interest in her own parental rights.
Thus, we conclude Amerson’s action is merely an assertion of her right to custody of M.H., which cannot form the basis for habeas jurisdiction. See Lehman, 458 U.S. at 515-16,102 S.Ct. at 3239-40.

us-scotus-507-292.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-507-292.summary: The Court held that an alien juvenile detained pending deportation has no substantive-due-process right to release into the custody of a private individual rather than a government-operated or government-selected facility. It also held that the regulation’s presumptive preference for parents, close relatives, and state-appointed guardians was consistent with the Attorney General’s broad statutory detention discretion.
excerpts: Where a juvenile has no available parent, close relative, or legal guardian, where the government does not intend to punish the child, and where the conditions of governmental custody are decent and humane, such custody surely does not violate the Constitution. It is rationally connected to a governmental interest in “preserving and promoting the welfare of the child,” Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U. S. 745, 766 (1982), and is not punitive since it is not excessive in relation to that valid purpose.

The list begins with parents, whom our society and this Court’s jurisprudence have always presumed to be the preferred and primary custodians of their minor children. See Parham v. J R., 442 U. S. 584, 602-603 (1979). The list extends to other close blood relatives, whose protective relationship with children our society has also traditionally respected.

That grants the Attorney General discretion to determine when temporary detention pending deportation proceedings is appropriate, and makes his exercise of that discretion “presumptively correct and unassailable except for abuse.” Carlson v. Landon, 342 U. S. 524, 540 (1952). We assuredly cannot say that the decision to rely on universally accepted presumptions as to the custodial competence of parents and close relatives, and to defer to the expertise of the States regarding the capabilities of other potential custodians, is an abuse of this broad discretion simply because it does not track policies applicable outside the immigration field.

us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.citation: Henne ex rel. Henne v. Wright, 904 F.2d 1208 (8th Cir. 1990)
us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive-due-process principles to determine whether parents have a fundamental right to give a child at birth a surname lacking a legally established parental connection. It recognized constitutionally protected parental child-rearing interests but held that those interests are not absolute and do not establish the asserted naming right.
excerpts: Whether there is a fundamental right to give a child a surname at birth with which the child has no legally established parental connection will dictate the appropriate level of constitutional scrutiny for evaluating Neb.Rev.Stat. § 71-640.01. Specifically, if the statute significantly infringes a right deemed fundamental under the fourteenth amendment right of privacy then we must rigorously scrutinize the asserted justifications for the statute.

While Meyer and Pierce extended constitutional protection to parental decisions relating to child rearing, the parental rights recognized in those cases centered primarily around the training and education of children. For example, the law at issue in Meyer prevented parents from having their children taught in a foreign language, 262 U.S. at 396-403, 43 S.Ct. at 626-28, and the law at issue in Pierce prevented parents from sending their children to non-public schools, 268 U.S. at 529-36, 45 S.Ct. at 571-74.

us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.citation: Lux ex rel. Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.summary: The court applied the substantive due process principle that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It considered that asserted right in reviewing the qualified-immunity defense to the § 1983 claim arising from the child’s separation from her father.
excerpts: Carrie alleges that her due process and liberty rights were violated when she was separated from her father as a result of DSS’s investigation and the subsequent dependency and neglect proceedings. She cites Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403 (8th Cir.1986), in which we recognized that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Id. at 407 (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-491-110.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-491-110.citation: Michael H. v. Gerald D., 491 U.S. 110 (1989)
us-scotus-491-110.summary: The plurality held that California’s conclusive marital-paternity presumption was a substantive rule implementing family-integrity policy, rather than a procedural due-process defect. It rejected Michael’s claim that his biological connection and relationship with Victoria gave him a constitutionally protected liberty interest requiring recognition as her legal father or conferring parental rights against the intact marital family.
excerpts: This Court has struck down as illegitimate certain “irrebut-table presumptions.” See, e. g., Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972); Vlandis v. Kline, 412 U. S. 441 (1973); Cleveland Board of Education v. LaFleur, 414 U. S. 632 (1974). Those holdings did not, however, rest upon procedural due process. A conclusive presumption does, of course, foreclose the person against whom it is invoked from demonstrating, in a particularized proceeding, that applying the presumption to him will in fact not further the lawful governmental policy the presumption is designed to effectuate.

We therefore reject Michael’s procedural due process challenge and proceed to his substantive claim. Michael contends as a matter of substantive due process that, because he has established a parental relationship with Victoria, protection of Gerald’s and Carole’s marital union is an insufficient state interest to support termination of that relationship. This argument is, of course, predicated on the assertion that Michael has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in his relationship with Victoria.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-852-f2d-1039.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-852-f2d-1039.summary: The court rejected the parents’ claim that the Fourteenth Amendment gives them a fundamental right to supervise their children’s education free from state testing requirements. It also applied rational-basis review to Arkansas’s differing regulation of home schools and private schools, upholding the classification.
excerpts: Second, we find no persuasive arguments advanced that there is a fundamental right of parents to supervise their children’s education to the extent that the Murphys contend. The recognition of such a right would fly directly in the face of those cases in which the Supreme Court has recognized the broad power of the state to compel school attendance and regulate curriculum and teacher certification. See Board of Education v. Allen, 392 U.S. at 245-46, 88 S.Ct. at 1927-28; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 534, 45 S.Ct. 571, 573, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925). Thus, again, strict scrutiny cannot be invoked in this case.

Given that strict scrutiny analysis does not apply, we move to the question of whether Arkansas has a rational reason to subject home schooling to regulatory requirements, while at the same time freeing private schools from virtually any regulation. This step by the legislature in Arkansas may at first glance offend common sense, and, sitting as a legislature, we might not have made this same decision. However, our job is not to sit as a legislature and the constitutional standard of rationality under the equal protection clause is a relaxed one.

us-ca8-810-f2d-1437.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-810-f2d-1437.summary: The court recognized that parents and children possess a constitutionally protected liberty interest in their care and companionship. It held that this interest is not absolute and that damages claims arising from the summary separation of children from parents were barred by qualified immunity where the legality of the conduct was legitimately uncertain.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has recognized a liberty interest which parents and children have in the care and companionship of each other. See, e.g., Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258 (1983) (“ * * * the Court has found that the relationship of love and duty in a recognized family unit is an interest in liberty entitled to constitutional protection.

us-ca8-787-f2d-403.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-787-f2d-403.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It held that the alleged reduction of visitation and foster-placement decisions did not establish a substantive due process violation, and that Missouri’s available post-deprivation procedures provided constitutionally adequate protection for the parents’ interests.
excerpts: This court has previously recognized that “[pjarents have a fundamental ‘liberty interest’ in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983) (citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)). “That [the Fitzgeralds may have] been deprived of a constitutionally protected right, of course, does not answer the whole question of whether [they have] a claim for relief. [They] must also show that [they were] deprived of the right without due process of law.” Id.

The Fitzgeralds’ procedural due process claim is based on the defendants’ failure to provide the Fitzgeralds with a hearing prior to reducing their periodic visits with Wisa or prior to permitting Wisa to remain with her DFS-selected foster parent. We recognize the possibility that visitation and placement decisions may be subject to due process scrutiny, as such decisions may infringe upon a parent’s interest in the “care, custody, and management of their child.” Santosky v. Kramer, supra, 455 U.S. at 753, 102 S.Ct. at 1394-95.

us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.citation: Bohn v. County of Dakota, 772 F.2d 1433 (8th Cir. 1985)
us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.summary: The court held that the privacy and autonomy of the parent-child relationship constitute protectible liberty interests under the Due Process Clause. It therefore evaluated the procedures used to determine child abuse under the Mathews v. Eldridge framework, balancing the family interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the government's interests.
excerpts: The privacy and autonomy of familial relationships involved in a case like this are unarguably among the protectible interests which due process protects. We can conceive of no more important relationship, no more basic bond in American society, than the tie between parent and child.

Having identified the protectible interests at stake, we next turn to the procedural protections that are due under Minn. Stat.Ann. § 626.556. To assist the courts in evaluating the propriety of such procedures, the Supreme Court in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 96 S.Ct. 893, 47 L.Ed.2d 18 (1976), identified three factors:

us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.citation: Horton v. Marshall Public Schools, 769 F.2d 1323 (8th Cir. 1985)
us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.summary: The court held that the school district’s policy violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause by creating an irrebuttable presumption that children without a parent or legal guardian residing in the district were not domiciled there, despite reasonable alternative means of determining domicile. The court rejected the claim that the policy impermissibly burdened a nontraditional family-living arrangement because it did not require children to live with a parent or legal guardian.
excerpts: rict court’s interpretation of the term “domicile” in the school attendance context to mean “residence”, there is no authority for so limiting a child’s domicile under Arkansas case law. See Spriggs v. Altheimer, Arkansas School District No. 22, supra. Accordingly, it is not “universally true” that children who do not have a parent or legal guardian living in the Marshall school district are not domiciled in the district (i.e. residing in the district with a present intent to remain). Since, as in Vlandis, reasonable alternative means of determining the child’s domicile exist, the Marshall school district policy creates an unconstitutional irrebuttable presumption.

3. Nontraditional Family-Living Arrangement. Plaintiffs further contend that the Marshall Public School District’s policy unconstitutionally interferes with their right to adopt a nontraditional family-living arrangement. See Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 431 U.S. 494, 506, 97 S.Ct. 1932, 1939, 52 L.Ed.2d 531 (1977). us-scotus-463-248.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-463-248.summary: The Court held that an unmarried biological father who had neither developed a substantial relationship with his child nor taken affirmative steps to establish one has no absolute constitutional right to notice and a hearing before the child’s adoption. New York’s statutory scheme, including its putative-father registry and defined notice categories, did not violate the Due Process or Equal Protection Clauses.
excerpts: When an unwed father demonstrates a full commitment to the responsibilities of parenthood by “com[ing] forward to participate in the rearing of his child,” Caban, 441 U. S., at 392, his interest in personal contact with his child acquires substantial protection under the Due Process Clause.

The question presented is whether New York has sufficiently protected an unmarried father’s inchoate relationship with a child whom he has never supported and rarely seen in the two years since her birth. The appellant, Jonathan Lehr, claims that the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, as interpreted in Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972), and Caban v. Mohammed, 441 U. S. 380 (1979), give him an absolute right to notice and an opportunity to be heard before the child may be adopted. We disagree.

In this case, however, it is a parent who claims that the State has improperly deprived him of a protected interest in liberty. This Court has examined the extent to which a natural father’s biological relationship with his child receives protection under the Due Process Clause in precisely three cases: Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972), Quilloin v. Walcott, 434 U. S. 246 (1978), and Caban v. Mohammed, 441 U. S. 380 (1979).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-ca8-702-f2d-710.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-702-f2d-710.summary: The court held that a parent has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of her child. Because the government relocated and concealed the child without providing any opportunity for the parent to challenge that action, the court found a due-process issue. It further held that the domestic-relations exception did not bar federal-question jurisdiction where state remedies could not provide effective relief against federal officials.
excerpts: Parents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children. See, e.g., Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 1394, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982). We need not decide whether a parent’s visitation rights are constitutionally protected, because Donna has more than a right to visitation.

But here plaintiff got no process at all. At no time was she allowed to challenge, before some impartial authority, the government’s conclusion that it was necessary to take Mike into the WPP, and to keep him there, in order to protect Michael’s life. We can readily agree with the Marshals Service that advance notice of a person’s being taken into the program need not be given. That would destroy the whole premise of secrecy on which the Program is based. But it should have been possible to devise some kind of post-deprivation process in which Donna could be heard.

Underlying the various reasons advanced to justify the domestic-relations exception is one basic premise: There is a state forum in which the plaintiff may obtain relief. Here, the state court cannot grant effective relief to Donna Ruffalo. Michael refuses to obey the court’s custody order, and ordinary processes for discovering his whereabouts are being impeded by the action of the federal government in providing him a new identity.

us-scotus-455-745.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-455-745.summary: The Court held that parental rights are a constitutionally protected liberty interest and that terminating them permanently and irrevocably requires heightened procedural protection. Under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, the State must prove the grounds for termination by at least clear and convincing evidence, rather than New York’s fair-preponderance standard.
excerpts: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.

Today we hold that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment demands more than this. Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.

At the factfinding hearing, the State must establish, among other things, that for more than a year after the child entered state custody, the agency “made diligent efforts to encourage and strengthen the parental relationship.” Fam. Ct. Act §§ 614.1.(c), 611. The State must further prove that during that same period, the child's natural parents failed “substantially and continuously or repeatedly to maintain contact with or plan for the future of the child although physically and financially able to do so.” §614.1.(d).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-452-18.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-452-18.citation: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981)
us-scotus-452-18.summary: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every parental-status termination proceeding; whether due process calls for appointed counsel is to be decided case by case by the trial court, subject to appellate review, and counsel was not required on the facts of this case.
excerpts: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding. We therefore adopt the standard found appropriate in Gagnon v. Scar- pelli, and leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court, subject, of course, to appellate review.
In view of all these circumstances, we hold that the trial court did not err in failing to appoint counsel for Ms. Lassiter.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-442-584.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-442-584.summary: The Court held that a child has a substantial liberty interest in avoiding unnecessary confinement for mental-health treatment, but that interest is ordinarily intertwined with the parents’ interests and responsibilities for the child’s welfare. Applying due-process balancing, the Court upheld Georgia’s voluntary-commitment scheme because parental authority and professional evaluation provided sufficient protection against arbitrary commitment without a mandatory adversary hearing.
excerpts: It is not disputed that a child, in common with adults, has a substantial liberty interest in not being confined unnecessarily for medical treatment and that the state’s involvement in the commitment decision constitutes state action under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Our jurisprudence historically has reflected Western civilization concepts of the family as a unit with broad parental authority over minor children. Our cases have consistently followed that course; our constitutional system long ago rejected any notion that a child is “the mere creature of the State” and, on the contrary, asserted that parents generally “have the right, coupled with the high duty, to recognize and prepare [their children] for additional obligations.” Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 535 (1925).

In applying these criteria, we must consider first the child’s interest in not being committed. Normally, however, since this interest is inextricably linked with the parents’ interest in and obligation for the welfare and health of the child, the private interest at stake is a combination of the child’s and parents’ concerns. Next, we must examine the State’s interest in the procedures it has adopted for commitment and treatment of children. Finally, we must consider how well Georgia’s procedures protect against arbitrariness in the decision to commit a child to a state mental hospital.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-scotus-442-640.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-442-640.citation: Secretary of Public Welfare v. Institutionalized Juveniles, 442 U.S. 640 (1979)
us-scotus-442-640.summary: The Court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause to Pennsylvania’s procedures for the voluntary institutionalization of children for mental-health treatment. It held that parental consent does not eliminate the child’s liberty interest and that an independent neutral factfinder must determine whether statutory medical-admission requirements are satisfied, with periodic review of the child’s continuing need for commitment.
excerpts: We conclude .that the risk of error inherent in the parental decision to have a child institutionalized for mental health care is sufficiently great that some kind of inquiry should be made by a ‘neutral factfinder’ to determine whether the statutory requirements for admission are satisfied. . . . That inquiry must carefully probe the child’s background using all available sources, including, but not limited to, parents, schools, and other social agencies.

Of course, the review must also include an interview with the child. It is necessary that the decision-maker have the authority to refuse to admit any child who does not satisfy the medical standards for admission. Finally, it is necessary that the child’s continuing need for commitment be reviewed periodically by a similarly independent procedure.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Pennsylvania Mental Health Procedures Act of 1976, § 201

us-scotus-434-246.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-434-246.summary: The Court held that Georgia could deny an unwed biological father veto authority over his child’s adoption under a “best interests of the child” standard, rather than requiring a finding of unfitness. Given the father’s lack of a developed family relationship with the child and the child’s established family life with the mother and stepfather, the statutory scheme did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: Thus, the underlying issue is whether, in the circumstances of this case and in light of the authority granted by Georgia law to married fathers, appellant’s interests were adequately protected by a “best interests of the child” standard. We examine this issue first under the Due Process Clause and then under the Equal Protection Clause.

We have recognized on numerous occasions that the relationship between parent and child is constitutionally protected. See, e. g., Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, 231-233 (1972) Stanley v. Illinois, supra; Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390, 399-401 (1923). “It is cardinal with us that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents, whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause; Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-557-f2d-170.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-557-f2d-170.citation: M. S. v. Wermers, 557 F.2d 170 (8th Cir. 1977)
us-ca8-557-f2d-170.summary: The court recognized parents’ constitutionally protected authority to direct the care, custody, education, and upbringing of their minor children. It applied that principle to conclude that parents may be informed of and attempt to address a minor child’s litigation, consistent with preserving the family relationship.
excerpts: In addition to restriction by the state, minors are subject to parental custody and control. “Constitutional interpretation has consistently recognized that the parents’ claim to authority in their own household to direct the rearing of their children is basic to the structure of society. It is cardinal that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder.” Carey v. New York, -U.S.-,---, 97 S.Ct. 2010, 2028, 52 L.Ed.2d 675 (1977).

Judicial decisions have enveloped the sanctity of the family and parental authority with constitutional protection because the institution of the family has long been recognized as a cornerstone of our law. Moore v. East Cleveland,-U.S.-, 97 S.Ct. 1932, 52 L.Ed.2d 531 (1977); Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205, 92 S.Ct. 1526, 32 L.Ed.2d 15 (1972); Ginsberg v. New York, supra; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 45 S.Ct. 571, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925).

us-scotus-431-816.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-431-816.citation: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform, 431 U.S. 816 (1977)
us-scotus-431-816.summary: The Court construed the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause in the context of foster-child placement and family integrity. It held that constitutional family protections principally reflect biological parent-child relationships, although nonbiological relationships may sometimes possess comparable emotional and familial significance; the foster parents’ asserted liberty interest therefore required analysis under the constitutional concept of family.
excerpts: It is, of course, true that “freedom of personal choice in matters of . . . family life is one of the liberties protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.” Cleveland Board of Education v. LaFleur, 414 U. S. 632, 639-640 (1974). There does exist a “private realm of family life which the state cannot enter,” Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U. S. 158, 166 (1944), that has been afforded both substantive and procedural protection.

First, the usual understanding of “family” implies biological relationships, and most decisions treating the relation between parent and child have stressed this element. Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645, 651 (1972), for example, spoke of “[t]he rights to conceive and to raise one’s children” as essential rights, citing Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923), and Skinner v. Oklahoma ex rel. Williamson, 316 U. S. 535 (1942).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-ca8-547-f2d-1007.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-547-f2d-1007.summary: The court treated the right to conceive and raise one's children as a fundamental liberty interest protected by due process. It considered that parental-rights interest in evaluating a challenge to Missouri’s deadly-force rules governing police pursuit of fleeing suspects.
excerpts: Among the rights that have been declared fundamental in due process analysis are the right to abort a pregnancy (encompassed within the right to privacy), Roe v. Wade, supra; to be free of restrictive maternity leave regulations that burden “the freedom of personal choice in matters of marriage and family life,” Cleveland Board of Education v.
