LaFleur, 414 U.S. 632, 639-640, 94 S.Ct. 791, 796, 39 L.Ed.2d 52 (1974); and the “rights to conceive and raise one’s children,” Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645, 651, 92 S.Ct. 1208, 1212, 31 L.Ed.2d 551 (1972).

us-scotus-420-636.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-420-636.summary: The Court held that § 402(g) violated the Fifth Amendment because it denied widowers survivors’ benefits available to widows based on an archaic and overbroad sex-based assumption about family support and caregiving. The Court also recognized that fathers, like mothers, have a constitutionally protected interest in the care, custody, and management of their children.
excerpts: The gender-based distinction made by § 402 (g) is indistinguishable from that invalidated in Frontiero v. Richardson, 411 U. S. 677 (1973). Frontiero involved statutes which provided the wife of a male serviceman with dependents’ benefits but not the husband of a servicewoman unless she proved that she supplied more than one-half of her husband’s support. The Court held that the statutory scheme violated the right to equal protection secured by the Fifth Amendment.

Given the purpose of enabling the surviving parent to remain at home to care for a child, the gender-based distinction of § 402 (g) is entirely irrational. The classification discriminates among surviving children solely on the basis of the sex of the surviving parent. Even in the typical family hypothesized by the Act, in which the husband is supporting the family and the mother is caring for the children, this result makes no sense. The fact that a man is working while there is a wife at home does not mean that he would, or should be required to, continue to work if his wife dies. It is no less important for a child to be cared for by its sole surviving parent when that parent-is male rather than female.

norms.b_justification: Weinberger v. Wiesenfeld interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 402(g) and held that its sex-based distinction in surviving-parent benefits violated equal protection. That holding is consistent in function with the current formulation concerning unconstitutional sex classifications in benefits and family-support contexts, although no verbatim current statutory text is supplied.

us-scotus-406-205.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-406-205.summary: The Court held that Wisconsin’s compulsory-attendance law could not constitutionally require Amish children to attend high school beyond the eighth grade when doing so substantially burdened the parents’ religiously grounded direction of their children’s education and upbringing. The State’s interest in universal education was subject to balancing against the parents’ fundamental interests and the Free Exercise Clause.
excerpts: There is no doubt as to the power of a State, having a high responsibility for education of its citizens, to impose reasonable regulations for the control and duration of basic education. See, e. g., Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 534 (1925). Providing public schools ranks at the very apex of the function of a State. Yet even this paramount responsibility was, in Pierce, made to yield to the right of parents to provide an equivalent education in a privately operated system.

As that case suggests, the values of parental direction of the religious upbringing and education of their children in their early and formative years have a high place in our society. See also Ginsberg v. New York, 390 U. S. 629, 639 (1968); Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923); cf. Rowan v. Post Office Dept., 397 U. S. 728 (1970). Thus, a State’s interest in universal education, however highly we rank it, is not totally free from a balancing process when it impinges on fundamental rights and interests
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Exercise Clause), as applied to the States through amend. XIV

us-scotus-405-645.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-405-645.summary: The Court held that an unwed father who had sired and raised his children could not be presumed unfit solely because of his unmarried status. Before removing his children, Illinois had to provide a hearing on his parental fitness, and denying that hearing while affording it to other parents violated due process and equal protection.
excerpts: The private interest here, that of a man in the children he has sired and raised, undeniably warrants deference and, absent a powerful countervailing interest, protection.

We must therefore examine the question that Illinois would have us avoid: Is a presumption that distinguishes and burdens all unwed fathers constitutionally repugnant? We conclude that, as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him and that, by denying him a hearing and extending it to all other parents whose custody of their children is challenged, the State denied Stanley the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.

The private interest here, that of a man in the children he has sired and raised, undeniably warrants deference and, absent a powerful countervailing interest, protection. It is plain that the interest of a parent in the companionship, care, custody, and management of his or her children “come[s] to this Court with a momentum for respect lacking when appeal is made to liberties which derive merely from shifting economic arrangements.” Kovacs v. Cooper, 336 U. S. 77, 95 (1949) (Frankfurter, J., concurring).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-321-158.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-321-158.summary: The Court recognized that parents ordinarily have primary custody, care, and nurture of their children, including authority to provide religious training. It held that this parental liberty and the family’s private sphere are not absolute, and that Massachusetts could restrict a custodian’s control through generally applicable child-labor laws enacted to protect children, even when the activity was religiously motivated.
excerpts: It is cardinal with us that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents, whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder.

It is cardinal with us that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents, whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder. Pierce v. Society of Sisters, supra. And it is in recognition of this that these decisions have respected the private realm of family life which the state cannot enter.

But the family itself is not beyond regulation in the public interest, as against a claim of religious liberty. Reynolds v. United States, 98 U. S. 145; Davis v. Beason, 133 U. S. 333. And neither rights of religion nor rights of parenthood are beyond limitation. Acting to guard the general interest in youth’s well being, the state as parens patriae may restrict the parent’s control by requiring school attendance, regulating or prohibiting the child’s labor and in many other ways. Its authority is not nullified merely because the parent grounds his claim to control the child’s course of conduct on religion or conscience.

norms.b_justification: Prince interpreted the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause in addressing parental custody, family privacy, and the state's authority to intervene in child welfare. Its recognition of a protected private realm of family life, subject to legitimate state regulation, is consistent in function with the current family-integrity rule, including extended and foster-family association.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-268-510.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-268-510.citation: Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510 (1925)
us-scotus-268-510.summary: The Court held that Oregon’s compulsory public-schooling law unreasonably interfered with parents’ and guardians’ liberty to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control. The Fourteenth Amendment’s protection of liberty barred the State from requiring all children to receive instruction exclusively from public teachers absent a reasonable relation to a competent state purpose.
excerpts: The child is not the mere creature of the State; those who nurture him and direct his destiny have the right, coupled with the high duty, to recognize and prepare him for additional. obligations.

Under the doctrine of Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390, we think it entirely plain That the Act of 1922 unreasonably- interferes- with the liberty of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control. As often heretofore pointed out, rights guaranteed '- by the Constitution may not be abridged by legislation which has no reasonable relation to some purpose within the competency of the. State.

The fundamental theory of liberty upon, which all governments in this Union repose excludes any general power of the State to standardize its children by forcing them to accept instruction from public teachers only; The child is not the mere creature of the State; those who nurture him and direct his destiny have the right, coupled with the high duty, to recognize and prepare him for additional. obligations.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-262-390.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-262-390.summary: The Court held that the liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment includes the right to acquire useful knowledge, establish a home, and bring up children. Nebraska’s prohibition on teaching German to young children unreasonably infringed that protected liberty and was not a valid exercise of the state’s police power.
excerpts: Without doubt, it denotes not merely freedom from bodily restraint but also the right of the individual to contract, to engage in any of the common occupations of life, to acquire useful knowledge, to marry, establish a home and bring up children, to worship God according to the dictates of his own conscience, and generally to enjoy those privileges long recognized at common law as essential to the orderly pursuit of happiness by free men.

The established doctrine is that this liberty may not be interfered with, under the guise of protecting the public interest, by legislative action which is arbitrary or without reasonable relation to some purpose within the competency of the State to effect. Determination by the legislature of what constitutes proper exercise of police power is not final or conclusive but is subject to supervision by the courts.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-441-380.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-441-380.summary: The Court held that New York Domestic Relations Law § 111 violated the Fourteenth Amendment because it categorically gave unmarried mothers, but not unmarried fathers with substantial parental relationships, the power to block adoption by withholding consent. The gender distinction was not substantially related to the State’s asserted interests in facilitating adoption and identifying appropriate consent requirements.
excerpts: The appellant, Abdiel Caban, challenges the constitutionality of § 111 of the New York Domestic Relations Law (McKinney 1977), under which two of his natural children were adopted by their natural mother and stepfather without his consent. We find the statute to be unconstitutional, as the distinction it invariably makes between the rights of unmarried mothers and the rights of unmarried fathers has not been shown to be substantially related to an important state interest.

In sum, we believe that § 111 is another example of “over-broad generalizations” in gender-based classifications. See Califano v. Goldfarb, 430 U. S. 199, 211 (1977); Stanton v. Stanton, 421 U. S. 7, 14-15.(1975). The effect of New York’s classification is to discriminate against unwed fathers even when their identity is known and they have manifested a significant paternal interest in the child. The facts of this case illustrate the harshness of classifying unwed fathers as being invariably less qualified and entitled than mothers to exercise a concerned judgment as to the fate of their children.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-731-f2d-527.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-731-f2d-527.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process principles to a state custody and parental-rights proceeding. It held that alleged ineffective assistance by appointed counsel and inadequate notice did not establish a due-process violation because Bruner failed to show material prejudice, and the state-court modification also made some claimed prejudice moot.
excerpts: Deborah J. Bruner brought an action under Section 1983 of Title 42 against the Director of the Nebraska Department of Public Welfare. She asserts that she had not been afforded due process in state court proceedings concerning her parental rights. The district court, the Honorable Warren K. Urbom presiding, held that Bruner had not been denied due process of law.

In federal court Bruner alleged that she had been denied effective assistance of counsel because her appointed counsel allegedly failed to interview and call material witnesses, discuss potential defenses with her, adequately apprise her of the consequences of missing hearings, develop a plan for Bruner’s resumption of custody of her son, or to object to evidence presented at the hearings in which custody was determined. Bruner also alleges that she was denied due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings dealing with custody of her son.

The district court also rejected Bruner’s allegations of a denial of due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings. Apparently Bruner missed four of fifteen hearings. The court found that her absences did not significantly affect the state court judge’s decision that Bruner was unable to care for her son’s needs; consequently, Bruner was not prejudiced, regardless of the adequacy of the notice.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-405-f3d-700.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-405-f3d-700.summary: The court held that Iowa’s residency restriction for certain convicted sex offenders did not implicate a fundamental constitutional right involving family choice or family living arrangements. Because the statute did not operate directly on the family relationship, strict scrutiny was unwarranted, and the restriction did not violate substantive or procedural due process.
excerpts: The Does first invoke “the right to personal choice regarding the family.” They cite the Supreme Court’s statement in Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609, 617-18, 104 S.Ct. 3244, 82 L.Ed.2d 462 (1984), that “certain intimate human relationships must be secured against undue intrusion by the State because of the role of such relationships in safeguarding the individual freedom that is central to our constitutional scheme,” and the Court’s discussion of “marital privacy” in Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479, 485-86, 85 S.Ct. 1678, 14 L.Ed.2d 510 (1965).

We do not believe that the residency restriction of § 692A.2A implicates any fundamental right of the Does that would trigger strict scrutiny of the statute. In evaluating this argument, it is important to consider the Supreme Court’s admonition that “ ‘[sjubstantive due process’ analysis must begin with a careful description of the asserted right, for ‘[t]he doctrine of judicial self-restraint requires us to exercise the utmost care whenever we are asked to break new ground in this field.’ ” Flores, 507 U.S. at 302, 113 S.Ct. 1439 (quoting Collins v. Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115, 125, 112 S.Ct. 1061, 117 L.Ed.2d 261 (1992)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-370-f3d-723.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-370-f3d-723.summary: The court applied the substantive-due-process conscience-shocking standard to claims arising from state child-welfare placement decisions. It held that the defendants’ failure to investigate abuse reports and failure to conduct a background check or home study were not sufficiently egregious to violate the plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights.
excerpts: The conduct at issue in this case consists in part of defendants’ failure to respond to two reports of sexual abuse and Allen’s failure to conduct a background check of the Huffmans prior .to the placement of plaintiffs with them. Each defendant received only a single and isolated complaint of possible sexual abuse in the Huffman home. The complaints were made by Shirley, the mother who previously had abandoned plaintiffs and who was attempting to reassert her parental rights. In these circumstances, defendants’ failure to investigate is not so outrageous or egregious as to shock the conscience and thus the failure to investigate did not violate plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights.

Similarly, Allen’s failure to conduct a home study prior to the court-ordered placement did not violate plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights. The juvenile court never ordered DFS to conduct such a study prior to placing the children in the custody of Rhonda and Jean as requested by the family. In light of the prior successful placement of certain plaintiffs with the Huffmans in 1977, the failure to conduct a home study and background check rises at most to the level o
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Substantive Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-539-126.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-539-126.summary: The Court addressed whether prison visitation restrictions impermissibly burdened an asserted constitutional right of familial or intimate association. Without defining the scope of that right in incarceration, it upheld the regulations because they bore a rational relation to legitimate penological interests under Turner v. Safley.
excerpts: We have said that the Constitution protects “certain kinds of highly personal relationships,” Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U. S. 609, 618, 619-620 (1984). And outside the prison context, there is some discussion in our cases of a right to maintain certain familial relationships, including association among members of an immediate family and association between grandchildren and grandparents. See Moore v. East Cleveland, 431 U. S. 494 (1977) (plurality opinion); Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923).

We do not hold, and we do not imply, that any right to intimate association is altogether terminated by incarceration or is always irrelevant to claims made by prisoners. We need not attempt to explore or define the asserted right of association at any length or determine the extent to which it survives incarceration because the challenged regulations bear a rational relation to legitimate penological interests. This suffices to sustain the regulation in question. See Turner v. Safley, 482 U. S. 78, 89 (1987).

us-scotus-483-587.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-483-587.summary: The Court upheld the DEFRA amendment against a Fifth Amendment challenge involving family living arrangements and the parent-child relationship. It held that heightened scrutiny was unwarranted and that the provision satisfied rational-basis review.
excerpts: Appellees argue (and the District Court .ruled), however, that finding that Congress acted rationally is not enough to sustain this legislation. Rather, they claim that some form of “heightened scrutiny” is appropriate because the amendment interferes with a family’s fundamental right to live in the type of family unit it chooses. We conclude that the District Court erred in subjecting the DEFRA amendment to any form of heightened scrutiny.

As in Lyng, the standard of review here is whether “Congress had a rational basis” for its decision. Id., at 639. And as in Lyng, “the justification for the statutory classification is obvious.” Id., at 642. The provisions at issue do not violate the Due Process Clause.
provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause and equal-protection component

us-ca8-820-f2d-923.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-820-f2d-923.citation: Harpole v. Arkansas Department of Human Services, 820 F.2d 923 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-820-f2d-923.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment due-process principles concerning familial association and recognized that parents and children may possess a liberty interest in each other’s companionship. It held, however, that Harpole did not establish a constitutionally protected loss arising from the death of her adult son, particularly where the alleged governmental interference was indirect.
excerpts: Both the Supreme Court and this court have recognized a liberty interest which parents and children have in each other’s companionship. See, e.g., Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983); Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462-63 (8th Cir.1987). Familial relationships have been protected from many forms of governmental intrusion.

The First Circuit, in Ortiz v. Burgos, 807 F.2d 6 (1st Cir.1986), divided constitutionally protected interests in familial relationships into two categories. In the first category are cases protecting the right to make private decisions affecting the family, such as whether to bear children. “The emphasis in these cases on choice suggests that the right is one of preemption; rather than an absolute right to a certain family relationship, family members have the right, when confronted with the state’s attempt to make choices for them, to choose for themselves.” Id. at 8. The second category contains cases dealing with governmental attempts to directly affect the parent-child relationship by means such as determining paternity or terminating parental rights.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-809-f2d-508.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-809-f2d-508.summary: The court held that Congress could condition federal AFDC funding on the family-unit filing regulation under its Spending Clause authority, despite the States’ traditional role in child-support matters. It further held that conflicting state child-support restrictions were preempted where they substantially interfered with the federal scheme, and that the regulation did not directly and substantially infringe protected family choices or violate due process.
excerpts: The spending clause gives Congress the “Power To lay and collect Taxes * * * to * * * provide for the * * * general Welfare of the United States.” U.S. Const, art. I, § 8, cl. 1. In the course of exercising its spending power Congress unquestionably may impose conditions on the receipt of federal funds by the states.

Our review under the supremacy clause takes on a special character because of the involvement of state family law, which will be overridden by conflicting federal law only when Congress has “ ‘positively required’ ” such a result “ ‘by direct enactment,’ ” Hisquierdo v. Hisquierdo, 439 U.S. 572, 581, 99 S.Ct. 802, 808, 59 L.Ed.2d 1 (1979) (quoting Wetmore v. Markoe, 196 U.S. 68, 77, 25 S.Ct. 172, 176, 49 L.Ed. 390 (1904)), and when the state law does “ ‘major damage’ ” to a “ ‘clear and substantial’ ” federal interest.

us-scotus-431-494.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-431-494.citation: Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 431 U.S. 494 (1977)
us-scotus-431-494.summary: The Court held that East Cleveland’s restrictive family-occupancy ordinance violated substantive due process because it intruded into the protected liberty of extended family members to live together. Although preventing overcrowding and related burdens were legitimate objectives, the ordinance bore only a tenuous relationship to those goals.
excerpts: Our decisions establish that the Constitution protects the sanctity of the family precisely because the institution of the family is deeply rooted in this Nation’s history and tradition.

East Cleveland, in contrast, has chosen to regulate the occupancy of its housing by slicing deeply into the family itself. This is no mere incidental result of the ordinance. On its face it selects certain categories of relatives who may live together and declares that others may not. In particular, it makes a crime of a grandmother’s choice to live with her grandson in circumstances like those presented here.

When thus examined, this ordinance cannot survive. The city seeks to justify it as a means of preventing overcrowding, minimizing traffic and parking congestion, and avoiding an undue financial burden on East Cleveland's school system. Although these are legitimate goals, the ordinance before us serves them marginally, at best.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-602-899.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-602-899.citation: Department of State v. Muñoz, 602 U.S. 899 (2024)
us-scotus-602-899.summary: The Court held that a U.S. citizen has no fundamental liberty interest in having a noncitizen spouse admitted to the United States. Although the asserted interest implicated marriage and spousal cohabitation, it was not deeply rooted in the Nation’s history and tradition, given the Government’s longstanding sovereign authority over admission and exclusion.
excerpts: Held: A citizen does not have a fundamental liberty interest in her noncitizen spouse being admitted to the country. Pp. 5–18. (a) Under the doctrine of consular nonreviewability, an executive officer’s decision “to admit or to exclude an alien” “is final and conclusive,” United States ex rel. Knauff v. Shaughnessy, 338 U. S. 537, 547,

Because Muñoz cannot clear the second step of Glucksberg, the Court need not decide whether such a category of implied rights protected by the Due Process Clause exists. Glucksberg requires a demonstration that the asserted right be “deeply rooted in this Nation’s history and tradition.” 521 U. S., at 721. This Nation’s history and tradition recognizes the Government’s sovereign authority to set the terms governing the admission and exclusion of noncitizens, and Muñoz points to no subsidiary tradition that curbs this authority in the case of noncitizen spouses.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-582-563.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-582-563.summary: The Court held that Arkansas could not require the female spouse of a woman who gave birth to be omitted from the child’s birth certificate when the State required a male spouse to be listed in the same circumstances. Under Obergefell, same-sex married couples must receive access to the same rights, benefits, and responsibilities associated with civil marriage, including birth-certificate recognition.
excerpts: As this Court explained in Obergefell v. Hodges, 576 U. S. ___ (2015), the Constitution entitles same-sex couples to civil marriage “on the same terms and conditions as opposite-sex couples.” Id., at ___ (slip op., at 23). In the decision below, the Arkansas Supreme Court considered the effect of that holding on the State’s rules governing the issuance of birth certificates.

The Arkansas Supreme Court’s decision, we conclude, denied married same-sex couples access to the “constellation of benefits that the Stat[e] ha[s] linked to marriage.” Obergefell, 576 U. S., at ___ (slip op., at 17). As already explained, when a married woman in Arkansas conceives a child by means of artificial insemination, the State will—indeed, must—list the name of her male spouse on the child’s birth certificate.

us-ca8-845-f3d-365.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-845-f3d-365.citation: United States v. Hobbs, 845 F.3d 365 (8th Cir. 2016)
us-ca8-845-f3d-365.summary: The court treated marriage as an important constitutional right when evaluating a sweeping supervised-release no-contact condition. Although it did not decide the applicable standard of constitutional review, it held that the condition was an abuse of discretion because it substantially restricted that important right.
excerpts: The sentencing court’s wide discretion notwithstanding, “we are particularly reluctant to uphold sweeping restrictions on important constitutional rights.” Crume, 422 F.3d at 733. Currently, most sweeping restrictions seem to involve the Internet. See, e.g., United States v. West, 829 F.3d 1013,1020-21 (8th Cir. 2016) (ban on creating websites overbroad); Crume, 422 F.3d at 733 (ban on Internet access overbroad). Others involve library access and the parent-child relationship. See, e.g., United States v. Bender, 566 F.3d 748, 753 (8th Cir. 2009) (library access); United States v. Davis, 452 F.3d 991, 995 (8th Cir. 2006) (parent-child relationship). The sweeping restriction in this case involves another important constitutional right— marriage. Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1, 12, 87 S.Ct. 1817, 18 L.Ed.2d 1010 (1967).

us-scotus-576-644.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-576-644.summary: The Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires States to license marriages between two people of the same sex and to recognize same-sex marriages lawfully performed in another State. It applied both substantive due process and equal-protection principles, concluding that the fundamental right to marry extends to same-sex couples.
excerpts: The Court now holds that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry.

The Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to license a marriage between two people of the same sex and to recognize a marriage between two people of the same sex when their marriage was lawfully licensed and performed out of State. Pp. 656–681.

The fundamental liberties protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause extend to certain personal choices central to individual dignity and autonomy, including intimate choices defning personal identity and beliefs. See, e. g., Eisenstadt v. Baird, 405 U. S. 438, 453; Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U. S. 479, 484–486.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 — Due Process Clause
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 — Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-576-86.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-576-86.summary: The Court vacated and remanded in a challenge to the denial of a visa for a citizen’s foreign spouse. The plurality concluded that the denial did not implicate a constitutionally protected liberty interest in marriage because the Government had not prohibited the marriage; the controlling concurrence found that, even assuming such an interest, the process provided was constitutionally sufficient.
excerpts: Unlike the States in Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967), Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U. S. 374 (1978), and Turner v. Safey, 482 U. S. 78 (1987), the Federal Government here has not attempted to forbid a marriage. Although Din and the dissent borrow language from those cases invoking a fundamental right to marriage, they both implicitly concede that no such right has been infringed in this case.

Nothing in the cases Din cites establishes a free-foating and categorical liberty interest in marriage (or any other formulation Din offers) suffcient to trigger constitutional protection whenever a regulation in any way
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-133-f3d-631.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-133-f3d-631.summary: The court applied the fundamental right to marry under the Fourteenth Amendment. It held that the city’s termination of Singleton based on his wife’s conduct did not directly or substantially interfere with, or significantly discourage, the marriage and therefore did not violate substantive due process.
excerpts: Singleton claims that his termination violated his substantive due process right of privacy in his marital relationship. The fundamental right of privacy embodies the “principle that personal decisions that profoundly affect bodily integrity, identity, and destiny should be largely beyond the reach of government.” Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833, 927, 112 S.Ct. 2791, 2846, 120 L.Ed.2d 674 (1992) (Blackmun, J., concurring in part, concurring in the judgment in part, and dissenting in part). The Supreme Court has recognized “that the right to marry is part of the fundamental ‘right of privacy implicit in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process clause.” Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U.S. 374, 384, 98 S.Ct. 673, 680, 54 L.Ed.2d 618 (1977).

This right, however, does not invalidate every state action that has some impact on marriage. See Gorrie v. Bowen, 809 F.2d 508, 522-23 (8th Cir.1987) (“Not every regulation that involves or somehow regulates on the basis of family membership is unconstitutional.”). Rather, the government is free to impose “reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into the marital relationship____” Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 386, 98 S.Ct. at 681. Government action “must interfere ‘directly and substantially5 with family choices before it is unconstitutional,” Gorrie, 809 F.2d at 523 (quoting Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 387, 98 S.Ct. at 681) (citation omitted), but action having only a collateral effect on family decisions typically does not violate that right.

us-scotus-482-78.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-482-78.summary: The Court held that prisoners retain the fundamental constitutional right to marry, although incarceration permits substantial restrictions on its exercise. Applying a deferential reasonable-relationship standard, the Court invalidated Missouri’s requirement that an inmate demonstrate “compelling reasons” before marrying because the restriction was not reasonably related to legitimate penological objectives.
excerpts: In support of the marriage regulation, petitioners first suggest that the rule does not deprive prisoners of a constitutionally protected right. They concede that the decision to marry is a fundamental right under Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U. S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967), but they imply that a different rule should obtain “in ... a prison forum.

We disagree with petitioners that Zablocki does not apply to prison inmates. It is settled that a prison inmate “retains those [constitutional] rights that are not inconsistent with his status as a prisoner or with the legitimate penological objectives of the corrections system.” Pell v. Procunier, supra, at 822. The right to marry, like many other rights, is subject to substantial restrictions as a result of incarceration.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Fundamental right to marry, as recognized in Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U.S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967)

us-scotus-434-374.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-434-374.summary: The Court held that Wisconsin’s requirement that certain parents obtain court permission before marrying violated the Equal Protection Clause because it significantly interfered with the fundamental right to marry. Regulations that do not significantly interfere with entry into marriage may still be valid.
excerpts: the right to marry is of fundamental importance for all individuals

In evaluating §§ 245.10 (1), (4), (5) under the Equal Protection Clause, “we must first determine what burden of justification the classification created thereby must meet, by looking to the nature of the classification and the individual interests affected.” Memorial Hospital v. Maricopa County, 415 U. S. 250, 253 (1974). Since our past decisions make clear that the right to marry is of fundamental importance, and since the classification at issue here significantly interferes with the exercise of that right, we believe that “critical examination” of the state interests advanced in support of the classification is required.

By reaffirming the fundamental character of the right to marry, we do not mean to suggest that every state regulation which relates in any way to the incidents of or prerequisites for marriage must be subjected to rigorous scrutiny. To the contrary, reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into the marital relationship may legitimately be imposed.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-414-632.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-414-632.citation: Cleveland Board of Education v. LaFleur, 414 U.S. 632 (1974)
us-scotus-414-632.summary: The Court held that freedom of personal choice in matters of marriage and family life, including the decision whether to bear or beget a child, is protected by the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. Mandatory maternity-leave rules may not needlessly, arbitrarily, or capriciously burden that constitutional liberty through conclusive presumptions about pregnant teachers’ ability to work.
excerpts: This Court has long recognized that freedom of personal choice in matters of marriage and family life is one of the liberties protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Roe v. Wade, 410 U. S. 113; Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1, 12; Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U. S. 479; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510; Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390. See also Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U. S. 158; Skinner v. Oklahoma, 316 U. S. 535.

By acting to penalize the pregnant teacher for deciding to bear a child, overly restrictive maternity leave regulations can constitute a heavy burden on the exercise of these protected freedoms. Because public school maternity leave rules directly affect “one of the basic civil rights of man,” Skinner v. Oklahoma, supra, at 541, the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires that such rules must not needlessly, arbitrarily, or capriciously impinge upon this vital area of a teacher’s constitutional liberty.

us-scotus-409-434.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-409-434.summary: The Court distinguished Boddie v. Connecticut, holding that indigent access to divorce implicates the fundamental marital relationship and associated constitutional interests. By contrast, access to a bankruptcy discharge does not involve a comparable fundamental interest.
excerpts: The denial of access to the judicial forum in Boddie touched directly, as has been noted, on the marital relationship and on the associational interests that surround the establishment and dissolution of that relationship. On many occasions we have recognized the fundamental importance of these interests under our Constitution.

us-scotus-401-371.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-401-371.summary: The Court held that due process prohibits Connecticut from denying indigent individuals access to divorce proceedings solely because they cannot pay filing fees and service costs. Because marriage is a fundamental relationship and the State monopolizes its legal dissolution, access to the courts is constitutionally required.
excerpts: given the basic position of the marriage relationship in this society’s hierarchy of values and the concomitant state monopolization of the means for legally dissolving this relationship, due process does prohibit a State from denying, solely because of inability to pay, access to its courts to individuals who seek judicial dissolution of their marriages.

We now reverse. Our conclusion is that, given the basic position of the marriage relationship in this society’s hierarchy of values and the concomitant state monopolization of the means for legally dissolving this relationship, due process does prohibit a State from denying, solely because of inability to pay, access to its courts to individuals who seek judicial dissolution of their marriages.

Recognition of this theoretical framework illuminates the precise issue presented in this case. As this Court on more than one occasion has recognized, marriage involves interests of basic importance in our society. See, e. g., Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967); Skinner v. Oklahoma, 316 U. S. 535 (1942); Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923). It is not surprising, then, that the States have seen fit to oversee many aspects of that institution.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-388-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-388-1.summary: The Court held that Virginia’s laws prohibiting and criminalizing interracial marriage violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court treated marriage as a constitutionally protected fundamental freedom that the State could not restrict through racial classifications.
excerpts: The freedom to marry has long been recognized as one of the vital personal rights essential to the orderly pursuit of happiness by free men.

This case presents a constitutional question never addressed by this Court: whether a statutory scheme adopted by the State of Virginia to prevent marriages between persons solely on the basis of racial classifications violates the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. For reasons which seem to us to reflect the central meaning of those constitutional commands, we conclude that these statutes cannot stand consistently with the Fourteenth Amendment.

While the state court is no doubt correct in asserting that marriage is a social relation subject to the State’s police power, Maynard v. Hill, 125 U. S. 190 (1888), the State does not contend in its argument before this Court that its powers to regulate marriage are un--limited notwithstanding the commands of the Fourteenth Amendment. Nor could it do so in light of Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923), and Skinner v. Oklahoma, 316 U. S. 535 (1942).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause and Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-381-479.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-381-479.summary: The Court held that Connecticut’s prohibition on the use of contraceptives, including its application to physicians who advised married couples, violated the constitutionally protected marital right of privacy. The Court grounded that protection in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, informed by the privacy surrounding the marital relationship and home.
excerpts: This law, however, operates directly on an intimate relation of husband and wife and their physician's role in one aspect of that relation.

The Connecticut statutes here involved deal with a particularly important and sensitive area of privacy — that of the marital relation and the marital home. This Court recognized in Meyer v. Nebraska, supra, that the right “to marry, establish a home and bring up children” was an essential part of the liberty guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment. 262 U. S., at 399. In Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, the Court held unconstitutional an Oregon Act which forbade parents from sending their children to private schools because such an act “unreasonably interferes with the liberty of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control.

norms.b_justification: Griswold interpreted the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause and recognized the right to marry and establish a home as an essential liberty. That principle is functionally consistent with the current formulation of marriage as a fundamental right, although the quoted language does not appear in a current statutory text.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-523-420.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-523-420.summary: The Court upheld § 1409’s differing requirements for children born abroad out of wedlock to citizen fathers and citizen mothers. It held that the distinctions, including paternity documentation and timely legitimation requirements, were supported by the important governmental interests in reliable proof of biological relationship and developing ties between the child, the citizen parent, and the United States.
excerpts: The petitioner in this case challenges the constitutionality of the statutory provisions governing the acquisition of citizenship at birth by children born out of wedlock and outside of the United States. The specific challenge is to the distinction drawn by §309 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 66 Stat. 238, as amended, 8 U. S. C. § 1409, between the child of an alien father and a citizen mother, on the one hand, and the child of an alien mother and a citizen father, on the other.

We find no merit in the challenge because the statute does not impose any limitation on the time within which the members of either class of children may prove that they qualify for citizenship. It does establish different qualifications for citizenship for the two classes of children, but we are persuaded that the qualifications for the members of each of those classes, so far as they are implicated by the facts of this case, are well supported by valid governmental interests. We therefore conclude that the statutory distinction is neither arbitrary nor invidious.

There is no doubt that ensuring reliable proof of a biological relationship between the potential citizen and its citizen parent is an important governmental objective. See Trimble v. Gordon, 430 U. S. 762, 770-771 (1977); Fiallo, 430 U. S., at 799, n. 8. Nor can it be denied that the male and female parents are differently situated in this respect. The blood relationship to the birth mother is immediately obvious and is typically established by hospital records and birth certificates; the relationship to the unmarried father may often be undisclosed and unrecorded in any contemporary public record.

us-ca8-68-f3d-208.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-68-f3d-208.summary: The court applied intermediate scrutiny to WELSA’s different treatment of nonmarital children seeking to inherit by representation through their fathers. It held that the paternal inheritance limitation was substantially related to the federal interest in accurately and efficiently resolving heirship claims, because of the distinctive problems of proving paternity.
excerpts: As in Lalli v. Lalli, the peculiar problems of proof of paternity as opposed to maternity justify the different treatment of paternal inheritance by illegitimate children under WELSA. Refusing to expand heirship status to include illegitimate children claiming by right of representation through their fathers is substantially related to the federal government’s important interest in accurately and efficiently settling the claims involving the White Earth Reservation allotments.
provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (equal-protection component)

us-scotus-486-456.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-486-456.summary: The Court applied intermediate scrutiny to Pennsylvania’s statute limiting paternity actions by children born out of wedlock. It held that such a limitation must provide a reasonable opportunity to establish paternity and must be substantially related to the State’s interest in preventing stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: To withstand intermediate scrutiny, a statutory classification must be substantially related to an important governmental objective.

In considering whether state legislation violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, U. S. Const., Arndt. 14, § 1, we apply different levels of scrutiny to different types of classifications. At a minimum, a statutory classification must be rationally related to a legitimate governmental purpose.

To withstand intermediate scrutiny, a statutory classification must be substantially related to an important governmental objective. Consequently we have invalidated classifications that burden illegitimate children for the sake of punishing the illicit relations of their parents, because “visiting this condemnation on the head of an infant is illogical and unjust.
provisions: U.S. Const., amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-476-852.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-476-852.summary: The Court held that Texas could not deny Reed’s inheritance claim under an unconstitutional classification based on nonmarital birth merely because her father died before Trimble and she filed her claim afterward. The State’s interests in orderly estate administration and finality did not justify excluding her while the estate proceedings remained in progress.
excerpts: Although the question presented in this case is framed in terms of “retroactivity,” its answer is governed by a rather clear distinction that has emerged from our cases considering the constitutionality of statutory provisions that impose special burdens on illegitimate children. In these cases, we have unambiguously concluded that a State may not justify discriminatory treatment of illegitimates in order to express its disapproval of their parents’ misconduct.

The state interest in the orderly disposition of decedents’ estates may justify the imposition of special requirements upon an illegitimate child who asserts a right to inherit from her father, and, of course, it justifies the enforcement of generally applicable limitations on the time and the manner in which claims may be asserted. After an estate has been finally distributed, the interest in finality may provide an additional, valid justification for barring the belated assertion of claims, even though they may be meritorious and even though mistakes of law or fact may have occurred during the probate process. We find no such justification for the State’s rejection of appellant’s claim in this case.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-462-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-462-1.summary: The Court held that Tennessee’s two-year limitation period for paternity and child-support actions brought on behalf of certain children born out of wedlock violated the Equal Protection Clause. The classification imposed a disability on nonmarital children that was not sufficiently related to the State’s asserted interests in avoiding stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: This case requires us to decide the constitutionality of a provision of a Tennessee statute that imposes a 2-year limitations period on paternity and child support actions brought on behalf of certain illegitimate children.

In several of these cases, we have held the classifications invalid. See, e. g., Mills v. Habluetzel, supra; Trimble v. Gordon, supra; Jimenez v. Weinberger, supra; New Jersey Welfare Rights Org. v. Cahill, supra; Gomez v. Perez, supra; Weber v. Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., supra; Glona v. American Guarantee & Liability Insurance Co., supra; Levy v. Louisiana, supra. Our consideration of these cases has been animated by a special concern for discrimination against illegitimate children.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-456-91.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-456-91.summary: The Court held that Texas’s one-year limitation for establishing paternity and obtaining child support denied equal protection because it made the opportunity for children born outside marriage effectively illusory. Although the State may impose greater restrictions on such claims because paternity must be proved, those restrictions must be substantially related to a legitimate interest in preventing stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: Our decision in Gomez held that “a State may not invidiously discriminate against illegitimate children by denying them substantial benefits accorded children generally.” 409 U. S., at 538. Specifically, we held that a State which grants an opportunity for legitimate children to obtain paternal support must also grant that opportunity to illegitimate children. If Gomez and the equal protection principles which underlie it are to have any meaning, it is clear that the support opportunity provided by the State to illegitimate children must be more than illusory.

Therefore, in support suits by illegitimate children more than in support suits by legitimate children, the State has an interest in preventing the prosecution of stale or fraudulent claims, and may impose greater restrictions on the former than it imposes on the latter. Such restrictions will survive equal protection scrutiny to the extent they are substantially related to a legitimate state interest. See Lalli v. Lalli, supra, at 265; Trimble v. Gordon, supra, at 767; Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U. S. 495, 510 (1976).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-664-f2d-667.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-664-f2d-667.citation: Gross ex rel. Scott v. Harris, 664 F.2d 667 (8th Cir. 1981)
us-ca8-664-f2d-667.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), which requires determining entitlement to child insurance benefits by referring to the law of the insured’s domicile governing intestate succession. It held that the former Missouri provisions conditioning an illegitimate child’s paternal inheritance—and thus eligibility for benefits—on the father’s marriage to the mother and recognition of the child were unconstitutional under the equal-protection principles applied in Trimble.
excerpts: 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) states: (2)(A) In determining whether an applicant is the child or parent of a fully or currently insured individual for purposes of this subchapter, the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which such insured individual is domiciled at the time such applicant files application, or, if such insured individual is dead, by the courts of the State in which he was domiciled at the time of his death, or, if such insured individual is or was not so domiciled in any State, by the courts of the District of Columbia.

Our inquiry, however, is not ended by a simple comparison of the statutes. In order to resolve this litigation, it remains for us to determine (1) whether the statute is unconstitutional in whole or only in part, and (2) whether the Trimble decision may be applied retrospectively so that the appellants may benefit from that decision. We shall address these issues seriatim.

us-ca8-658-f2d-641.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-658-f2d-641.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s dependency rules, including the provision deeming a child dependent when the child could inherit from the insured parent under applicable state intestacy law. It relied on equal-protection precedent invalidating Arkansas’s discriminatory intestacy rule and concluded that the child’s eligibility could not be defeated by that unconstitutional nonmarital-status classification.
excerpts: In addressing appellant’s contention that her daughter is entitled to child’s insurance benefits, we note initially that under the statute a child is deemed dependent on the deceased wage earner unless the child is illegitimate and is not living with the insured parent or is not receiving support from that parent. 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(3)(A). A child is deemed legitimate and, consequently, dependent if she may inherit personal property from the insured parent under the law of the state where that parent was domiciled at the time of his death. Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U.S. 495, 514-15 n.17, 96 S.Ct. 2755, 2766-67 n.17, 49 L.Ed.2d 651 (1976); 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and the dependency provisions in 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1)(C)(ii) and § 402(d)(3)(A), including the state-law inheritance rule for determining legitimacy and dependency. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively amend those provisions; later changes elsewhere in § 416 are unrelated, so the interpreted rule remains identical in wording and function.

us-scotus-445-23.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-445-23.summary: The Court construed the Civil Service Retirement Act’s “lived with” requirement for children born out of wedlock and affirmed on statutory grounds, avoiding resolution of the constitutional challenge. It nonetheless applied the equal-protection rule that classifications based on nonmarital birth must bear an evident and substantial relation to the interests served by the statute.
excerpts: The Civil Service Retirement Act provides survivors’ annuities to all legitimate children, but grants the same benefits to children born out' of wedlock only if they “lived with the employee ... in a regular parent-child relationship.” Such a classification based on illegitimacy is unconstitutional unless it bears “an evident and substantial relation to the particular .. . interests this statute is designed to serve.” Lalli v. Lalli, 439 U. S. 259, 268 (1978) (plurality opinion); see id., at 279 (Brennan, J., dissenting). See also Trimble v. Gordon, 430 U. S. 762, 767 (1977).

The Court of Claims granted the appellee’s motion for summary judgment. 218 Ct. Cl. 705, 590 F. 2d 343. Ignoring the statutory issue, the court granted relief on the authority of its earlier decision in Gentry v. United States, 212 Ct. Cl. 1, 546 F. 2d 343 (1976), rehearing denied, 212 Ct. Cl. 27, 551 F. 2d 852 (1977), which held that the “lived with” requirement of 5 U. S. C. § 8341 (a) (3) (A) unconstitutionally discriminated against illegitimate children. We postponed consideration of our jurisdiction pending hearing on the merits, 441 U. S. 960 (1979), and now affirm on the statutory ground presented to but not addressed by the Court of Claims.

us-scotus-441-347.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-441-347.summary: The Court upheld Georgia’s restriction allowing an unmarried biological father to sue for the wrongful death of his child only if he had legitimated the child. The classification was not invidious discrimination based on illegitimacy or sex because it furthered legitimate interests in establishing paternity and preventing fraudulent or duplicative claims, and was rationally related to those interests.
excerpts: With these principles in mind, it is clear that the Georgia statute does not invidiously discriminate against the appellant simply because he is of the male sex. The fact is that mothers and fathers of illegitimate children are not similarly situated. Under Georgia law, only a father can by voluntary unilateral action make an illegitimate child legitimate. Unlike the mother of an illegitimate child whose identity will rarely be in doubt, the identity of the father will frequently be unknown. Lalli v. Lalli, 439 U. S. 259.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-439-259.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-439-259.summary: The Court applied heightened equal-protection review to New York’s inheritance classification based on nonmarital birth. It upheld § 4-1.2 because requiring a judicial declaration of paternity during the father’s lifetime was substantially related to the State’s legitimate interests in reliable paternity determinations and orderly estate administration.
excerpts: We concluded that the Illinois statute discriminated against illegitimate children in a manner prohibited by the Equal Protection Clause. Although, as decided in Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U. S. 495, 506 (1976), and reaffirmed in Trimble, supra, at 767, classifications based on illegitimacy are not subject to “strict scrutiny,” they nevertheless are invalid under the Fourteenth Amendment if they are not substantially related to permissible state interests. Upon examination, we found that the Illinois law failed that test.

At the outset we observe that § 4-1.2 is different in important respects from the statutory provision overturned in Trimble. The Illinois statute required, in addition to the father’s acknowledgment of paternity, the legitimation of the child through the intermarriage of the parents as an absolute precondition to inheritance. This combination of requirements eliminated “the possibility of a middle ground between the extremes of complete exclusion and case-by-case determination of paternity.” Trimble, 430 U. S., at 770-771. As illustrated by the facts in Trimble, even a judicial declaration of paternity was insufficient to permit inheritance.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)
N.Y. Estates, Powers, and Trusts Law § 4-1.2

us-scotus-430-787.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-430-787.citation: Fiallo ex rel. Rodriguez v. Bell, 430 U.S. 787 (1977)
us-scotus-430-787.summary: The Court construed the Immigration and Nationality Act’s definitions of “child” and “parent” to exclude the relationship between an illegitimate child and his natural father from the Act’s family-based immigration preferences. It held that this exclusion did not violate the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component, emphasizing Congress’s exceptionally broad power over immigration and the rational concerns about family ties, paternity proof, and fraudulent applications.
excerpts: The Act grants special preference immigration status to aliens who qualify as the “children” or “parents” of United States citizens or lawful permanent residents. Under § 101 (b) (1), a “child” is defined as an unmarried person under 21 years of age who is a legitimate or legitimated child, a stepchild, an adopted child, or an illegitimate child seeking preference by virtue of his relationship with his natural mother. The definition does not extend to an illegitimate child seeking preference by virtue of his relationship with his natural father.

We hold that §§ 101 (b) (1) (D) and 101 (b) (2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 are not unconstitutional by virtue of the exclusion of the relationship between an illegitimate child and his natural father from the preferences accorded by the Act to the “child” or “parent” of a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident.

The inherent difficulty of determining the paternity of an illegitimate child is compounded when it depends upon events that may have occurred in foreign countries many years earlier. Congress may well have given substantial weight, in adopting the classification here challenged, to these problems of proof and the potential for fraudulent visa applications that would have resulted from a more generous drawing of the line.

us-scotus-430-762.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-430-762.summary: The Court held that Illinois Probate Act § 12 violated the Fourteenth Amendment because it allowed intestate inheritance from a father only for legitimate children, while permitting inheritance from both parents for legitimate children. Classifications based on nonmarital birth receive heightened, though less than strict, scrutiny and must substantially further legitimate state objectives; the statute’s discriminatory exclusion was not adequately justified where paternity had already been adjudicated.
excerpts: We noted probable jurisdiction to consider the arguments that § 12 violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by invidiously discriminating on the basis of illegitimacy and sex. 424 U. S. 964 (1976). We now reverse. As we conclude that the statutory discrimination against illegitimate children is unconstitutional, we do not reach the sex discrimination argument.

In this context, the standard just stated is a minimum; the Court sometimes requires more. “Though the latitude given state economic and social regulation is necessarily broad, when state statutory classifications approach sensitive and fundamental personal rights, this Court exercises a stricter scrutiny . . . .” Ibid.

That adjudication should be equally sufficient to establish Deta Mona’s right to claim a child’s share of Gordon’s estate, for the State’s interest in the accurate and efficient disposition of property at death would not be compromised in any way by allowing her claim in these circumstances. The reach of the statute extends well beyond the asserted purposes. See Jimenez v. Weinberger, 417 U. S. 628, 637 (1974).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-427-495.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-427-495.summary: The Court upheld the Social Security Act’s dependency presumptions for survivor benefits against a Fifth Amendment equal-protection challenge based on nonmarital birth. It held that the classifications were constitutionally permissible because they were reasonably related to the likelihood of dependency at the insured parent’s death, and that legitimacy classifications do not receive heightened scrutiny.
excerpts: This case presents the issue of the constitutionality, under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, of those provisions of the Social Security Act that condition the eligibility of certain illegitimate children for a surviving child’s insurance benefits upon a showing that the deceased wage earner was the claimant child’s parent and, at the time of his death, was living with the child or was contributing to his support.

us-scotus-417-628.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-417-628.summary: The Court construed the Social Security Act’s rules for establishing eligibility for child’s insurance benefits and held that conclusively excluding one subclass of nonmarital children, while granting benefits to comparable subclasses without a further dependency showing, violated the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component. The judgment was vacated and remanded to allow the children to establish eligibility as the claimant’s children.
excerpts: The contested Social Security scheme provides, in essence, that legitimate or legitimated children (42 U. S. C. § 402 (d) (3)), illegitimate children who can inherit their parent’s personal property under the intestacy laws of the State of the insured’s domicile (42 U. S. C. § 416 (h) (2) (A)), and those children who cannot inherit only because their parents’ ceremonial marriage was invalid for nonobvious defects (42 U. S. C. § 416 (h) (2) (B)), are entitled to receive benefits without any further showing of parental support. However, illegitimate children such as Eugenio and Alicia who were not living with or being supported by the applicant at the time the claimant’s period of disabilhy began, and who do not fall into one of the foregoing categories, are not entitled to receive any benefits. 42 U. S. C. § 416 (b)(3).

Even if children might rationally be classified on the basis of whether they are dependent upon their disabled parent, the Act’s definition of these two subclasses of illegitimates is “over-inclusive” in that it benefits some children who are legitimated, or entitled to inherit, or illegitimate solely because of a defect in the marriage of their parents, but who are not dependent on their disabled parent. Conversely, the Act is “underinclusive” in that it conclusively excludes some illegitimates in appellants’ subclass who are, in fact, dependent upon their disabled parent. Thus, for all that is shown in this record, the two subclasses of illegitimates stand on equal footing, and the potential for spurious claims is the same as to both; hence to conclusively deny one subclass benefits presumptively available to the other denies the former the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the due process provision of the Fifth Amendment. Schneider v. Rusk, 377 U. S. 163, 168 (1964); Bolling v. Sharpe, 347 U. S. 497, 499 (1954).

us-scotus-411-619.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-411-619.citation: New Jersey Welfare Rights Organization v. Cahill, 411 U.S. 619 (1973)
us-scotus-411-619.summary: The Court held that New Jersey could not deny welfare benefits to children on the basis of nonmarital birth. Applying equal-protection principles, it concluded that benefits indispensable to the health and well-being of illegitimate children could not constitutionally be withheld from them.
excerpts: Thus, in Weber we held that under the Equal Protection Clause a State may not exclude illegitimate children from sharing equally with other children in the recovery of workmen’s compensation benefits for the death of their parent. Similarly, in Levy v. Louisiana, 391 U. S. 68 (1968), we held that a State may not create a right of action in favor of children for the wrongful death of a parent and' exclude illegitimate children from the benefit of such a right.

Those decisions compel the conclusion that appellants’ claim of the denial of equal protection must be sustained, for there can be no doubt that the benefits extended under the challenged program are as indispensable to the health and well-being of illegitimate children as to those who are legitimate. Accordingly, we grant the motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis, reverse the judgment of the District Court, and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-409-535.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-409-535.summary: The Court held that once Texas created a judicially enforceable right to needed support from natural fathers, it could not deny that right to children solely because their fathers were unmarried to their mothers. Such discrimination against nonmarital children lacked a constitutionally sufficient justification under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
excerpts: Under these decisions, a State may not invidiously discriminate against illegitimate children by denying them substantial benefits accorded children generally. We therefore hold that once a State posits a judicially enforceable right on behalf of children to needed support from their natural fathers there is no constitutionally sufficient justification for denying such an essential right to a child simply because its natural father has not married its mother.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-406-164.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-406-164.citation: Weber v. Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., 406 U.S. 164 (1972)
us-scotus-406-164.summary: The Court held that Louisiana violated the Equal Protection Clause by relegating dependent, unacknowledged nonmarital children to an inferior recovery category under its workers’ compensation statute. Because the children were equally dependent on and biologically related to the deceased father, their nonmarital status did not justify denying them equal benefits with legitimate children.
excerpts: The question before us, on writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of Louisiana, concerns the right of dependent unacknowledged, illegitimate children to recover under Louisiana workmen's compensation laws benefits for the death of their natural father on an equal footing with his dependent legitimate children. We hold that Louisiana’s denial of equal recovery rights to dependent unacknowledged illegitimates violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

An unacknowledged illegitimate child may suffer as much from the loss of a parent as a child born within wedlock or an illegitimate later acknowledged. So far as this record shows, the dependency and natural affinity of the unacknowledged illegitimate children for their father were as great as those of the four legitimate children whom Louisiana law has allowed to recover. The legitimate children and the illegitimate children all lived in the home of the deceased and were equally dependent upon him for maintenance and support.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-401-532.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-401-532.summary: The Court upheld Louisiana’s intestate-succession rules denying an acknowledged but nonlegitimated child the automatic right to inherit from her father. It held that the classification did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment because Louisiana had a rational basis in promoting family life and regulating the disposition of property.
excerpts: In this Court appellant argues that Louisiana’s statutory scheme for intestate succession that bars this illegitimate child from sharing in her father’s estate constitutes an invidious discrimination against illegitimate children that cannot stand under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution. Much reliance is placed upon the Court’s decisions in Levy v. Louisiana, 391 U. S. 68 (1968), and Glona v. American Guarantee & Liability Insurance Co., 391 U. S. 73 (1968). For the reasons set out below, we find appellant’s reliance on those cases misplaced, and we decline to extend the rationale of those cases where it does not apply. Accordingly, we affirm the decision below.

Nor is Glona v. American Guarantee & Liability Insurance Co., 391 U. S. 73 (1968), analogous to this case. In Glona the majority relied on Louisiana’s “curious course” of sanctions against illegitimacy to demonstrate that there was no “rational basis” for prohibiting a mother from recovering for the wrongful death of her son. Id., at 74-75. Even if we were to apply the “rational basis” test to the Louisiana intestate succession statute, that statute clearly has a rational basis in view of Louisiana’s interest in promoting family life and of directing the disposition of pro
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses)

us-scotus-391-68.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-391-68.citation: Levy v. Louisiana ex rel. Charity Hospital, 391 U.S. 68 (1968)
us-scotus-391-68.summary: The Court held that Louisiana violated the Equal Protection Clause by denying illegitimate children the right to recover damages for the wrongful death of their mother. Birth out of wedlock was unrelated to the injury, and the children were persons and dependents entitled to equal protection.
excerpts: We start from the premise that illegitimate children are not “nonpersons.” They are humans, live, and have their being. They are clearly “persons” within the meaning of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The rights asserted here involve the intimate, familial relationship between a child and his own mother. When the child’s claim of damage for loss of his mother is in issue, why, in terms of “equal protection,” should the tortfeasors go free merely because the child is illegitimate? Why should the illegitimate child be denied rights merely because of his birth out of wedlock
We conclude that it is invidious to discriminate against them when no action, conduct, or demeanor of theirs is possibly relevant to the harm that was done the mother.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-391-73.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-391-73.citation: Glona v. American Guarantee & Liability Insurance, 391 U.S. 73 (1968)
us-scotus-391-73.summary: The Court held that Louisiana violated the Equal Protection Clause by denying a mother the right to recover for the wrongful death of her illegitimate child solely because of the child’s nonmarital birth. The classification lacked a rational connection to the asserted purpose of discouraging illegitimacy and impermissibly denied relief based on the legal rather than biological relationship.
excerpts: Yet we see no possible rational basis (Morey v. Doud, 354 U. S. 457, 465-466) for assuming that if the natural mother is allowed recovery for the wrongful death of her illegitimate child, the cause of illegitimacy will be served. It would, indeed, be farfetched to assume that women have illegitimate children so that they can be compensated in damages for their death. A law which creates an open season on illegitimates in the area of automobile accidents gives a windfall to tortfeasors.

To say that the test of equal protection should be the “legal” rather than the biological relationship is to avoid the issue. For the Equal Protection Clause necessarily limits the authority of a State to draw such “legal” lines as it chooses.
Where the claimant is plainly the mother, the State denies equal protection of the laws to withhold relief merely because the child, wrongfully killed, was born to her out of wedlock.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-582-47.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-582-47.summary: The Court held that § 1409(a) and (c), which imposed different physical-presence requirements on unmarried U.S.-citizen fathers and mothers transmitting citizenship to children born abroad, violated the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component. Applying heightened scrutiny, the Court found no exceedingly persuasive justification for the gender-based disparity and ordered the longer requirement applied prospectively to both parents unless Congress enacted a new rule.
excerpts: The defender of legislation that differentiates on the basis of gender must show “at least that the [challenged] classifcation serves important governmental objectives and that the discriminatory means employed are substantially related to the achievement of those objectives.” Virginia, 518 U. S., at 533 (quoting Mississippi Univ. for Women v. Hogan, 458 U. S. 718, 724 (1982); alteration in original); see Tuan Anh Nguyen v. INS, 533 U. S. 53, 60, 70 (2001). Moreover, the classifcation must substantially serve an important governmental interest today, for “in interpreting the [e]qual [p]rotection [guarantee], [we have] recognized that new insights and societal understandings can reveal unjustifed inequality . . . that once passed unnoticed and unchallenged.” Obergefell v. Hodges, 576 U. S. 644, 673 (2015). Here, the Government has supplied no “exceedingly persuasive justifcation,” Virginia, 518 U. S., at 531 (internal quotation marks omitted), for § 1409(a) and (c)'s “gender-based” and “genderbiased” disparity, Westcott, 443 U. S., at 84 (internal quotation marks omitted).

The Government must show, at least, that its gender-based “ `classifcation serves “important governmental objectives and that the discriminatory means employed” are “substantially related to [achieving] those objectives.” ' ” Virginia, 518 U. S., at 533. The classifcation must serve an important governmental interest today, for “new insights and societal understandings can reveal unjustifed inequality . . . that once passed unnoticed and unchallenged.” Obergefell v. Hodges, 576 U. S. 644, 673. Pp. 59–64.

In the 1940 Act, Congress discarded the father-controls assumption concerning married parents, but codifed the mother-as-sole-guardian perception regarding unmarried parents. The Roosevelt administration, which proposed § 1409, explained: “[T]he mother [of a nonmarital child] stands in the place of the father . . . [,] has a right to the custody and control of such a child as against the putative

us-scotus-533-53.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-533-53.citation: Tuan Anh Nguyen v. Immigration & Naturalization Service, 533 U.S. 53 (2001)
