us-scotus-533-53.summary: The Court upheld 8 U.S.C. § 1409(a), which imposes additional requirements for citizenship transmission to children born abroad and out of wedlock when the citizen parent is the father. Applying the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component, the Court held that the differing requirements for citizen fathers and mothers are justified by their different evidentiary relationships to biological parenthood at birth.
excerpts: This case presents a question not resolved by a majority of the Court in a case before us three Terms ago. See Miller v. Albright, 523 U. S. 420 (1998). Title 8 U. S. C. § 1409 governs the acquisition of United States citizenship by persons born to one United States citizen parent and one noncitizen parent when the parents are unmarried and the child is born outside of the United States or its possessions. The statute imposes different requirements for the child’s acquisition of citizenship depending upon whether the citizen parent is the mother or the father. The question before us is whether the statutory distinction is consistent with the equal protection guarantee embedded in the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

Fathers and mothers are not similarly situated with regard to the proof of biological parenthood. The imposition of a different set of rules for making that legal determination with respect to fathers and mothers is neither surprising nor troublesome from a constitutional perspective. Cf. Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U. S. 432, 439 (1985) (explaining that the Equal Protection Clause “is essentially a direction that all persons similarly situated should be treated alike”); F S. Royster Guano Co. v. Virginia, 253 U. S. 412, 415 (1920).
provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (equal-protection component)

us-ca8-828-f2d-493.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.citation: Estate of Brandon v. Commissioner, 828 F.2d 493 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.summary: The court held that a settlement qualifies for the estate-tax marital deduction only to the extent it reflects an enforceable surviving-spouse claim under properly interpreted state law. It remanded for an independent determination whether Arkansas’s gender-based dower-election statute was constitutional under the Equal Protection Clause at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr.
excerpts: Specifically, we agree that “under even the most narrow reading of Bosch, either a good faith settlement or a judgment of a lower state court must be based on an enforceable right, under state law properly interpreted, in order to qualify as ‘passing’ pursuant to the estate tax marital deduction.” Ahmanson, supra, 674 F.2d at 775.

Bosch and Ahmanson support the conclusion that the Tax Court was required, in this instance, to make an independent determination as to the enforceability of Chanoy Brandon’s dower claims against the estate under state law at the time the settlement was reached. Specifically, the Tax Court was required to consider the constitutionality of the Arkansas dower statute at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr. Having carefully reviewed the Tax Court’s opinion, we find that the Tax Court failed to do so.

The Tax Court’s reliance upon Estate of Barrett v. Commissioner, supra, holding that the test for determining the enforceability of the surviving spouse’s claims against the estate is whether or not the settlement agreement was made as the result of good faith, arm’s-length negotiations, was improper, because that case appears to have been overruled sub silentio by Bosch. We therefore remand for a determination of the constitutionality of ARK.STAT.ANN. § 60-501 at the time the settlement was reached.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), particularly whether an enforceable state-law interest “passes” to the surviving spouse for purposes of the marital deduction. The later amendments listed affect other subsections and do not alter § 2056(a) or its relevant function; the Equal Protection issue likewise does not change that statutory language.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-465-728.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-465-728.summary: The Court held that the pension-offset exception in the Social Security Act revived an unconstitutional sex-based distinction by incorporating the pre-1977 rule that required husbands and widowers, but not wives and widows, to show dependency. The Court treated the right to benefits distributed without unjustified sex classifications as sufficient injury for standing and held that equal treatment could be achieved by withdrawing the favorable treatment rather than extending it.
excerpts: Califano v. Goldfarb, 430 U. S. 199 (1977), held that a gender-based classification in the spousal-benefit provisions of the Social Security Act violated the right to the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. In this case, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama held that amendments to the Act, adopted in 1977 partly in response to our decision, unjustifiably revive the gender-based classification that was invalidated in Goldfarb and therefore also violate the Fifth Amendment.

There can be no dispute that in January 1977 men were eligible for benefits only upon a showing of dependency whereas women were subject to no such requirement. See former 42 U. S. C. §§ 402(c) and (f); Califano v. Goldfarb, supra, at 201-202, and nn. 1, 2. And Congress further indicated its intent to revive those eligibility criteria by including an unusual severability clause that would, in the event the classification were held invalid, sacrifice the exception’s protection of reliance interests to the goal served by the offset provision itself — preventing an undue financial burden on the system.
provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (equal-protection component)

us-scotus-450-455.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-450-455.summary: The Court held that Louisiana’s former “head and master” statute, which gave husbands exclusive control over jointly owned community property, violated the Equal Protection Clause because it expressly discriminated on the basis of sex. The party defending the classification bore the burden of providing an exceedingly persuasive justification showing that it substantially furthered an important governmental interest.
excerpts: By granting the husband exclusive control over the disposition of community property, Art. 2404 clearly embodies the type of express gender-based discrimination that we have found unconstitutional absent a showing that the classification is tailored to further an important governmental interest.

Instead the burden remains on the party seeking to uphold a statute that expressly discriminates on the basis of sex to advance an “exceedingly persuasive justification” for the challenged classification. Personnel Administrator of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U. S. 256, 273 (1979).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-630-f2d-636.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-630-f2d-636.summary: The court applied intermediate scrutiny to Iowa’s gender-based statutory-rape classification under the Equal Protection Clause. It held that the State had not shown that limiting liability to male defendants and female victims was substantially related to important objectives such as preventing pregnancy or emotional harm.
excerpts: Gender-based classifications are subject to scrutiny under the equal protection clause, Reed v. Reed, 404 U.S. 71, 75, 92 S.Ct. 251, 253, 30 L.Ed.2d 225 (1971), including those classifications which discriminate against men. Orr v. Orr, 440 U.S. 268, 279, 99 S.Ct. 1102, 1111, 59 L.Ed.2d 306 (1979).

The state contends that the statutory rape provisions of § 698.1 had, in essence, two objectives; protecting certain young, unmarried females from unwanted pregnancies and from the possibly traumatic emotional effects of sexual intercourse with an older man who may wield undue influence oyer her. Although the state has provided no actual evidence of the statute’s purpose, it seems apparent from the face of the statute that those were the objectives intended.

In this case, the general doubts expressed by the First Circuit regarding a pregnancy rationale are reinforced by the peculiar structure of the Iowa statute. That statute superimposes strict age limitations upon its gender distinction, thereby excluding from punishment the class of males most likely to have intercou
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-446-142.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-446-142.citation: Wengler v. Druggists Mutual Insurance, 446 U.S. 142 (1980)
us-scotus-446-142.summary: The Court held that Missouri’s workers’ compensation survivor-benefit scheme violated the Fourteenth Amendment because it presumed dependency for widows but required widowers to prove incapacity or dependency. The gender-based distinction was not substantially related to an important governmental objective.
excerpts: The Missouri law, as the Missouri courts recognized, also discriminates against men who survive their employed wives’ dying in work-related accidents. To receive benefits, the surviving male spouse must prove his incapacity or dependency. The widow of a deceased wage earner, in contrast, is presumed dependent and is guaranteed a weekly benefit for life or until remarriage.

However the discrimination is described in this case, our precedents require that gender-based discriminations must serve important governmental objectives and that the discriminatory means employed must be substantially related to the achievement of those objectives. Califano v. Westcott, 443 U. S. 76, 85 (1979); Orr v. Orr, 440 U. S. 268, 279 (1979); Califano v. Webster, 430 U. S. 313, 316-317 (1977); Craig v. Boren, 429 U. S. 190, 197 (1976).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-443-76.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-443-76.summary: The Court held that § 407 of the AFDC-UF program unlawfully discriminated on the basis of sex by denying subsistence benefits to families because the unemployed parent was the mother rather than the father. The gender classification was not substantially related to an important governmental objective and rested on impermissible sex-role stereotypes, violating the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component.
excerpts: For mothers who are the primary providers for their families, and who are unemployed, § 407 is obviously gender biased, for it deprives them and their families of benefits solely on the basis of their sex. The Secretary’s argument, at bottom, turns on the fact that the impact of the gender qualification is felt by family units rather than individuals. But this Court has not hesitated to strike down gender classifications that result in benefits being granted or denied to family units on the basis of the sex of the qualifying parent.

We conclude that the gender classification of § 407 is not substantially related to the attainment of any important and valid statutory goals. It is, rather, part of the “baggage of sexual stereotypes,” Orr v. Orr, 440 U. S., at 283, that presumes the father has the “primary responsibility to provide a home and its essentials,” Stanton v. Stanton, 421 U. S. 7, 10 (1975), while the mother is the “ 'center of home and family life/ ” Taylor v. Louisiana, 419 U. S. 522, 534 n. 15 (1975). Legislation that rests on such presumptions, without more, cannot survive scrutiny under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

us-scotus-440-268.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-440-268.summary: The Court held that Alabama’s alimony statutes, which authorized courts to require husbands but not wives to pay alimony, violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. Sex was not an adequate proxy for need or a valid means of compensating women for marital discrimination where individualized financial hearings were available.
excerpts: The question presented is the constitutionality of Alabama alimony statutes which provide that husbands, but not wives, may be required to pay alimony upon divorce. On February 26, 1974, a final decree of divorce was entered, dissolving the marriage of William and Lillian Orr. That decree directed appellant, Mr. Orr, to pay appellee, Mrs. Orr, $1,240 per month in alimony.

But in this case, even if sex were a reliable proxy for need, and even if the institution of marriage did discriminate against women, these factors still would “not adequately justify the salient features of” Alabama’s statutory scheme, Craig v. Boren, supra, at 202-203. Under the statute, individualized hearings at which the parties’ relative financial circumstances are considered ialready occur. See Russell v. Russell, 247 Ala. 284, 286, 24 So. 2d 124, 126 (1945); Ortman v. Ortman, 203 Ala. 167, 82 So. 417 (1919).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-430-313.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-430-313.summary: The Court upheld the Social Security formula that allowed female wage earners to exclude more low-earning years when calculating old-age benefits. It held that the sex-based distinction satisfied intermediate scrutiny because it directly compensated women for the effects of longstanding employment discrimination, and Congress could make the revised formula prospective only.
excerpts: To withstand scrutiny under the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, “classifications by gender must serve important governmental objectives and must be substantially related to achievement of those objectives.” Craig v. Boren, 429 U. S. 190, 197 (1976). Reduction of the disparity in economic condition between men and women caused by the long history of discrimination against women has been recognized as such an important governmental objective.

The challenged statute operated directly to compensate women for past economic discrimination. Retirement benefits under the Act are based on past earnings. But as we have recognized: “Whether from overt discrimination or from the socialization process of a male-dominated culture, the job market is inhospitable to the woman seeking any but the lowest paid jobs.” Kahn v. Shevin, 416 U. S., at 353. See generally id., at 353-354, and nn. 4-6. Thus, allowing women, who as such have been unfairly hindered from earning as much as men, to eliminate additional low-earning years from the calculation of their retirement benefits works directly to remedy some part of the effect of past discrimination.

norms.b_justification: Califano v. Webster interpreted the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component as applied to gender classifications in 42 U.S.C. § 415(b)(3) and § 416(a), applying the important-objective/substantial-relation standard. Its remedial treatment of sex-based economic discrimination is consistent in wording and function with the current formulation of the judge-made equal-protection rule, even though no current statutory text is provided verbatim.

provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (equal-protection component)

us-scotus-430-199.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-430-199.summary: The Court held that requiring widowers, but not widows, to prove dependency to obtain Social Security survivor benefits violated the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component. The gender distinction impermissibly reduced the family protection produced by female workers’ employment and rested on archaic assumptions about dependency rather than a sufficient governmental justification.
excerpts: The gender-based distinction drawn by § 402 (f)(1)(D)—burdening a widower but not a widow with the task of proving dependency upon the deceased spouse—presents an equal protection question indistinguishable from that decided in Weinberger v. Wiesenfeld, supra. That decision and the decision in Frontiero v. Richardson, 411 U. S. 677 (1973), plainly require affirmance of the judgment of the District Court.

Precisely the same reasoning condemns the gender-based distinction made by § 402 (f)(1)(D) in this case. For that distinction, too, operates “to deprive women of protection for their families which men receive as a result of their employment” : social security taxes were deducted from Hannah Goldfarb’s salary during the quarter century she worked as a secretary, yet, in consequence of § 402 (f)(1)(D), she also “not only failed to receive for her [spouse] the same protection which a similarly situated male worker would have received [for his spouse] but she also was deprived of a portion of her own earnings in order to contribute to the fund out of which benefits would be paid to others.

norms.b_justification: Califano v. Goldfarb interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 402(f)(1)(D) and applied the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection principle to invalidate a sex-based dependency requirement disadvantaging widowers. Its rule is consistent in wording and function with the current formulation concerning sex classifications in family-related benefits, support, and protection.

us-scotus-429-501.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-429-501.summary: The Court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause to Utah’s child-support age-of-majority statute, which imposed a support obligation until age 21 for males but only age 18 for females. It held that Utah’s post-remand treatment failed to comply with the Court’s prior mandate addressing that unconstitutional sex distinction.
excerpts: This appeal brings before us for the second time the Utah Supreme Court’s construction of Utah Code Ann. § 15-2-1 (1973), which established 21 as the age of majority for males, and 18 as the age for females, as applied to a parent’s obligation to support his children. In our first opinion, we held that this distinction between males and females violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution.

On the remand, the Utah Supreme Court did not consider the issue presented to it and held, instead, that the age-of-majority statute was constitutional as applied to females without considering the discrimination. That action does not comply with our mandate.

norms.b_justification: Stanton interpreted Utah Code Ann. § 15-2-1 (1973) and held that its sex-based ages of majority, as applied to parental support obligations, violated the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause. That holding is consistent in function with the current judge-made rule concerning unconstitutional sex-based classifications in family-support matters, even though no current statutory text is supplied.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-421-7.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-421-7.summary: The Court held that Utah’s sex-based statute establishing majority at age 18 for females and age 21 for males violated the Equal Protection Clause when applied to a parent’s child-support obligation. Relying on Reed v. Reed, the Court rejected generalized assumptions about the different maturity, education, and family responsibilities of boys and girls as an adequate justification.
excerpts: This case presents the issue whether a state statute specifying for males a greater age of majority than it specifies for females denies, in the context of a parent’s obligation for support payments for his children, the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by § 1 of the Fourteenth Amendment.

We turn to the merits. The appellant argues that Utah’s statutory prescription establishing different ages of majority for males and females denies equal protection; that it is a classification based solely on sex and affects a child’s “fundamental right” to be fed, clothed, and sheltered by its parents; that no compelling state interest supports the classification; and that the statute can withstand no judicial scrutiny, “close” or otherwise, for it has no relationship to any ascertainable legislative objective.

Reed, we feel, is controlling here. That case presented an equal protection challenge to a provision of the Idaho probate code which gave preference to males over females when persons otherwise of the same entitlement applied for appointment as administrator of a decedent’s estate. No regard was paid under the statute to the applicants’ respective individual qualifications.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-466-429.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-466-429.summary: The Court held that a state custody decision may not remove a child from a fit natural mother based on the racial composition of her household or anticipated private racial prejudice. Although the State has a substantial interest in the child’s best interests, race-based custody classifications require compelling justification and cannot give effect to private biases.
excerpts: The Constitution cannot control such prejudices but neither can it tolerate them. Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

A core purpose of the Fourteenth Amendment was to do away with all governmentally imposed discrimination based on race. See Strauder v. West Virginia, 100 U. S. 303, 307-308, 310 (1880). Classifying persons according to their race is more likely to reflect racial prejudice than legitimate public concerns; the race, not the person, dictates the category. See Personnel Administrator of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U. S. 256, 272 (1979). Such classifications are subject to the most exacting scrutiny; to pass constitutional muster, they must be justified by a compelling governmental interest and must be “necessary ... to the accomplishment” of their legitimate purpose, McLaughlin v. Florida, 379 U. S. 184, 196 (1964). See Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1, 11 (1967).

The question, however, is whether the reality of private biases and the possible injury they might inflict are permissible considerations for removal of an infant child from the custody of its natural mother. We have little difficulty concluding that they are not. The Constitution cannot control such prejudices but neither can it tolerate them. Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-812-f2d-1079.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-812-f2d-1079.citation: Williams v. St. Louis County, 812 F.2d 1079 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-812-f2d-1079.summary: The court held that when an indigent plaintiff presents a non-frivolous state-law claim, denying in forma pauperis status or comparable fee relief without apparent justification makes an otherwise adequate state postdeprivation remedy inadequate. The court relied on this access-to-courts principle to vacate dismissal of the plaintiff’s § 1983 action.
excerpts: To refuse to waive filing fees and grant in forma pauperis status in these circumstances raises concerns of a constitutional magnitude even outside the context of an assessment of the adequacy of state remedies under Parratt. See Boddie v. Connecticut, 401 U.S. 371, 91 S.Ct. 780, 28 L.Ed.2d 113 (1971); United States v. Kras, 409 U.S. 434, 93 S.Ct. 631, 34 L.Ed.2d 626 (1973). We need not address those concerns here, however; instead, we hold only that where an indigent plaintiff presents a non-frivolous state-law claim, the denial of in forma pauperis status or similar relief for no apparent reason renders an otherwise-adequate postdeprivation remedy inadequate under Parratt.

us-scotus-419-393.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-419-393.summary: The Court held that Iowa’s one-year durational-residency requirement for initiating a divorce or dissolution proceeding did not violate the Constitution. The requirement was sufficiently related to Iowa’s interests in ensuring a genuine connection to the State, avoiding becoming a divorce mill, and securing interstate recognition of its divorce decrees under the Full Faith and Credit Clause.
excerpts: State statutes imposing durational residency requirements were, of course, invalidated when imposed by States as a qualification for welfare payments, Shapiro, supra; for voting, Dunn, supra; and for medical care, Maricopa County, supra. But none of those cases intimated that the States might never impose durational residency requirements, and such a proposition was in fact expressly disclaimed.

Such a requirement additionally furthers the State’s parallel interests both in avoiding officious intermeddling in matters in which another State has a paramount interest, and in minimizing the susceptibility of its own divorce decrees to collateral attack. A State such as Iowa may quite reasonably decide that it does not wish to become a divorce mill for unhappy spouses who have lived there as short a time as appellant had when she commenced her action in the state court after having long resided elsewhere.

For that purpose, this Court has often stated that “judicial power to grant a divorce — jurisdiction, strictly speaking — is founded on domicil.” Williams, supra; Andrews v. Andrews, 188 U. S. 14 (1903); Bell v. Bell, 181 U. S. 175 (1901). Where a divorce decree is entered after a finding of domicile in ex parte proceedings, this Court has held that the finding of domicile is not binding upon another State and may be disregarded in the face of “cogent evidence” to the contrary.

us-scotus-410-656.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-410-656.summary: The Court held that Oregon’s filing-fee requirement did not unconstitutionally deny indigent litigants access to judicial relief. Applying United States v. Kras rather than Boddie v. Connecticut, the Court treated the fee as permissible under the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: We emphasized the special nature of the marital relationship and its concomitant associational interests, and noted that they were not affected in that case and that the objective sought by appellant Kras could be obtained through alternative means that did not require a fee. Boddie, of course, was not concerned with post-hearing review. We now conclude that Kras, rather than Boddie, governs the present appeal

us-scotus-406-337.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-406-337.summary: The Court applied Boddie v. Connecticut’s due-process access principle to an annulment proceeding involving paternity and child custody. An indigent litigant could not be denied meaningful access to appellate review because of inability to pay the required appeal costs or bond.
excerpts: T]he crucial foundation on which Boddie rests also forbids denial of an indigent’s right of appeal in civil cases merely because he is too poor to pay appeal costs. Once the right to unhampered access to the judicial process has been established, that right is diluted unless the indigent litigant has an opportunity to assert and obtain review of the errors committed at trial.” Meltzer v. LeCraw & Co., 402 U. S. 954, 955-956, 958 (opinion of Black, J.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-495-604.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-495-604.summary: The Court held that California’s exercise of personal jurisdiction over a nonresident personally served while physically present in California was consistent with the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, even though the suit was unrelated to his activities in the State. Traditional transient-presence jurisdiction remains constitutionally permissible when process is properly served.
excerpts: Among the most firmly established principles of personal jurisdiction in American tradition is that the courts of a State have jurisdiction over nonresidents who are physically present in the State. The view developed early that each State had the power to hale before its courts any individual who could be found within its borders, and that once having acquired jurisdiction over such a person by properly serving him with process, the State could retain jurisdiction to enter judgment against him, no matter how fleeting his visit.

To determine whether the assertion of personal jurisdiction is consistent with due process, we have long relied on the principles traditionally followed by American courts in marking out the territorial limits of each State’s authority. That criterion was first announced in Pennoyer v. Neff, supra, in which we stated that due process “mean[s] a course of legal proceedings according to those rules and principles which have been established in our systems of jurisprudence for the protection and enforcement of private rights,” id., at 733, including the “well-established principles of public law respecting the jurisdiction of an independent State over persons and property,” id., at 722.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-874-f2d-510.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-874-f2d-510.citation: DeMent ex rel. DeMent v. Oglala Sioux Tribal Court, 874 F.2d 510 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-874-f2d-510.summary: The court applied the PKPA and held, following Thompson v. Thompson, that 28 U.S.C. § 1738A does not create an implied federal cause of action to resolve conflicting custody decisions; the claim should be raised in the subsequent custody proceeding. The court also held that exercising personal jurisdiction over a nonmember, nonresident parent in a tribal custody proceeding may violate due process under the Indian Civil Rights Act, analogizing to Kulko.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has held that, in an action for child support, exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident nondomiciliary parent of a minor child domiciled within a state may violate the due process under the federal Constitution. Kulko v. California Superior Court, 436 U.S. 84, 101, 98 S.Ct. 1690, 1701, 56 L.Ed.2d 132 (1978) (the Supreme Court refused to enforce a California child support decree because the father’s contacts with the state were too attenuated to satisfy traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice).

Similarly, we believe that a tribal court exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonmember nonresident parent of a minor child domiciled within the Indian reservation may violate due process under section 1302(8) of the ICRA. We believe that DeMent may have a valid due process claim under the ICRA.

norms.b_justification: The decision construed 28 U.S.C. § 1738A, including subsection (f), concerning a State court’s authority to modify a custody determination made by a court of another State. Subsection (f) was not amended after the 1989 decision, and the later amendments affected other provisions without changing the interpreted language or its function.

us-scotus-436-84.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-436-84.summary: The Court held that California could not exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident, nondomiciliary parent in a child-support action based on his consent to his children’s relocation to California. Applying the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts standard, the Court concluded that the father’s limited California contacts and conduct did not make it fair, just, or reasonable to require him to defend the support action there.
excerpts: A father who agrees, in the interests of family harmony and his children’s preferences, to allow them to spend more time in California than was required under a separation agreement can hardly be said to have “purposefully availed himself” of the “benefits and protections” of California’s laws.

The issue before us is whether, in this action for child support, the California state courts may exercise in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident, nondomiciliary parent of minor children domiciled within the State. For reasons set forth below, we hold that the exercise of such jurisdiction would violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Like any standard that requires a determination of “reasonableness,” the “minimum contacts” test of International Shoe is not susceptible of mechanical application; rather, the facts of each case must be weighed to determine whether the requisite “affiliating circumstances” are present. Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U. S. 235, 246 (1958).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-scotus-354-416.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-354-416.summary: The Court held that an ex parte Nevada divorce decree could dissolve the marriage but could not extinguish the wife’s support rights under New York law because Nevada lacked personal jurisdiction over her. The Full Faith and Credit Clause therefore did not require New York to recognize the decree insofar as it purported to terminate that support obligation.
excerpts: Since the wife was not subject to its jurisdiction, the Nevada divorce court had no power to extinguish any right which she had under the law of New York to financial support from her husband.

Since the wife was not subject to its jurisdiction, the Nevada divorce court had no power to extinguish any right which she had under the law of New York to financial support from her husband. It has long been the constitutional rule that a court cannot adjudicate a personal claim or obligation unless it has jurisdiction over the person of the defendant.

Art. IV, § 1. “Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State. And the Congress may by general Laws prescribe the Manner in which such Acts, Records and Proceedings shall be proved, and the Effect thereof.” Congress has provided that judgments shall have the same force and effect in every court throughout the United States that they have in the State where they were rendered. 28 U. S. C. § 1738.

norms.b_justification: Vanderbilt interpreted U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 and 28 U.S.C. § 1738, holding that a state court cannot adjudicate a personal claim against a nonresident absent personal jurisdiction. That jurisdictional principle is functionally consistent with the current family-law personal-jurisdiction rule reflected in Kulko, despite the absence of verbatim current text.

us-scotus-345-528.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-345-528.summary: The Court held that Ohio was not required to give full faith and credit to the Wisconsin custody award because Wisconsin lacked personal jurisdiction over the mother, who was neither domiciled, resident, nor present there and did not appear. Although the ex parte divorce could be recognized as dissolving the marriage, the custody component could not bind the nonresident mother.
excerpts: The question presented is whether, in a habeas corpus proceeding attacking the right of a mother to retain possession of her minor children, an Ohio court must give full faith and credit to a Wisconsin decree awarding custody of the children to their father when that decree is obtained by the father in an ex parte divorce action in a Wisconsin court which had no personal jurisdiction over the mother. For the reasons hereafter stated, our answer is no.

Separated as our issue is from that of the future interests of the children, we have before us the elemental question whether a court of a state, where a mother is neither domiciled, resident nor present, may cut off her immediate right to the care, custody, management and companionship of her minor children without having jurisdiction over her in personam. Rights far more precious to appellant than property rights will be cut off if she is to be bound by the Wisconsin award of custody.

I]t is now too well settled to be open to further dispute that the 'full faith and credit’ clause and the act of Congress passed pursuant to it do not entitle a judgment in personam to extra-territorial effect if it be made to appear that it was rendered without jurisdiction over the person sought to be bound.” Baker v. Baker, Eccles & Co., 242 U. S. 394, 401, and see 403; Thompson v. Whitman, 18 Wall. 457; D’Arcy v. Ketchum, 11 How. 165.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-381-81.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-381-81.citation: Simons v. Miami Beach First National Bank, 381 U.S. 81 (1965)
us-scotus-381-81.summary: The Court held that Florida’s refusal to recognize the petitioner’s claimed dower interest did not violate the Full Faith and Credit Clause. The New York separation decree created only support obligations, and Florida law treated inchoate dower rights as extinguished by the ex parte divorce decree.
excerpts: It follows that insofar as petitioner’s argument rests on rights created by the New York decree or by New York law, the denial of her dower by the Florida courts was not a violation of the Full Faith and Credit Clause. Cf. Armstrong v. Armstrong, 350 U. S. 568.

Insofar as petitioner argues that since she was not subject to the jurisdiction of the Florida divorce court its decree could not extinguish any dower right existing under Florida law, Vanderbilt v. Vanderbilt, 354 U. S. 416, 418, the answer is that under Florida law no dower right survived the decree. The Supreme Court of Florida has said that dower rights in Florida property, being inchoate, are extinguished by a divorce decree predicated upon substituted or constructive service. Pawley v. Pawley, 46 So. 2d 464.

us-scotus-350-568.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-350-568.summary: The Court held that Ohio did not deny full faith and credit to the Florida divorce decree because the Florida court had not adjudicated the wife’s right to alimony. The Court therefore avoided deciding the constitutional question concerning the effect of an ex parte divorce decree on alimony rights.
excerpts: The sole question presented by the petition for certio-rari was whether the Ohio courts were required to give full faith and credit to the ex parte Florida divorce decree, which petitioner alleges not only granted him a divorce but also decreed that the wife was not entitled to alimony. As we interpret the Florida decree, however, the Florida court did not purport to adjudicate the absent wife's right to alimony. The Ohio courts, therefore, in awarding alimony to the wife, did not in fact fail to give full faith and credit to the Florida decree. Accordingly, we do not reach the constitutional question sought to be presented.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-342-402.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-342-402.summary: The Court held that Illinois had to give sister-state judicial proceedings the effect required by the Full Faith and Credit Clause, including avoiding relitigation of adjudicated issues concerning the parties’ marriages and divorce. The clause did not displace Illinois law governing the consequence of those established facts for the alimony obligation.
excerpts: As the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires Illinois to recognize the validity of records and judicial proceedings of sister states, the conclusion will not vary because the post-divorce recorded events underlying this litigation took place in other states than Illinois. This is not an alleged conflict of decisions between states such as existed in certain tax and estate cases. Rather the situation -more nearly approaches Barber v. Barber, 323 U. S. 77. There Tennessee refused full faith and credit to a North Carolina judgment for arrears of alimony on the ground of its lack of finality in North Carolina.

Illinois’ conclusion as to this claim for alimony must be reached under Illinois law on the basis of giving the various proceedings the effect to which the Constitution entitles them. In this way the Full Faith and Credit Clause performs its intended function of avoiding relitigation in other states of adjudicated issues, while leaving to the law of the forum state the application of the predetermined facts to the new problem. Riley v. New York Trust Co., 315 U. S. 343, 348-349.

us-scotus-342-126.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-342-126.summary: The Court held that a sister-state divorce decree is presumptively entitled to full faith and credit, and the party attacking it bears a heavy burden of showing that the issuing court lacked jurisdiction. An ex parte divorce obtained without the petitioner’s domicile in the issuing State and without the other spouse’s appearance, service, or submission is a nullity and need not be recognized.
excerpts: But the burden of undermining the decree of a sister state “rests heavily upon the assailant.” Williams v. North Carolina, supra, p. 234; Esenwein v. Commonwealth, 325 U. S. 279, 280-281. A judgment presumes jurisdiction over the subject matter and over the persons. See Titus v. Wallick, 306 U. S. 282, 287. As stated for the Court by Justice Stone in Adam v. Saenger, 303 U. S. 59, 62, “If it appears on its face to be a record of a'court of general jurisdiction, such jurisdiction over the cause and the parties is to be presumed unless disproved by extrinsic evidence, or by the record itself.

If Mrs. Mann did not have a Florida domicile and her husband did not submit, under the Sherrer doctrine, 334 U. S. 343, to the State’s jurisdiction, Florida had no power to terminate the marriage. If there was no jurisdiction to grant a divorce, there was no divorce. The sham divorce was a nullity, no more binding on the Vermont courts than would have been a private letter to the lady by the local Florida judge. And while Vermont could, if that State chose, deny relief to Cook,because of his “unclean hands,” the Constitution of the United States has nothing to do with that defense.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-340-581.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-340-581.summary: The Court held that Florida’s divorce decree was entitled to full faith and credit in New York. Because Florida would not permit the daughter, as a stranger to the divorce action, to collaterally attack the decree for lack of jurisdiction, New York could not permit that attack either.
excerpts: It is clear from the foregoing that, under our decisions, a state by virtue of the clause must give full faith and credit to an out-of-state divorce by barring either party to that divorce who has been personally served or who has entered a personal appearance from collaterally attacking the decree. Such an attack is barred where the party attacking would not be permitted to make a collateral attack in the courts of the granting state.

We conclude that Florida would not permit Mrs. Muel-berger to attack the Florida decree of divorce between her father and his second wife as beyond the jurisdiction of the rendering court. In that case New York cannot permit such an attack by reason of the Full Faith and Credit Clause. When a divorce cannot be attacked for lack of jurisdiction by parties actually before the court or strangers in the rendering state, it cannot be attacked by them anywhere in the Union. The Full Faith and Credit Clause forbids.

us-scotus-336-674.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-336-674.summary: The Court held that Connecticut gave proper respect to the Nevada divorce decree while permitting Connecticut to independently determine whether the decedent was domiciled in Nevada when the decree was entered. Because the nonparticipating spouse had not been personally served, she was not barred from challenging Nevada’s jurisdictional domicile finding in a later property and widowhood proceeding.
excerpts: Upon full consideration of the record, the opinion of the Supreme Court of Errors, and the argument of counsel, we have concluded that the Connecticut courts gave proper weight to the claims of power by the Nevada court, that the burden of proving that the decedent had not acquired a domicile in Nevada was placed upon respondent, that this issue of fact was fairly tried according to appropriate procedure, and that the findings of the Connecticut courts are amply supported in evidence.

Sherrer v. Sherrer, 334 U. S. 343, and Coe v. Coe, 334 U. S. 378, decided by this Court last term, are not in point. No personal service was made upon respondent, nor did she in any way participate in the Nevada proceedings. She was not, therefore, precluded in the present action from challenging the finding of the Nevada court that Herbert N. Rice was, at the time of the divorce, domiciled in that state.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-334-343.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-334-343.summary: The Court held that full faith and credit barred Massachusetts from collaterally attacking Florida’s divorce decree on the ground that the petitioner lacked Florida domicile. Because the husband appeared, contested domicile, had a full opportunity to litigate and appeal, and the decree was valid under Florida law, Massachusetts had to recognize it.
excerpts: Those cases stand for the proposition that the requirements of full faith and credit bar a defendant from collaterally attacking a divorce decree on jurisdictional grounds in the courts of a sister State where there has been participation by the defendant in the divorce proceedings, where the defendant has been accorded full opportunity to contest the jurisdictional issues, and where the decree is not susceptible to such collateral attack in the courts of the State which rendered the decree.

But the recognition of the importance of a State’s power to determine the incidents of basic social relationships into which its domiciliaries enter does not resolve the issues of this case. This is not a situation in which a State has merely sought to exert such power over a domiciliary. This is, rather, a case involving inconsistent assertions of power by courts of two States of the Federal Union and thus presents considerations which go beyond the interests of local policy, however vital.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-334-378.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-334-378.summary: The Court held that Massachusetts had to give full faith and credit to Nevada’s divorce decree because it was valid and final in Nevada and both spouses participated in the Nevada proceedings with a full opportunity to litigate domicile and jurisdiction. The decree therefore could not be subjected to collateral attack in Massachusetts by relitigating those jurisdictional facts.
excerpts: It is clear that the decree of divorce in question is valid and final in the State in which it was rendered and, under the law of Nevada, may not be subjected to the collateral attack permitted in this case in the Massachusetts courts. Respondent does not urge the contrary.

Thus, here, as in the Sherrer case, the decree of divorce is one which was entered after proceedings in which there was participation by both plaintiff and defendant and in which both parties were given full opportunity to contest the jurisdictional issues. It is a decree not susceptible to collateral attack in the courts of the State in which it was rendered. In the Sherrer case, we concluded that the requirements of full faith and credit preclude the courts of a sister State from subjecting such a decree to collateral attack by readjudicating the existence of jurisdictional facts. That principle is no less a
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-334-541.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-334-541.summary: The Court held that Nevada’s ex parte divorce decree was entitled to full faith and credit insofar as it changed the parties’ marital status, because the husband was domiciled in Nevada and due process was satisfied. However, Nevada lacked jurisdiction to extinguish the wife’s rights under an earlier New York support judgment, so the divorce was divisible and ineffective as to alimony.
excerpts: The result in this situation is to make the divorce divisible — to give effect to the Nevada decree insofar as it affects marital status and to make it ineffective on the issue of alimony.

The requirements of procedural due process were satisfied and the domicile of the husband in Nevada was foundation for a decree effecting a change in the marital capacity of both parties in all the other States of the Union, as well as in Nevada. Williams v. North Carolina, 317 U. S. 287. But the fact that marital capacity was changed does not mean that every other legal incidence of the marriage was necessarily affected.

The result in this situation is to make the divorce divisible — to give effect to the Nevada decree insofar as it affects marital status and to make it ineffective on the issue of alimony. It accommodates the interests of both Nevada and New York in this broken marriage by restricting each State to the matters of her dominant concern.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-334-555.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-334-555.summary: The Court applied the divisible-divorce rule under the Full Faith and Credit Clause, holding that Nevada’s ex parte divorce could not adjudicate the respondent’s rights under the prior New York separation judgment. New York therefore was not required to recognize the Nevada decree insofar as it purported to eliminate those rights.
excerpts: For the reasons stated in Estin v. Estin, ante, p. 541, we hold that Nevada had no power to adjudicate respondent’s rights in the New York judgment and thus New York was not required to bow to that provision of the Nevada decree. It is therefore unnecessary to pass upon New York’s attempt to enjoin petitioner from securing a divorce or to reach the question whether the New York judgment was entitled to full faith and credit in the Nevada proceedings.

us-scotus-325-226.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-325-226.summary: The Court held that a sister-state divorce decree is entitled to full faith and credit only if the rendering court had jurisdiction, including a valid domicile. North Carolina could therefore determine for itself whether Nevada domicile existed and collaterally impeach the decree on that jurisdictional fact, while treating the decree as conclusive on other matters.
excerpts: Under our system of law, judicial power to grant a divorce — jurisdiction, strictly speaking — is founded on domicil.

But the Clause does not make a sister-State judgment a judgment in another State. The proposal to do so was rejected by the Philadelphia Convention. 2 Farrand, The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, 447-48. “To give it the force of a judgment in another state, it must be made a judgment there.” M’Elmoyle v. Cohen, 13 Pet. 312, 325. It can be made a judgment there only if the court purporting to render the original judgment had power to render such a judgment. A judgment in one State is conclusive upon the merits in every other State, but only if the court of the first State had power to pass on the merits — had jurisdiction, that is, to render the judgment.

Under our system of law, judicial power to grant a divorce — jurisdiction, strictly speaking — is founded on domicil. Bell v. Bell, 181 U. S. 175; Andrews v. Andrews, 188 U. S. 14. The framers of the Constitution were familiar with this jurisdictional prerequisite, and since 1789 neither this Court nor any other court in the English-speaking world has questioned it. Domicil implies a nexus between person and place of such permanence as to control the creation of legal relations and responsibilities of the utmost significance.

us-scotus-325-279.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-325-279.citation: Esenwein v. Commonwealth ex rel. Esenwein, 325 U.S. 279 (1945)
us-scotus-325-279.summary: The Court held that Pennsylvania was required to accord prima facie validity to the Nevada divorce decree under the Full Faith and Credit Clause. That obligation did not prevent Pennsylvania from determining that the decree lacked a jurisdictional foundation because the husband was not bona fide domiciled in Nevada.
excerpts: The Full Faith and Credit Clause placed the Pennsylvania courts under duty to accord -prima facie validity to the Nevada decree. The burden is on the litigant who would escape the operation of a judgment decreed in another State. Pennsylvania recognized that burden, but its courts were warranted in finding that the respondent sustained her burden of impeaching the foundation of the Nevada decree on the jurisdictional prerequisite of bona fide domicil. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court rightly indicated that if merely the Nevada decree had been in evidence, it was entitled to carry the day.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-323-77.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-323-77.summary: The Court held that a North Carolina money judgment for accrued and unpaid alimony was a final, unconditional judgment entitled to full faith and credit in Tennessee. Although future alimony orders could be prospectively modified, the accrued installments and judgment for those installments were not subject to modification or recall under North Carolina law.
excerpts: The constitutional command is that “Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State.” Article IV, § 1 of the Constitution also provides that “Con
provisions: Act of May 26, 1790, ch. 11, 1 Stat. 122 (then 28 U.S.C. § 687)

us-scotus-317-287.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-317-287.summary: The Court held that a divorce decree issued by Nevada must receive full faith and credit when Nevada was the spouses’ bona fide domicile and the decree was valid and binding there. North Carolina could not refuse recognition merely because it would not have granted a divorce on the same grounds, although the Court reserved whether recognition could be denied if Nevada domicile was not bona fide.
excerpts: Nor did it hold that a decree of divorce granted by the courts of one state need not be given full faith and credit in another if the grounds for the divorce would not be recognized by the courts of the forum. It does not purport to challenge or disturb the rule, earlier established by Christmas v. Russell, supra, and subsequently fortified by Fauntleroy v. Lum, supra, that, even though the cause of action could not have been entertained in the state of the forum, a judgment obtained thereon in a sister state is entitled to full faith and credit.

This Court, of course, is the final arbiter when the question is raised as to what is a permissible limitation on the full faith and credit clause. Alaska Packers Assn. v. Industrial Accident Comm’n, supra, p. 547; Milwaukee County v. White Co., supra, p. 274. But the question for us is a limited one. In the first place, we repeat that in this case we must assume that petitioners had a bona fide domicil in Nevada, not that .the Nevada domicil was a sham. We thus have no question on the present record whether a divorce decree granted by the courts of one state to a resident, as distinguished from a domiciliary, is entitled to full faith and credit in another state.
provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-scotus-305-32.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-305-32.summary: The Court held that Virginia’s divorce decree was entitled to recognition and enforcement in the District of Columbia under full faith and credit because the husband had sufficient Virginia domicile and the wife had received notice and litigated his standing to sue. It distinguished Haddock because the wife appeared and had been adjudged to have disrupted the marital relationship.
excerpts: Nor can it be said that the domicil was not adequate to support, in virtue of the rule of full faith and credit established by Congress, a decree enforceable in the courts of the District of Columbia. Depending on the connection in which used, various meanings have been attributed to the phrase matrimonial domicil.

In view of these facts, and of her conduct, adjudged repugnant to the marital relation, it would be unreasonable to hold that his domicil in Virginia was not sufficient to entitle him to obtain a divorce having the same force in the District as in that State.

norms.b_justification: Davis interpreted the Full Faith and Credit Clause of U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1, as implemented by 28 U.S.C. § 1738, and applied the domicile-based validity of an out-of-state divorce decree. Its holding is functionally consistent with the current rule requiring recognition of such decrees, including the distinction between marital status and ancillary support or property rights.

us-scotus-292-216.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-292-216.summary: The Court held that a marriage valid under the law of the state where it was solemnized generally must be recognized elsewhere, despite a domiciliary statute prohibiting remarriage by a divorced person or prohibiting remarriage for a specified period. Such a statute ordinarily has only territorial effect and does not invalidate an otherwise valid out-of-state marriage.
excerpts: First. Marriages not polygamous or incestuous, or otherwise declared void by statute, will, if valid by the law of the State where entered into, be recognized as valid in every other jurisdiction. Meister v. Moore, 96 U.S. 76; Travers v. Reinhardt, 205 U.S. 423, 440. The mere statutory prohibition by the State of the domicile either generally of the remarriage of a divorced person, or of remarriage within a prescribed period after the entry of the decree, is given only territorial effect. Such a statute does not invalidate a marriage solemnized in another State in conformity with the laws thereof.

norms.b_justification: Loughran v. Loughran applies the interstate-recognition rule for marital status: a marriage valid where celebrated is generally recognized elsewhere, while a forum’s remarriage prohibition has only territorial effect. That approach is functionally consistent with the current judge-made full-faith-and-credit and divisible-divorce framework, although no verbatim current statutory text is provided.

us-scotus-215-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-215-1.summary: The Court held that the Full Faith and Credit Clause did not require Nebraska to treat a Washington divorce decree as having transferred title to Nebraska land. The decree could establish rights arising from the divorce, but it could not itself operate as an in rem conveyance of property located outside Washington, particularly absent personal jurisdiction over the nonappearing property holder.
excerpts: The question is in narrow compass. The full faith and credit clause of the Constitution of the United States is invoked by plaintiff to sustain the deed executed under the decree of the court of the State of Washington.

The argument in support of this is that the Washington court, having had jurisdiction of the parties and the subject-matter, in determination of the equities- between the parties to the lands in controversy, decreed a conveyance to be made to her.
No personal service was had upon E.- W. Fall, and he did not appear. A decree was passed in favor of plaintiff, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court.

norms.b_justification: Fall v. Eastin interpreted U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 and applied full faith and credit to a divorce decree while distinguishing the decree’s marital adjudication from its attempted disposition of out-of-state property. That property/status distinction is functionally consistent with the current divisible-divorce rule, and no later change to the constitutional provision is shown.

us-scotus-192-125.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-192-125.citation: German Savings & Loan Society v. Dormitzer, 192 U.S. 125 (1904)
us-scotus-192-125.summary: The Court considered whether Washington had given full faith and credit to a Kansas divorce decree. It applied the distinction between recognition of the marital-status determination and the decree’s effect on property rights, holding that the Kansas decree did not conclusively establish the children’s claimed interest in Washington community property.
excerpts: This is a writ of error to the Suprefne'Court of Washington on the ground that full faith and credit has not been given to a decree of divorce rendered in the State of Kansas. See 23 Washington, 132. The record is long, but all .that is material to the case in this court can be stated in a few words.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 and applied full faith and credit to a sister-state divorce decree based on the rendering court’s jurisdiction, rather than on whether the forum recognized the divorce grounds. That is consistent in function with the current domicile-based full-faith-and-credit rule; the later divisible-divorce doctrine does not contradict the holding.

us-scotus-181-155.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-181-155.summary: The Court held that Kentucky’s divorce decree was entitled to full faith and credit in another state as an absolute decree of divorce. It applied the domicile-based rule that a state may dissolve a marriage when one spouse is domiciled there, even if the other spouse was not personally within the state.
excerpts: There can be no doubt that this decree was by law and usage entitled to full faith and credit as an absolute decree of divorce in the State of Kentucky. The Court of Appeals of that State has held that, under its statutes, a wife residing in the State- was entitled to obtain a decree of divorce against a husband who' had left the State, or who had never been within it;

norms.b_justification: Atherton v. Atherton interpreted the Full Faith and Credit Clause as requiring recognition of a sister-state divorce decree where the rendering court had jurisdiction based on domicile, including when the forum would not recognize the underlying divorce ground. That holding is consistent in function with the current divisible-divorce framework, which gives full faith and credit to marital-status determinations while treating support and property rights separately.

provisions: U.S. Const. art. IV, § 1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause)

us-ca8-72-f4th-269.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-72-f4th-269.citation: Lisa Crain v. Shirley Crain, 72 F.4th 269 (8th Cir. 2023)
us-ca8-72-f4th-269.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the domestic-relations exception and held that it did not bar federal diversity jurisdiction over a dispute involving marital-property distribution and interpretation of an agreement incorporated into a divorce decree. The court emphasized that the exception is narrow and applies only when the action’s subject is divorce, alimony, child support, or related marital-property distribution.
excerpts: We now turn to the domestic relations exception. This exception “‘divests the federal courts of jurisdiction over any action for which the subject is a divorce, allowance of alimony, or child support,’ including ‘the distribution of marital property.’” Wallace v. Wallace, 736 F.3d 764, 766 (8th Cir. 2013) (citation omitted). We have had limited occasion to analyze the domestic relations exception, but generally, we apply it only in narrow circumstances.

us-ca8-736-f3d-764.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-736-f3d-764.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the domestic-relations exception to diversity jurisdiction and held that the identity-theft claims were inextricably intertwined with the parties’ divorce proceedings. Because the requested damages and equitable relief would undermine or modify the state court’s marital-debt allocation, federal subject-matter jurisdiction was precluded.
excerpts: The domestic relations exception, first articulated in Barber v. Barber, 62 U.S. ([2]1 How.) 582, 584, 16 L.Ed. 226 (185[8]), divests the federal courts of jurisdiction over any action for which the subject is a divorce, allowance of alimony, or child support,” including “the distribution of marital property.” Kahn, 21 F.3d at 861.

If the federal district court were to' award Michael the injunctive and declaratory relief he requests here, the award, at least in part, would undermine the judgment of the state court. These remedies would essentially require that the federal court remove the label “marital debt” and reallocate the debt division the state court has already “deem[ed] just after considering” the conduct at issue here.

us-scotus-547-293.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-547-293.summary: The Court described the domestic-relations exception as a longstanding, judicially created limitation on federal jurisdiction and noted that Ankenbrandt had curtailed expansive interpretations of it. The case itself principally narrowed the separate probate exception.
excerpts: Among longstanding limitations on federal jurisdiction otherwise properly exercised are the so-called “domestic relations” and “probate” exceptions. Neither is compelled by the text of the Constitution or federal statute. Both are judicially created doctrines stemming in large measure from misty understandings of English legal history.

In Ankenbrandt v. Richards, 504 U. S. 689 (1992), this Court reined in the “domestic relations exception.” Earlier, in Markham v. Allen, 326 U. S. 490 (1946), the Court endeavored similarly to curtail the “probate exception.

us-scotus-542-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-542-1.citation: Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow, 542 U.S. 1 (2004)
us-scotus-542-1.summary: The Court discussed the domestic-relations exception, explaining that it generally prevents federal courts from issuing divorce, alimony, and child-custody decrees. It clarified that its holding rested on prudential standing rather than formally applying the exception, but the standing analysis was informed by the federal courts’ deference to state family-law determinations.
excerpts: One of the principal areas in which this Court has customarily declined to intervene is the realm of domestic relations. Long ago we observed that “[t]he whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States.” In re Burrus, 136 U. S. 586, 593-594 (1890). See also Mansell v. Mansell, 490 U. S. 581, 587 (1989) (“[Domestic relations are preeminently matters of state law”); Moore v. Sims, 442 U. S. 415, 435 (1979) (“Family relations are a traditional area of state concern”).

Our holding does not rest, as The Chief Justice suggests, see post, at 19-22 (opinion concurring in judgment), on either the domestic relations exception or the abstention doctrine. Rather, our prudential standing analysis is informed by the variety of contexts in which federal courts decline to intervene because, as Ankenbrandt v. Richards, 504 U. S. 689 (1992), contemplated, the suit “depend[s] on a determination of the status of the parties,” id., at 706. We deemed it appropriate to review the dispute in Palmore because it “raise[d] important federal concerns arising from the Constitution’s commitment to eradicating discrimination based on race.” 466 U. S., at 432. In this case, by contrast, the disputed family law rights are entwined inextricably with the threshold standing inquiry.

us-ca8-115-f3d-1397.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-115-f3d-1397.citation: United States v. Crawford, 115 F.3d 1397 (8th Cir. 1997)
us-ca8-115-f3d-1397.summary: The court held that the domestic-relations exception, which is limited to diversity cases involving divorce, alimony, and child-custody decrees, did not apply to a federal prosecution under the CSRA because jurisdiction rested on federal-question criminal jurisdiction. It also held that Younger abstention was unwarranted because the CSRA supplements, rather than interferes with, state enforcement of child-support obligations.
excerpts: Moreover, Crawford’s reliance upon the “domestic relations exception” is misplaced. In Ankenbrandt v. Richards, 504 U.S. 689, 701-04, 112 S.Ct. 2206, 2213-15, 119 L.Ed.2d 468 (1992), the Supreme Court reaffirmed the validity of the “domestic relations exception” in diversity cases, but specifically limited application of that exception to divorce and alimony decrees and child custody orders. That exception is irrelevant to federal prosecutions under the CSRA because the district courts’ jurisdiction in such cases does not rest upon diversity, but rather is based upon 18 U.S.C. § 3231 (“The district courts of the United States shall have original jurisdiction, exclusive of the courts of the States, of all offenses against the laws of the United States.

Similarly, contrary to Crawford’s argument based upon the Younger abstention doctrine, we discern no interference with the states’ abilities to apply and enforce their criminal laws. “[T]he CSRA does not displace any approach taken by the state in addressing the problem of delinquent parents but rather supplements such state initiatives by fortifying law enforcement efforts and existing state penalties.” Hampshire, 95 F.3d at 1004. In sum, the district court correctly rejected Crawford’s argument that principles of federalism and comity compel abstention. Accord Johnson, 114 F.3d at 480-82 (rejecting substantially the same arguments). We therefore hold that the district court appropriately declined to abstain.
provisions: Domestic-relations exception to diversity jurisdiction; 18 U.S.C. § 3231

us-ca8-94-f3d-510.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-94-f3d-510.summary: The court applied Younger and related abstention principles to dismiss Amerson’s equitable claims because parallel state proceedings concerning termination of parental rights were pending. It also held that federal relief, including damages dependent on invalidating the state judgment, was impermissible in this domestic-relations context and would improperly require review of the state custody determination.
excerpts: We conclude without extended discussion that the district court’s detailed discussion of the abstention principles cited above is correct as applied to Amerson’s equitable claims, including those for injunctive relief. The relief Amerson seeks is redress for “alleged tortious interference with her parental rights.” (Appellant’s Br. at 6.) Because the state courts have terminated her parental rights, redress for this alleged interference cannot be granted without first disturbing the state court adjudication terminating her parental rights, a matter of substantial public concern.

Additionally, several state court proceedings and appeals concerning the same issues asserted here were pending at the time of the district court’s decision. See Younger, 401 U.S. at 43-54, 91 S.Ct. at 750-55 (holding that, with a few exceptions, federal courts cannot interfere with pending state court criminal proceedings). See also Ankenbrandt, 504 U.S. at 705, 112 S.Ct. at 2215-16 (noting that Younger abstention has been extended to the civil context). Thus, the district court did not err in applying these principles of abstention to Amerson’s equitable claims.

The Supreme Court has long rejected federal court interference in state domestic relations policy. See Ankenbrandt, 504 U.S. at 701-02, 112 S.Ct. at 2213-14 (noting that claims seeking to restore a child to the custody of a parent are within the subject of domestic relations, which belongs to the states); Lannan v. Maul, 979 F.2d 627, 630-31 (8th Cir.1992) (discussing Ankenbrandt and noting that the domestic relations exception is narrow and “divests federal courts of power to issue divorce, alimony decrees and child custody orders”).

us-ca8-979-f2d-627.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-979-f2d-627.summary: The court applied the narrow domestic-relations exception, holding that it does not bar federal jurisdiction over a collateral third-party beneficiary contract claim merely because the contract arose from a divorce-related property settlement. The court also considered whether Younger abstention was warranted because related family-law proceedings were pending in state court.
excerpts: The domestic relations exception, upon which the district court relied to decline jurisdiction, was recently addressed by the United States Supreme Court in the case of Ankenbrandt v. Richards, - U.S. -, 112 S.Ct. 2206, 119 L.Ed.2d 468 (1992) (Ankenbrandt). We held this appeal in abeyance pending the Supreme Court’s decision in Ankenbrandt. In Ankenbrandt, the Supreme Court determined that it was “unwilling to cast aside an understood rule that has been recognized for nearly a century and a half” and held that it would continue to recognize the domestic relations exception to federal jurisdiction. Id. 112 S.Ct. at 2210. However, the Court concluded that a tort action arising out of the domestic relations of the parties did not fall within the domestic relations exception.

Thus, we conclude that the domestic relations exception, as articulated by the Supreme Court in Ankenbrandt, is a narrow one. Id. at 2215 n. 6 (Noting that better reasoned views among Courts of Appeals have similarly limited the domestic relations exception). The case at bar is similar to Ankenbrandt. The issues presented here do not involve a domestic relations dispute between a feuding couple concerning a divorce, alimony, or child custody decree. Rather, it concerns a third-party beneficiary claim based on contract law. We hold, therefore, that the district court erred in holding that it lacked jurisdiction because the domestic relations exception does not encompass collateral issues, such as the alleged breach of contract presented here.

Although the federal district court did not specifically invoke the abstention doctrine announced in Younger v. Harris, as an alternative ground for its holding, the district court concluded that the issues raised were substantially related to and intertwined with issues pending before state courts. See page 630. Lannan argues, however, that the district court erred in declining jurisdiction because neither he, as conservator, nor Ashley Brewer, is a party to any other state court litigation or was a party to the divorce litigation between her parents. Moreover, Lannan argues this is a breach of contract claim which has no significant relationship to any action pending in state court.

us-scotus-504-689.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-504-689.citation: Ankenbrandt ex rel. L. R. v. Richards, 504 U.S. 689 (1992)
us-scotus-504-689.summary: The Court held that the domestic-relations exception does not bar a diversity tort action seeking damages for alleged child abuse when the plaintiff does not request a divorce, alimony, or child-custody decree. It also held that Younger abstention was improper because no state proceeding was pending, while noting that Burford abstention might apply in limited circumstances involving difficult state-law questions concerning domestic status.
excerpts: the domestic relations exception encompasses only cases involving the issuance of a divorce, alimony, or child custody decree,

The courts below cited Younger v. Harris, 401 U. S. 37 (1971), to support their holdings to abstain in this case. In so doing, the courts clearly erred. Younger itself held that, absent unusual circumstances, a federal court could not interfere with a pending state criminal prosecution. Id., at 54. Though we have extended Younger abstention to the civil context, see, e. g., Middlesex County Ethics Comm. v. Garden State Bar Assn., 457 U. S. 423 (1982); Ohio Civil Rights Comm’n v. Dayton Christian Schools, Inc., 477 U. S. 619 (1986); Pennzoil Co. v. Texaco Inc., 481 U. S. 1 (1987), we have never applied the notions of comity so critical to Younger’s “Our Federalism” when no state proceeding was pending nor any assertion of important state interests made.

We thus conclude that the Court of Appeals erred by affirming the District Court’s rulings to decline jurisdiction based on the domestic relations exception to diversity jurisdiction and to abstain under the doctrine of Younger v. Harris, supra. The exception has no place in a suit such as this one, in which a former spouse sues another on behalf of children alleged to have been abused. Because the allegations in this complaint do not request the District Court to issue a divorce, alimony, or child custody decree, we hold that the suit is appropriate for the exercise of §1332 jurisdiction given the existence of diverse citizenship between petitioner and respondents and the pleading of the relevant amount in controversy.

us-ca8-623-f2d-517.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-623-f2d-517.summary: The court applied the domestic-relations exception to require dismissal of a federal custody dispute where resolving the constitutional claim would require factual reexamination and possible modification of the state custody arrangement. It held that the custody issue belonged exclusively in state court, particularly while related state proceedings were pending.
excerpts: Where a constitutional issue arises out of a custody dispute, and the initial determination involves a reexamination of the custody arrangement, the proper course is to dismiss the case and remand to the state court.

Since the primary issue is whether changed circumstances warrant modification of the custody arrangement, the constitutional question was obviously not presented in the posture of strict necessity. Under the circumstances, the district court should have declined to exercise jurisdiction.

Reexamination of custody arrangements is a matter which belongs exclusively in state court; domestic relations disputes have been traditionally subject to exclusive state jurisdiction. See Popovici v. Agler, 280 U.S. 379, 50 S.Ct. 154, 74 L.Ed. 489 (1930); Overman v. United States, 563 F.2d 1287, 1290 (8th Cir. 1977).

us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.citation: Overman v. United States, 563 F.2d 1287 (8th Cir. 1977)
us-ca8-563-f2d-1287.summary: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 659 waived sovereign immunity only for state garnishment proceedings enforcing child-support or alimony obligations, and did not authorize a broader damages or validity challenge against the United States or its disbursing officer. It further reasoned that § 660's expressly certified jurisdictional mechanism did not extend to § 659 actions, and remanded the remaining domestic-relations dispute to state court under the federal policy against federal adjudication of such matters.
excerpts: In 42 U.S.C. § 659 (Supp.1975), the United States waived its immunity from state garnishment actions directed at federal employees.
