The statute simply removed the bar of sovereign immunity to one narrow class of actions: enforcement of garnishment writs issued by state courts. See, e. g., Wilhelm v. United States Department of Air Force Accounting, 418 F.Supp. 162, 164 (S.D.Tex.1976). Nothing in the statute or legislative history, however, indicates any congressional intent to expose the Government to wider liability.

Congressman Ullman’s comment about certification is a reference to 42 U.S.C. § 660 (Supp. 1975). That provision provides federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8) (Supp. 1975), if certified by the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare. Since §§ 652(a)(8) and 659 are parallel provisions, that is, both are part of Pub.L. 93-647, § 606(a), 88 Stat. 2351, 2357, the presumption must be that if Congress had intended federal jurisdiction for cases arising under § 659 it would have explicitly provided for it, as it did for § 652(a)(8).

norms.b_justification: Overman interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 660’s grant of federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under § 652(a)(8) when certified by the Secretary, and the current text retains that same jurisdictional mechanism and venue provisions. The 1984 amendment only changed the agency name from Health, Education, and Welfare to Health and Human Services, a technical change that does not alter the provision’s wording in substance or function.

provisions: 42 U.S.C. § 660 (jurisdiction for actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8), upon certification)

us-scotus-280-379.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-280-379.citation: Ohio ex rel. Popovici v. Agler, 280 U.S. 379 (1930)
us-scotus-280-379.summary: The Court held that the constitutional and statutory provisions concerning suits against consuls did not confer federal jurisdiction over a divorce and alimony proceeding. Applying the domestic-relations limitation on federal jurisdiction, the Court concluded that state courts retained authority because federal courts had historically lacked jurisdiction over divorce.
excerpts: It has been understood that, “ the whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States,” Ex parte Burrus, 136 U. S. 586, 593, 594, and the jurisdiction of the Courts of the United States over divorces and alimony always has been denied. Barber v. Barber, 21 How. 582. Simms v. Simms, 175 U. S. 162, 167. De La Rama v. De La Rama, 201 U. S. 303, 307.

The words quoted from the Constitution do not of themselves and without more exclude the jurisdiction of the State. Plaquemines Tropical Fruit Co. v. Henderson, 170 U. S. 511. The statutes do- not purport to exclude the State Courts from jurisdiction except where they grant it to Courts of the United States. Therefore they do not affect the present case if it be true as has been unquestioned for three-quarters of a century that the Courts of the United States have no jurisdiction over divorce.

us-scotus-203-429.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-203-429.citation: New York Foundling Hospital v. Gatti, 203 U.S. 429 (1906)
us-scotus-203-429.summary: The Court held that its appellate jurisdiction under the habeas corpus statute was limited to cases involving personal freedom. A habeas proceeding seeking determination of an infant’s custody did not involve the child’s personal freedom and therefore was not reviewable by the Supreme Court.
excerpts: The jurisdiction is conferred to enable the cause of restraint to be inquired into, and the person imprisoned or wrongfully deprived of freedom restored to liberty. The subject was discussed by .Mr. Justice Miller in the case of In re Burrus, 136 U. S. 586, in which it was held that a District Court of the United States has no' authority to issue a writ of habeas corpus to restore an infant to the custody of its father when unlawfully detained by its grandparents.

A brief consideration of the history and nature of the writ will, we think, make manifest the purpose of Congress in using this restrictive language giving the right of appeal. The writ is usually granted in order to institute an investigation into the illegal imprisonment or wrongful detention of one alleging himself to be unlawfully restrained of his liberty.
provisions: Act of March 3, 1891, § 5 (appellate jurisdiction in habeas corpus cases involving “the question of personal freedom”)

us-scotus-201-303.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-201-303.citation: De la Rama v. De la Rama, 201 U.S. 303 (1906)
us-scotus-201-303.summary: The Court applied the established rule that federal courts generally lack jurisdiction over divorce and alimony matters. It held that the rule did not bar appellate jurisdiction over a territorial court, particularly where the decree involved a monetary claim exceeding the jurisdictional amount.
excerpts: An important question of jurisdiction is presented by the record in this case. It has been a long established rule that the courts of the United States have no jurisdiction upon the subject of divorce, or for the allowance of alimony, either as an original, proceeding in chancery) or an incident of a divorce or separation, both by reason of fact that the husband and wife cannot usually be citizens of different States, so long as the marriage relation continues

us-scotus-198-317.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-198-317.summary: The Court treated federal enforcement of an alimony judgment as permissible despite its connection to a marital-separation proceeding. Relying on Barber v. Barber, it recognized that federal courts may enforce such family-related judgments even while refraining from deciding the validity of an underlying divorce decree.
excerpts: The controversy before us is, in some respects, like that which was considered in Barber v. Barber, 21 How. 582. There a bill was filed in a Federal court in Wisconsin to enforce judgment for alimony under a decree of separation a mensa et thoro, rendered against a husband in New York. It was shown by the evidence that to avoid the payment of the alimony the husband had left the State of New York, the matrimonial domicil, and taken up his residence in the State of Wisconsin, where he obtained a decree of divorce on the ground of desertion by the. wife.

Whilst this court refrained from expressing an opinion as to the legality of the Wisconsin decree of divorce obtained under these circumstances, it enforced the New York judgment for alimony, and held it to be binding.

us-scotus-196-68.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-196-68.summary: The Court treated alimony as arising from the marital relationship and the legal duty of support, rather than from contract or an ordinary business transaction. It emphasized that alimony is ordinarily subject to the continuing authority and discretion of the court having jurisdiction over the marital relationship, reflecting the domestic-relations limitation on federal judicial authority.
excerpts: Alimony does not arise from any business transaction, but from the relation of marriage. It is not founded on contract, express or implied, but on the natural and legal duty of the husband to support the wife. The general obligation to support is made'specific by the decree of the court of appropriate jurisdiction. Generally speaking, alimony .may be altered by the court at any time, as the circumstances of the parties may require.

Permanent alimony is regarded rather as a portion of the husband’s estate to which the wife is equitably entitled, than as strictly a debt; alimony from time to time may be regarded as a portion.of his current income or earnings; and the considerations which affect either can be better weighed by the court having jurisdiction over the relation of husband and wife, than by a court of a different jurisdiction.

us-scotus-175-162.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-175-162.summary: The Court reaffirmed that federal Circuit Courts lack jurisdiction over suits for divorce or claims for alimony. It held that this domestic-relations limitation does not apply to the courts of a federal Territory or to the Supreme Court’s appellate jurisdiction over those courts.
excerpts: It may therefore be assumed as indubitable that the Circuit Courts of the United States have no jurisdiction, either of suits for divorce, or of claims for alimony, whether made in a suit for divorce, or by an original proceeding in equity, before a decree for such alimony in a state court. Within the States of the Union, the whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the State, and not to the laws of the United States.

But those considerations have no application to the jurisdiction of the courts of a Territory, or to the appellate jurisdiction of this court over those courts. In the Territories of the United States, Congress has the entire dominion and sovereignty, national and local, Federal and state, and has full legislative power over all subjects upon which the legislature of a State might legislate within the State; and may, at its discretion, intrust that power to the legislative assembly of a Territory.

us-scotus-136-586.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-136-586.summary: The Court treated parental custody, care, and nurture as protected parental rights relevant to habeas proceedings concerning a child. It recognized that habeas corpus could be used in limited circumstances involving an infant’s detention, including detention by a parent, but cautioned against treating ordinary parental custody as wrongful imprisonment absent necessity to preserve parental rights or the child’s interests.
excerpts: The whole subject of the, domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child,belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States.

The incongruity of, awarding proofs, at the instance of husband or wife, to take away an infant child from the parent having it in nurture and keeping, upon the allegation that such keeping is a wrongful imprisonment, is most palpable and striking. It is a bold figure of speech, or rather fiction, to which the law ought not to resort, unless indispensably necessary to be employed in preservation of parental rights, or the personal fondness of the child.

The courts, however, assume such supposititious imprisonment to exist as the foundation for jurisdiction, to a limited extent, over the detention of infants, even by their parents, on the ground that the writ is rather to be considered a proceeding in the name and behalf of the sovereign than by one'named person against the other.

us-scotus-62-582.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-62-582.citation: Barber v. Barber ex rel. Cronkhite, 62 U.S. 582 (1858)
us-scotus-62-582.summary: The Court distinguished a suit to enforce an existing alimony decree from a proceeding seeking an original divorce or alimony award. It held that federal courts lack jurisdiction over divorce or original alimony matters, but may act in equity to prevent an existing alimony decree from being defeated by fraud.
excerpts: Our first remark is — and we wish it to be remembered — that this is not a suit asking the court for the allowance of alimony. That has been done by a court of competent jurisdiction. The court in Wisconsin was asked to interfere to prevent that decree from being defeated by fraud. We disclaim altogether any jurisdiction in the courts of the United States upon the subject of divorce, or for the allowance of alimony, either as an original proceeding in chancery or as ah incident to divorce a vinculo, or to one from bed and board.

us-ca8-831-f3d-1005.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-831-f3d-1005.summary: The court applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine in a family-law context involving state divorce-related contempt proceedings. It held that the bankruptcy court construed the doctrine too broadly because Caldwell’s federal automatic-stay claim did not necessarily seek review of or relief from the state-court judgment.
excerpts: Under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, a lower federal court cannot exercise subject-matter jurisdiction over an action that “seek[s] review of, or relief from, state court judgments.” Hageman v. Barton, 817 F.3d 611, 614 (8th Cir. 2016). The bankruptcy court concluded the doctrine applied because, in order for Caldwell’s complaint to succeed in federal court, the court would have to overrule the state court’s determination that the automatic stay did not apply to the state court contempt proceedings. We conclude the bankruptcy court construed the Rooker-Feldman doctrine too broadly.

us-ca8-601-f3d-750.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-601-f3d-750.citation: Dodson v. University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences ex rel. University of Arkansas System Board of Trustees, 601 F.3d 750 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-601-f3d-750.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to a family-related dispute over the disposition and control of embryos. It affirmed dismissal of Count I because Dodson was a state-court loser alleging injuries caused by prior state-court judgments and could not use § 1983 to recast an attempted appeal.
excerpts: We affirm the dismissal of Count I because Dodson is a “state-court loser[] complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the district court proceedings commenced.” Friends of Lake View, 578 F.3d at 758.

us-ca8-457-f3d-794.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-457-f3d-794.citation: Porter ex rel. Pierce v. Knickrehm, 457 F.3d 794 (8th Cir. 2006)
us-ca8-457-f3d-794.summary: The court rejected applying Rooker-Feldman to a federal challenge concerning the procedures governing an incapacitated person's admission and continued placement in a state human-development center, rather than a direct attack on the state guardianship judgment. It held that the confined person possessed a substantial liberty interest and evaluated the adequacy of the procedures under the Mathews framework and Parham.
excerpts: Porter filed his complaint alleging that the procedures governing admission and continuing placement were constitutionally infirm. The Officials filed a motion to dismiss. The Officials argued that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine precluded Porter’s claim because they believed a grant of relief in the federal action would necessarily void earlier state actions granting guardianship.

Having determined that a liberty interest exists, we must determine what process is required to protect that interest. The question is whether the procedures afforded under Arkansas state law and the HDCs’ policies are constitutionally sufficient.

us-scotus-546-459.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-546-459.summary: The Court held that Rooker-Feldman bars lower federal courts from exercising appellate jurisdiction over state-court judgments, but does not prevent federal plaintiffs who were not parties or in privity with a state-court loser from proceeding. The citizen-plaintiffs therefore were not barred merely because the Colorado General Assembly had lost in the state litigation.
excerpts: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine prevents the lower federal courts from exercising jurisdiction over cases brought by “state-court losers” challenging “state-court judgments rendered before the district court proceedings commenced.” Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U. S. 280, 284 (2005). In this case, the District Court dismissed the plaintiffs’ suit on the ground that they were in privity with a state-court loser. We hold that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine does not bar the plaintiffs from proceeding, and vacate the District Court’s judgment.

This Court is vested, under 28 U. S. C. § 1257, with jurisdiction over appeals from final state-court judgments. We have held that this grant of jurisdiction is exclusive: “Review of such judgments may be had only in this Court.” District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U. S. 462, 482 (1988) (emphasis added); see also Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Locomotive Engineers, 398 U. S. 281, 286 (1970); Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U. S. 413, 416 (1923). Accordingly, under what has come to be known as the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, lower federal courts are precluded from exercising appellate jurisdiction over final state-court judgments.

us-scotus-544-280.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-544-280.citation: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
us-scotus-544-280.summary: The Court confined the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to cases brought by state-court losers who complain of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the federal action and invite federal district-court review and rejection of those judgments. The doctrine does not otherwise replace ordinary preclusion rules or expand abstention doctrines.
excerpts: cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the district court proceedings commenced and inviting district court review and rejection of those judgments.

The Rooker-Feldman doctrine, we hold today, is confined to cases of the kind from which the doctrine acquired its name: cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the district court proceedings commenced and inviting district court review and rejection of those judgments. Rooker-Feldman does not otherwise override or supplant preclusion doctrine or augment the circumscribed doctrines that allow federal courts to stay or dismiss proceedings in deference to state-court actions.

us-ca8-338-f3d-886.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-338-f3d-886.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that the children’s habitual residence was Israel and that returning them there did not create a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention as implemented by ICARA. It also held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the federal Hague proceeding because the state court had not decided the Convention-specific issues of habitual residence or wrongful removal and retention.
excerpts: Because we find that the children’s habitual residence was Israel at the time of their removal and that there is no grave risk of harm to the children if they are returned to Israel, we reverse the district court.

The state court determined neither the “habitual residence” of the children nor the issue of “wrongful removal or retention” as required by and defined in the Hague Convention and ICARA. Indeed, it was not asked to do so.

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention article 3 and ICARA’s wrongful-removal provisions, including the child’s habitual residence, through a fact-intensive assessment of the circumstances. Its application is functionally consistent with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances rule; the later formulation does not materially alter the habitual-residence inquiry.

us-ca8-335-f3d-684.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-335-f3d-684.citation: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle, 335 F.3d 684 (8th Cir. 2003)
us-ca8-335-f3d-684.summary: The court applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine in the context of a federal challenge involving state child-protection proceedings. It explained that a losing state-court party may not obtain de facto appellate review of a state judgment in federal district court, but indicated that Heartland’s request for injunctive relief was not necessarily barred because it did not interfere with the state-court judgment.
excerpts: On appeal from this order, Waddle first maintains that the District Court should have abstained from exercising jurisdiction over Heartland’s claim for preliminary in-junctive relief. He argues that the federal court is being asked to interfere with his responsibility to enforce the State’s child protection laws, and the District Court therefore should have abstained from hearing Heartland’s claims.

Under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, “a party losing in state court is barred from seeking what in substance would be appellate review of the state judgment in a United States district court, based on the losing party’s claim that the state judgment itself violates the loser’s federal rights.” Johnson v. De Grandy, 512 U.S. 997, 1005-06, 114 S.Ct. 2647, 129 L.Ed.2d 775 (1994). In other words, original federal jurisdiction over state-court judgments is reserved to the Supreme Court. Verizon Md. Inc. v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 535 U.S. 635, 644 n. 3, 122 S.Ct. 1753, 152 L.Ed.2d 871 (2002).

us-ca8-322-f3d-546.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-322-f3d-546.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman barred Ballinger’s § 1983 claims because they challenged a state-court custody judgment and could succeed only if the state court had wrongly decided the custody issues. The federal action would therefore operate as a prohibited appellate review of the state judgment.
excerpts: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine provides that, “with the exception of habe-as corpus petitions, lower federal courts lack subject matter jurisdiction over challenges to state court judgments.” Lemonds v. St. Louis County, 222 F.3d 488, 492 (8th Cir.2000) (citing Feldman, 460 U.S. at 476, 103 S.Ct. 1303; Rooker, 263 U.S. at 416, 44 S.Ct. 149). District courts may not review state court decisions, “even if those challenges allege that the state court’s action was unconstitutional,”

A claim brought in federal court is inextricably intertwined with a state court judgment “if the federal claim succeeds only to the extent that the state court wrongly decided the issue before it.” Id. at 493 (citing Pennzoil Co. v. Texaco, Inc., 481 U.S. 1, 25, 107 S.Ct. 1519, 95 L.Ed.2d 1 (1987) (Marshall, J., concurring)). Balling-er alleged in the complaint that Judge Pratt of the Circuit Court of Clay County violated Missouri law by awarding custody of John Ballinger to the Rheeses, who neither had “intervened in the action, nor filed a motion to modify.

Because “the relief requested in [Ballinger’s] federal [§ 1983] action would effectively reverse the state court decision or void its ruling,” Bechtold v. City of Rosemount, 104 F.3d 1062, 1065 (8th Cir.1997), the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars the district court from considering Balling-er’s claims, as the federal court action would amount to a “prohibited appeal of the state-court judgment,” id. at 1066 (citation omitted).

us-scotus-460-462.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-460-462.citation: District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
us-scotus-460-462.summary: The Court held that final judgments of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, like state-court judgments, are directly reviewable only by the Supreme Court under 28 U.S.C. § 1257. Lower federal courts therefore may not exercise appellate jurisdiction to review those judgments, establishing the Rooker-Feldman rule.
excerpts: These provisions make the judgments of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, like the judgments of state courts, directly reviewable in this Court. Cases no longer have to proceed from the local courts to the United States Court of Appeals and then to this Court under 28 U. S. C. § 1254. See Key v. Doyle, supra, at 64.

us-scotus-263-413.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-263-413.citation: Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
us-scotus-263-413.summary: The Court held that a federal district court, whose jurisdiction is strictly original, could not entertain an action seeking to reverse or modify a state-court judgment for alleged constitutional and legal errors. Such review would constitute appellate jurisdiction reserved to the Supreme Court, and a litigant could not circumvent the prescribed appellate process by attacking the judgment indirectly.
excerpts: It affirmatively appears from the bill that the judgment was rendered in a cause wherein the circuit court had jurisdiction'of both the subject matter and the parties; that a full hearing was had therein; that the judgment .was responsive to the issues, and that it was affirmed by the Supreme Court of the State on an appeal by the plaintiffs. . 191 Irfd.' 141. If the constitutional questions stated in the bill actually arose in the cause, it was the province and duty .of. the state courts’ to decide them; and their decision, whether right or wrong, ivas an exercise of , jurisdiction.

Under the legislation of Congress' no' court of the United States other than this Court could entertain á proceed-; ing to reverse or modify the judgment -for errors of that character. Judicial Code, §237, -as amended September 6, 1916, c. 448, § 2, 39 Stat. 726. To do so would be an exercise of appellate jurisdiction. The jurisdiction possessed by the District Courts is strictly original. Judicial Code, § 24. Besides, the period within which a proceeding might be' begun .for the correction of errors such as are charged in the bill had expired before it was filed, Act September 6,1916, c. 448, § 6, 39 Stat. 726, and, as is pointed out in Voorhees v. Bank of United States, supra, after that, period elapses an aggrieved litigant cannot be permitted to do indirectly what he no longer can do directly.
provisions: Judicial Code § 237, as amended September 6, 1916, ch. 448, § 2, 39 Stat. 726

us-ca8-110-f4th-1114.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-110-f4th-1114.citation: Devon Arseneau v. Elaine Pudlowski, 110 F.4th 1114 (8th Cir. 2024)
us-ca8-110-f4th-1114.summary: The court applied Younger abstention’s three-part framework to the family-custody dispute. It held that abstention was unwarranted because no state-court proceedings concerning the subject of the federal suit were ongoing, so the first Younger requirement was not satisfied.
excerpts: Younger abstention requires that federal courts “abstain from exercising their jurisdiction if (1) there is an ongoing state proceeding, (2) that implicates important state interests, and (3) that provides an adequate opportunity to raise any relevant federal questions.” Tony Alamo Christian Ministries v. Selig, 664 F.3d 1245, 1249 (8th Cir. 2012). There are no ongoing state court proceedings pertaining to the subject of this suit. Thus, the first component of Younger abstention is not met.

us-ca8-904-f3d-603.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-904-f3d-603.citation: Oglala Sioux Tribe v. Fleming, 904 F.3d 603 (8th Cir. 2018)
us-ca8-904-f3d-603.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that Younger abstention required federal-court abstention from challenges to South Dakota temporary child-custody proceedings. Because those proceedings were civil enforcement proceedings involving state custody of allegedly abused children, the court vacated the federal declaratory and injunctive relief and remanded for dismissal.
excerpts: We ultimately conclude that the district court should have abstained from exercising jurisdiction under principles of federal-state comity articulated in Younger v. Harris , 401 U.S. 37, 91 S.Ct. 746, 27 L.Ed.2d 669 (1971), and later cases. We thus vacate the court's orders granting partial summary judgment and declaratory and injunctive relief, and remand with instructions to dismiss the claims that gave rise to the orders.

South Dakota's temporary custody proceedings are civil enforcement proceedings to which Younger principles apply. In Moore , the Court held that a federal court should have abstained from intervening in a state-initiated proceeding to gain custody of children allegedly abused by their parents. 442 U.S. at 423, 435, 99 S.Ct. 2371. The Court observed

us-scotus-571-69.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-571-69.citation: Sprint Commc'ns, Inc. v. Jacobs, 571 U.S. 69 (2013)
us-scotus-571-69.summary: The Court held that federal courts generally must decide cases within their jurisdiction and may not abstain merely because parallel state proceedings are pending. Younger abstention is limited to exceptional categories, including state criminal prosecutions, certain civil enforcement proceedings, and proceedings uniquely supporting state courts’ judicial functions.
excerpts: state criminal prosecutions," "civil enforcement proceedings," and "civil proceedings involving certain orders that are uniquely in furtherance of the state courts' ability to perform their judicial functions

We reverse the judgment of the Court of Appeals. In the main, federal courts are obliged to decide cases within the scope of federal jurisdiction. Abstention is not in order simply because a pending state-court proceeding involves the same subject matter.

Circumstances fitting within the Younger doctrine, we have stressed, are "exceptional"; they include, as catalogued in NOPSI, "state criminal prosecutions," "civil enforcement proceedings," and "civil proceedings involving certain orders that are uniquely in furtherance of the state courts' ability to perform their judicial functions.

us-ca8-664-f3d-1245.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-664-f3d-1245.citation: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries v. Selig, 664 F.3d 1245 (8th Cir. 2012)
us-ca8-664-f3d-1245.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied Younger abstention to a § 1983 action challenging state child-welfare proceedings involving the removal of children and termination of parental rights. It held that ongoing state proceedings, important state interests in protecting children from abuse and neglect, and an adequate opportunity to raise federal claims in state court required dismissal of the federal action, including the church’s claims.
excerpts: Under current Younger v. Harris doctrine, federal courts should abstain from exercising their jurisdiction if (1) there is an ongoing state proceeding, (2) that implicates important state interests, and (3) that provides an adequate opportunity to raise any relevant federal questions. Plouffe v. Ligon, 606 F.3d 890, 894-95 (8th Cir.2010) (citing Middlesex County Ethics Comm. v. Garden State Bar Ass’n, 457 U.S. 423, 432, 102 S.Ct. 2515, 73 L.Ed.2d 116 (1982)). In such circumstances, principles of comity and federalism preclude federal actions seeking injunctive or declaratory relief.

us-ca8-536-f3d-844.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-536-f3d-844.summary: The court applied ICARA and the Hague Convention in holding that federal courts may adjudicate a Hague petition despite parallel state custody proceedings. Hague Convention article 16 requires custody proceedings to await resolution of the Hague litigation, and the pendency of state custody proceedings therefore does not justify Younger abstention.
excerpts: A party invokes the protections of the Convention in the United States by filing a petition in either federal or state court under ICARA (Hague petition). 42 U.S.C. § 11603(b) (“Any person seeking to initiate judicial proceedings under the Convention for the return of a child ... may do so by commencing a civil action by filing a petition for the relief sought in any court which has jurisdiction of such action and which is authorized to exercise its jurisdiction in the place where the child is located at the time the petition is filed.”); see § 11603(a) (vesting concurrent original jurisdiction over Hague petitions in the state and federal courts). ICARA further provides that “[t]he court in which an action is brought under [§ 11603(b)] shall decide the case in accordance with the Convention.” § 11603(d).

The Hague Convention requires that state court custody proceedings be stayed until the resolution of the Hague litigation. Hague Convention art. 16, T.I.A.S. No. 11670 (“[T]he judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been removed or in which it has been retained shall not decide on the merits of rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be returned under this Convention.”) (emphasis added); Yang v. Tsui, 416 F.3d 199, 201 (3d Cir.2005). While ICARA does not have a similar express provision, the purpose of the Convention is to “provide for a reasoned determination of where jurisdiction over a custody dispute is properly placed.

us-ca8-267-f3d-788.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-267-f3d-788.summary: The court held that Younger abstention principles did not permit outright dismissal of a Hague Convention return petition because Article 12 makes return relief non-discretionary once wrongful removal or retention is established. Although state custody proceedings were pending, the proper course was to remand for determination of whether the children were wrongfully removed.
excerpts: Younger abstention prohibits a federal court from interfering in pending state civil cases where (1) there is an ongoing state proceeding (2) that implicates important state interests and (3) there is an adequate opportunity in the state proceeding to raise the federal issues.

In the absence of discretion with respect to relief, abstention principles do not permit an outright dismissal of a Hague petition. See Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. v. Stroud, 179 F.3d 598, 603-04 (8th Cir.1999).

Because the Hague issue has not been addressed, we believe the appropriate course of action is to remand the matter to the district court to consider whether the Silverman children were wrongfully removed.
provisions: Younger abstention: ongoing state proceeding, important state interest, and adequate opportunity to raise federal issues

us-scotus-442-415.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-442-415.summary: The Court held that Younger abstention applies to pending state child-welfare proceedings because such civil proceedings involve important state interests and federal intervention threatens the federal system. The federal district court therefore should not have entertained the broad constitutional challenge while the state proceedings were pending, absent recognized exceptions such as bad faith, harassment, or a flagrantly unconstitutional statute.
excerpts: Family relations are a traditional area of state concern.

This litigation, involving suspected instances of child abuse, was initiated by state authorities in the Texas state courts in 1976. The state proceedings, however, were enjoined by the three-judge District Court below, which went on to find various parts of Title 2 unconstitutional on their face or as applied. We noted probable jurisdiction. 439 U. S. 925 (1978). This appeal first raises the question whether in light of the pending state proceedings, the Federal District Court should have exercised its jurisdiction. We conclude that it should not have done so and accordingly reverse and remand with instructions that the complaint be dismissed.

The Younger doctrine, which counsels federal-court abstention when there is a pending state proceeding, reflects a strong policy against federal intervention in state judicial processes in the absence of great and immediate irreparable injury to the federal plaintiff. Samuels v. Mackell, 401 U. S. 66, 69 (1971). That policy was first articulated with reference to state criminal proceedings, but as we recognized in Huffman v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U. S. 592 (1975), the basic concern — that threat to our federal system posed by displacement of state courts by those of the National Government — is also fully applicable to civil proceedings in which important state interests are involved.

us-ca8-575-f2d-200.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-575-f2d-200.summary: The Eighth Circuit affirmed dismissal under Younger abstention and related principles of federalism and comity. It held that abstention was not defeated merely because the federal plaintiffs were not named parties in the ongoing state family-law proceedings or because they claimed state remedies had been exhausted.
excerpts: As we read their brief, appellants, who are appealing pro se, contend that the three-judge district court erred in applying Younger principles to them because they were not named parties in the state court action. They also argue that state court remedies have been exhausted and that the principles of comity and federalism no longer apply. We reject both arguments and affirm.

The dismissal was grounded on the principles of federalism and comity set forth by the Supreme Court in Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37, 91 5. Ct. 746, 27 L.Ed.2d 669 (1971); Samuels v. Mackell, 401 U.S. 66, 91 S.Ct. 764, 27 L.Ed.2d 688 (1971); and Huffman v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U.S. 592, 95 S.Ct. 1200, 43 L.Ed.2d 482 (1975). Stivers and Cherry appeal the order of dismissal.

us-ca8-532-f2d-120.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-532-f2d-120.summary: The court applied Younger abstention and comity principles to bar declaratory and injunctive relief that would nullify a Missouri adoption decree. It emphasized that domestic relations are traditionally within the province of the states and that state collateral remedies had not been exhausted.
excerpts: The application for declaratory and injunctive relief is barred by the comity principles of Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37, 91 S.Ct. 746, 27 L.Ed.2d 669 (1971) and Huffmann v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U.S. 592, 95 S.Ct. 1200, 43 L.Ed.2d 482 (1975). To grant the relief sought would nullify the decree of a Missouri court. This decree relates to an area, domestic relations, which has traditionally been the province of the states.

us-scotus-401-37.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-401-37.summary: The Court held that federal courts generally may not enjoin a pending state criminal prosecution absent special circumstances. It applied the longstanding federalism-based abstention policy underlying the Anti-Injunction Act and reversed the injunction against the state prosecution.
excerpts: Without regard to the questions raised about Whitney v. California, supra, since overruled by Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U. S. 444 (1969), or the constitutionality of the state law, we have concluded that the judgment of the District Court, enjoining appellant Younger from prosecuting under these California statutes, must be reversed as a violation of the national policy forbidding federal courts to stay or enjoin pending state court proceedings except under special circumstances.

Since the beginning of this country’s history Congress has, subject to few exceptions, manifested a desire to permit state courts to try state cases free from interference by federal courts. In 1793 an Act unconditionally provided: “[N]or shall a writ of injunction be granted to stay proceedings in any court of a state . . . 1 Stat. 335, c. 22, § 5. A comparison of the 1793 Act with 28 U. S. C. § 2283, its present-day successor, graphically illustrates how few and minor have been the exceptions granted from the flat, prohibitory language of the old Act.

us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.citation: Lucas Alzu v. Amy Huff, No. 24-2517 (8th Cir. 2026)
us-ca8-24-2517-2026-01-23.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention principles governing wrongful removal, holding that the petitioner bears the burden of proving wrongful removal or retention. Monasky, 589 U.S. at 84. “Once the trial court correctly identifies the governing totality-of-the-circumstances standard, . . . [t]he habitual residence determination . . . should be judged on appeal by a clear-error review standard deferential to the factfinding court.” Id.; See also Tsuruta v. Tsuruta, 76 F.4th 1107, 1111 (8th Cir. 2023) (same).
The petitioner bears the burden of proving ‘that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention.’” Id. at 917, citing 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).
L]ocating a child’s home is a fact-driven inquiry[.] [C]ourts must be ‘sensitive to the unique circumstances of the case and informed by common sense.

us-ca8-76-f4th-1107.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-76-f4th-1107.citation: Naoteru Tsuruta v. Sarah Tsuruta, 76 F.4th 1107 (8th Cir. 2023)
us-ca8-76-f4th-1107.summary: The court applied the Hague Convention’s wrongful-removal framework and held that Japan was the child’s habitual residence before removal. Habitual residence is determined by where the child was “at home” based on the totality of the circumstances, and does not require an actual parental agreement.
excerpts: The Hague Convention does not govern custody battles, instead the Hague Convention determines the proper forum for custody battles. Id. at 916–17. Under the Hague Convention, “a child wrongfully removed from her country of ‘habitual residence’ ordinarily must be returned to that country[]” where custody will be determined. Monasky v. Taglieri, 140 S. Ct. 719, 723 (2020).

A child’s habitual residence is “[t]he place where a child is at home, at the time of removal or retention[.]” Monasky, 140 S. Ct. at 726. An actual agreement between the parents is not required to establish habitual residence, instead “a child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case.” Monasky, 140 S. Ct. at 723.

us-scotus-589-68.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-589-68.summary: The Court held that a child’s habitual residence under the Hague Convention is determined by the totality of the circumstances specific to the case, rather than by categorical requirements such as an actual parental agreement. It also held that a trial court’s habitual-residence determination is a fact-intensive mixed question subject to clear-error review on appeal.
excerpts: A child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case

Held: 1. A child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case, not on categorical requirements such as an actual agreement between the parents. Pp. 7–14. (a) The inquiry begins with the Convention’s text “and the context 2 MONASKY v. TAGLIERI Syllabus in which the written words are used.

In accord with decisions of the courts of other countries party to the Convention, we hold that a child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case. An actual agreement between the parents is not necessary to establish an infant’s habitual residence. We further hold that a first-instance habitualresidence determination is subject to deferential appellate review for clear error.

us-ca8-639-f3d-449.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-639-f3d-449.summary: The court applied ICARA to determine whether DJ had been wrongfully retained in the United States. It held that the United States was DJ’s habitual residence, so Martin was not entitled to an ICARA remedy requiring his return to Israel for custody adjudication.
excerpts: Martin brought this action in the district court petitioning for DJ’s return to Israel under ICARA. That act implements the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, 19 I.L.M. 1501 (1980) (Convention). ICARA does not control substantive custody disputes, but rather governs selection of the forum where such a dispute should be brought. Barzilay v. Barzilay, 600 F.3d 912, 916 (8th Cir.2010). The key question under ICARA is “whether a child has been wrongfully removed from the country of its habitual residence or wrongfully retained in a country other than that of its habitual residence.

The district court held a bench trial in June 2010, after which it found that DJ habitually resided in the United States. The court found “little evidence” about DJ’s connections with Israel. In contrast, it found DJ had “considerable connections with his current [Iowa] environment.” At the time DJ was seven years old and had been living in Iowa since he was two.

norms.b_justification: Stern interpreted ICARA, 22 U.S.C. § 9003, and the Hague Convention’s habitual-residence requirement through a fact-intensive assessment of the child’s connections to the competing countries. Its analysis—contrasting DJ’s limited connections with Israel against his substantial, longstanding connections to Iowa—is consistent in function with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances formulation, even though Stern predates and does not use Monasky’s exact wording.

provisions: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, habitual-residence requirement

us-ca8-559-f3d-871.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-559-f3d-871.summary: The court held that Australia was the child’s habitual residence when the allegedly wrongful retention occurred. It therefore affirmed the district court’s ruling on Sorenson’s Article 15 Hague Convention claim.
excerpts: Eric Sorenson appeals the district court’s rulings on his claim under Article 15 of the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (Hague Convention), 19 I.L.M. 1501 (1980), as implemented by the United States in the International Child Abduction Remedies Act, 42 U.S.C. § 11601-11610 (“ICARA”). Because we find that Australia was the child’s habitual residence at the time of the allegedly wrongful retention, we affirm the decision of the district court.

norms.b_justification: Sorenson interpreted Hague Convention Article 3’s habitual-residence requirement, as implemented by ICARA, through a fact-specific inquiry into the child’s circumstances and concluded that Australia was the habitual residence. That approach is functionally consistent with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances formulation, although the record does not contain verbatim current-text language.

us-ca8-312-f3d-914.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-312-f3d-914.summary: The court held that habitual residence under the Hague Convention and ICARA is a purely factual, case-specific inquiry, reviewed for clear error. The parent seeking return bears the preponderance-of-the-evidence burden to show that the children were removed from their habitual residence; because the children’s habitual residence was the United States, the court did not reach the Article 13(b) defense.
excerpts: habitual residence” has not been defined in either the Convention or the Act, and courts must look to the legislative history for guidance on the matter. The official history and commentary in the Federal Register explains that “ ‘habitual residence’ ... is, in fact, a familiar notion of the Hague Conference, where it is understood as a ;purely factual concept, to be differentiated especially from that of the ‘domicile.

In its conclusions of law, the district court found that the determination of habitual residence is a fact-based inquiry to be analyzed on a case-by-case basis. We agree with the court below that the Silverman children’s habitual residence is solely a question of fact, and we therefore review the district court’s holding for clear error.

Pursuant to the Hague Convention, Robert Silverman (Robert) must initially prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Julie Silverman (Julie) removed their children from their habitual residence, which Robert alleges is Israel. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention Article 3 and 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A), holding that habitual residence is a fact-based, case-by-case inquiry. That approach is consistent in wording and function with Monasky’s current totality-of-the-circumstances rule, even though the quoted language does not appear verbatim in the current text.

us-scotus-596-666.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-596-666.summary: The Court held that once a court finds that returning a child would pose a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b), it is not categorically required to consider all possible ameliorative measures before denying return. Any consideration of such measures is discretionary and must prioritize the child’s safety, respect the custody court’s role, and avoid undue delay, consistent with the Convention’s return framework.
excerpts: A court is not categorically required to examine all possible ameliorative measures before denying a Hague Convention petition for return of a child to a foreign country once the court has found that return would expose the child to a grave risk of harm.

Held: A court is not categorically required to examine all possible ameliorative measures before denying a Hague Convention petition for return of a child to a foreign country once the court has found that return would expose the child to a grave risk of harm. Pp. 8–16.

But Article 13(b) of the Convention leaves a court with the discretion to grant or deny return, providing that a court “is not bound to order the return of the child” if it finds that the party opposing return has established that return would expose the child to a “grave risk” of physical or psychological harm.

us-scotus-572-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-572-1.summary: The Court held that the Hague Convention’s one-year period for seeking return of a wrongfully removed child is not subject to equitable tolling, even when the abducting parent conceals the child’s location. After that period, return remains subject to Article 12’s “well settled” exception, and ICARA requires courts to decide the case under the Convention.
excerpts: When a parent abducts a child and flees to another country, the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction generally requires that country to return the child immediately if the other parent requests return within one year. The question in this case is whether that 1-year period is subject to equitable tolling when the abducting parent conceals the child's location from the other parent. We hold that equitable tolling is not available.

This case concerns another exception to the return remedy. Article 12 of the Convention states the general rule that when a court receives a petition for return within one year after the child's wrongful removal, the court "shall order the return of the child forthwith." Id., at 9. Article 12 further provides that the court, "where the proceedings have been commenced after the expiration of the period of one year [from the date of the wrongful removal], shall also order the return of the child, unless it is demonstrated that the child is now settled in its new environment." Ibid. Thus, at least in some cases, failure to file a petition for return within one year renders the return remedy unavailable.

us-scotus-560-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-560-1.summary: The Court held that a parent’s ne exeat right—the authority to consent before the other parent may remove the child to another country—is a right of custody under Articles 3 and 5(a) of the Hague Convention. Removal in breach of that right is wrongful and triggers the Convention’s return remedy, as implemented by ICARA.
excerpts: Mr. Abbott’s ne exeat right is a right of custody under the Convention.
The question is whether a parent has a “righ[t] of custody” by reason of that parent’s ne exeat right: the authority to consent before the other parent may take the child to another country.

A removal is “wrongful” where the child was removed in violation of “rights of custody.” The Convention defines “rights of custody” to “include rights relating to the care of the person of the ehild and, in particular, the right to determine the child’s place of residence.” Art. 5(a), id., at 7. A return remedy does not alter the preabduction allocation of custody rights but leaves custodial decisions to the courts of the country of habitual residence. Art. 19, id., at 11.

us-scotus-568-165.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-568-165.summary: The Court held that an appeal from an ICARA/Hague Convention return order is not rendered moot merely because the child has already been returned abroad. The return order and associated costs remain subject to meaningful appellate relief, including reversal and possible recovery of fees and expenses.
excerpts: The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction generally requires courts in the United States to order children returned to their countries of habitual residence, if the courts find that the children have been wrongfully removed to or retained in the United States. The question is whether, after a child is returned pursuant to such an order, any appeal of the order is moot.

Congress established procedures for implementing the Convention in ICARA. See 42 U. S. C. § 11601(b)(1). ICARA grants federal and state courts concurrent jurisdiction over actions arising under the Convention, § 11603(a), and directs them to “decide the case in accordance with the Convention,” § 11603(d). If those courts find children to have been wrongfully removed or retained, the children “are to be promptly returned.” § 11601(a)(4).

ICARA also provides that courts ordering children returned generally must require defendants to pay various expenses incurred by plaintiffs, including court costs, légal fees, and transportation costs associated with the return of the children. § 11607(b)(3).

us-ca8-913-f3d-777.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-913-f3d-777.summary: The court held that Schwartz’s federal ERISA and REA claims were barred by res judicata because the New Jersey court had already determined that the payments represented an equitable distribution of Schwartz’s pension and had addressed the asserted ERISA restrictions. The court also accepted that state and federal courts have concurrent jurisdiction to determine whether a divorce judgment qualifies as a QDRO, while declining to revisit the correctness of the state court’s determination.
excerpts: The court also found that while ERISA prohibits the assignment or alienation of pension-plan benefits, it "was not intended to prevent the assignment to a spouse or former spouse that is entitled to support,"

It concluded that state and federal courts have concurrent jurisdiction to determine whether a divorce decree, judgment, or order qualifies as a QDRO. Whether the state court "correctly determined that the prior order was an enforceable QDRO," the district court explained, is irrelevant to the application of res judicata.

us-scotus-581-214.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-581-214.summary: The Court held that the Uniformed Services Former Spouses’ Protection Act permits division of disposable military retired pay but excludes amounts waived to receive disability benefits. Federal law therefore preempts a state court from ordering a veteran to indemnify a former spouse for the resulting reduction in retirement-pay benefits.
excerpts: A federal statute provides that a State may treat as community property, and divide at divorce, a military veteran’s retirement pay. See 10 U. S. C. §1408(c)(1). The statute, however, exempts from this grant of permission any amount that the Government deducts “as a result of a waiver” that the veteran must make “in order to receive” disability benefits. §1408(a)(4)(B). We have held that a State cannot treat as community property, and divide at divorce, this portion (the waived portion) of the veteran’s retirement pay. See Mansell v. Mansell, 490 U. S. 581, 594–595 (1989).

This Court’s decision in Mansell v. Mansell, 490 U. S. 581, determines the outcome here. There, the Court held that federal law completely pre-empts the States from treating waived military retirement pay as divisible

us-ca8-720-f3d-715.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-720-f3d-715.citation: MidAmerican Pension & Employee Benefits Plans Administrative Committee v. Cox, 720 F.3d 715 (8th Cir. 2013)
us-ca8-720-f3d-715.summary: The court applied ERISA, as amended by the Retirement Equity Act, as controlling the distribution of the plan funds. It construed ERISA’s qualified preretirement survivor-annuity provisions, including the participant’s ability to waive that form of benefit, rather than applying contrary state divorce or property-law rules.

A plan participant “may elect at any time during the applicable election period to waive the ... qualified preretirement survivor annuity form of benefit[.]” 29 U.S.C. § 1055(c)(l)(A)(i). Such an election takes effect only i

us-scotus-569-483.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-569-483.summary: The Court held that FEGLIA preempts Virginia Code § 20-111.1(D), which imposed personal liability on a former spouse who received life-insurance proceeds under a federal employee’s unchanged beneficiary designation. FEGLIA’s order of precedence and federal control over beneficiary designations conflicted with the state-law remedy, notwithstanding the traditional state authority over domestic relations.
excerpts: This case presents the question whether the remedy created by § 20-111.1(D) is pre-empted by FEGLIA and its implementing regulations. We hold that it is.

State law is pre-empted "to the extent of any conflict with a federal statute." Crosby v. National Foreign Trade Council, 530 U.S. 363, 372, 120 S.Ct. 2288, 147 L.Ed.2d 352 (2000) (citing Hines v. Davidowitz, 312 U.S. 52, 66-67, 61 S.Ct. 399, 85 L.Ed. 581 (1941) ). Such a conflict occurs when compliance with both federal and state regulations is impossible, Florida Lime & Avocado Growers, Inc. v. Paul, 373 U.S. 132, 142-143, 83 S.Ct. 1210, 10 L.Ed.2d 248 (1963), or when the state law "stands as an obstacle to the accomplishment and execution of the full purposes and objectives of Congress," Hines, 312 U.S., at 67, 61 S.Ct. 399. This case raises a question of purposes and objectives pre-emption.

us-ca8-622-f3d-885.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-622-f3d-885.citation: Matschiner v. Hartford Life & Accident Insurance, 622 F.3d 885 (8th Cir. 2010)
us-ca8-622-f3d-885.summary: The court held that ERISA’s requirements governing the plan documents and administration preclude a federal common-law inquiry into whether a divorce decree waived a properly designated beneficiary’s entitlement to plan benefits. The court treated the Supreme Court’s reasoning in Kennedy and Egelhoff as controlling despite the plan being a group life-insurance welfare plan rather than a pension plan.
excerpts: In granting summary judgment to the Matsehiners, the district court relied on Eighth Circuit cases applying federal common law and concluded that the divorce decree divested Alan of his beneficiary rights to the life insurance proceeds even though RoJane submitted no designated beneficiary form reflecting this change. See Hill v. AT&T Corp., 125 F.3d 646, 648-50 (8th Cir.1997); Mohamed v. Kerr, 53 F.3d 911, 914 (8th Cir.1995). In Kennedy, a unanimous Supreme Court resolved a conflict in the circuits on this issue.

Consistent with its prior decision in Egelhoff v. Egelhoff ex rel. Breiner, 532 U.S. 141, 147-48, 121 S.Ct. 1322, 149 L.Ed.2d 264 (2001), the Court held that ERISA’s statutory mandates that a plan “specify the basis on which payments are made to and from the plan,” 29 U.S.C. § 1102(b)(4), and that the plan administrator act “in accordance with the documents and instruments” of the plan, § 1104(a)(1)(D), foreclose any federal common law inquiry into whether a properly designated beneficiary’s divorce decree waived his or her entitlement to plan benefits. 129 S.Ct. at 875-77. Hartford and the Secretary argue that principle is controlling here.

us-scotus-532-141.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-532-141.citation: Egelhoff v. Egelhoff ex rel. Breiner, 532 U.S. 141 (2001)
us-scotus-532-141.summary: The Court held that ERISA expressly preempts Washington’s statute automatically revoking an ex-spouse’s beneficiary designation upon divorce when applied to ERISA-covered plans. The statute relates to ERISA plans because it requires plan administrators to determine beneficiary status under state law rather than administer benefits according to the plan documents.
excerpts: Justice Thomas delivered the opinion of the Court. A Washington statute provides that the designation of a spouse as the beneficiary of a nonprobate asset is revoked automatically upon divorce. We are asked to decide whether the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), 88 Stat. 832, 29 U.S.C. §1001 et seq., preempts that statute to the extent it applies to ERISA plans. We hold that it does.

ERISA’s pre-emption section, 29 U. S. C. § 1144(a), states that ERISA “shall supersede any and all State laws insofar as they may now or hereafter relate to any employee benefit plan” covered by ERISA. We have observed repeatedly that this broadly worded provision is “clearly expansive.” New York State Conference of Blue Cross & Blue Shield Plans v. Travelers Ins. Co., 514 U. S. 645, 655 (1995); see, e. g., Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U. S. 374, 384 (1992) (listing cases in which we have described ERISA pre-emption in broad terms).

us-ca8-121-f3d-436.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-121-f3d-436.citation: Painter v. Golden Rule Insurance, 121 F.3d 436 (8th Cir. 1997)
us-ca8-121-f3d-436.summary: The court applied ERISA conflict-preemption principles, holding that state-law claims conflicting with ERISA’s specifically prescribed benefit remedies are preempted. It distinguished this analysis from broader “relate to” preemption.
excerpts: However, some ERISA eases involve the distinct question of conflict preemption — whether a state law is preempted because it conflicts with a specific portion of the complex ERISA statute. If there is a conflict, state law is preempted, whether or not “the statutory phrase ‘relate to’ provides further and additional support for the pre-emption claim.” Boggs v. Boggs, — U.S. -, -, 117 S.Ct. 1754, 1761, 138 L.Ed.2d 45 (1997). In our view, this is a ease of conflict preemption.

us-ca8-121-f3d-364.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-121-f3d-364.citation: Prudential Insurance v. Hinkel, 121 F.3d 364 (8th Cir. 1997)
us-ca8-121-f3d-364.summary: The court applied the federal-preemption rule recognized in Ridgway, holding that state divorce decrees and related state-law property claims cannot override federally established beneficiary designations for military life-insurance benefits. It therefore concluded that Hinkel was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
excerpts: In Ridgway, Sergeant Ridgway and his first wife were divorced and he was ordered to keep in force the insurance policies on his life for the benefit of the three children of the marriage. After his remarriage, Sergeant Ridgway changed the beneficiary designation on his SGLIA policy from his first wife, April, to his second wife, Donna. Both April and Donna filed claims for the proceeds of the policy. April’s claim was on behalf of the children, pursuant to the divorce decree. The Supreme Judicial Court of Maine held that Donna must hold the policy proceeds as constructive trustee on behalf of the children. The United States Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine. Ridgway, 454 U.S. at 63, 102 S.Ct. at 59.

us-scotus-490-581.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-490-581.summary: The Court held that the Uniformed Services Former Spouses’ Protection Act does not authorize state courts to treat military retired pay waived to obtain veterans’ disability benefits as community property divisible upon divorce. The Act’s definition of “disposable retired or retainer pay” excludes waived amounts, and that limitation controls the state-court property division authorized by § 1408(c)(1).
excerpts: the Former Spouses’ Protection Act does not grant state courts the power to treat as property divisible upon divorce military retirement pay that has been waived to receive veterans’ disability benefits.

In this appeal, we decide whether state courts, consistent with the federal Uniformed Services Former Spouses’ Protection Act, 10 U. S. C. § 1408 (1982 ed. and Supp. V) (Former Spouses’ Protection Act or Act), may treat as property divisible upon divorce military retirement pay waived by the retiree in order to receive veterans’ disability benefits. We hold that they may not.

In direct response to McCarty, Congress enacted the Former Spouses’ Protection Act, which authorizes state courts to treat “disposable retired or retainer pay” as community property. 10 U. S. C. § 1408(c)(1). “‘Disposable retired or retainer pay’” is defined as “the total monthly retired or retainer pay to which a military member is entitled,” minus certain deductions. § 1408(a)(4) (1982 ed. and Supp. V). Among the amounts required to be deducted from total pay are any amounts waived in order to receive disability benefits. § 1408(a)(4)(B).

us-scotus-481-619.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-481-619.summary: The Court held that Tennessee could consider and enforce a disabled veteran’s veterans’ disability benefits as a source of child support. Section 659(a) was a limited waiver permitting legal process against federal funds in appropriate support proceedings, and the exclusion in § 662(f)(2) did not preempt the state court’s child-support order. The state law therefore did not cause the kind of major damage to a clear and substantial federal interest required for Supremacy Clause preemption.
excerpts: The Court of Appeals correctly identified the constitutional standard for determining whether § 36-820, as construed by the Tennessee courts to authorize an award of a veteran’s disability benefits as child support, conflicts with federal law and is therefore pre-empted under the Supremacy Clause. We have consistently recognized that “[t]he whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States.

But § 659(a) does not refer to any legal process. The provision was intended to create a limited waiver of sovereign immunity so that state courts could issue valid orders directed against agencies of the United States Government attaching funds in the possession of those agencies:

norms.b_justification: Rose v. Rose interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 659(a), together with § 662(f)(2), concerning the federal waiver permitting state child-support process against qualifying federal payments, including veterans’ disability benefits. Although the section was generally amended after the decision and the former Title 38 citation was recodified from § 3101 to § 5301, the operative language and legal function of § 659(a) remain materially unchanged.

us-scotus-454-46.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-454-46.summary: The Court held that the Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance Act controlled the beneficiary designation and distribution of the policy proceeds. Because the federal scheme protected the designated beneficiary’s rights, the Supremacy Clause barred enforcement of a state divorce decree through a constructive trust that would redirect the proceeds to the insured’s children.
excerpts: Notwithstanding the limited application of federal law in the field of domestic relations generally, see McCarty v. McCarty, 453 U. S. 210, 220 (1981); Hisquierdo v. Hisquierdo, 439 U. S. 572, 581 (1979); In re Burrus, 136 U. S. 586, 593-594 (1890), this Court, even in that area, has not hesitated to protect, under the Supremacy Clause, rights and expectancies established by federal law against the operation of state law, or to prevent the frustration and erosion of the congressional policy embodied in the federal rights.

While “[sjtate family and family-property law must do ‘major damage’ to ‘clear and substantial’ federal interests before the Supremacy Clause will demand that state law be overridden,” Hisquierdo, 439 U. S., at 581, with references to United States v. Yazell, 382 U. S. 341, 352 (1966), “[t]he relative importance to the State of its own law is not material when there is a conflict with a valid federal law, for the Framers of our Constitution provided that the federal law must prevail.” Free v. Bland, 369 U. S., at 666.

us-scotus-453-210.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-453-210.summary: The Court held that federal law precludes state courts from dividing military nondisability retired pay as community property upon divorce. Applying Supremacy Clause preemption principles, it concluded that state family-property law conflicted with substantial federal interests embodied in the military retirement scheme.
excerpts: The question presented by this case is whether, upon the dissolution of a marriage, federal law precludes a state court from dividing military nondisability retired pay pursuant to state community property laws.

Thus, “[s]tate family and family-property law must do 'major damage’ to 'clear and substantial’ federal interests before the Supremacy Clause will demand that state law be overridden.” Hisquierdo, 439 U. S., at 581, with references to United States v. Yazell, 382 U. S. 341, 352 (1966).

us-scotus-439-572.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-439-572.summary: The Court held that California’s community-property allocation of an employee’s expected Railroad Retirement Act benefits was preempted because it conflicted with the federal statute’s allocation and protection of those benefits. Although domestic relations are generally governed by state law, the Supremacy Clause requires state family-property rules to yield when they cause major damage to clear and substantial federal interests.
excerpts: The pertinent questions are whether the right as asserted conflicts with the express terms of federal law and whether its consequences sufficiently injure the objectives of the federal program to require nonrecognition.

Insofar as marriage is within temporal control, the States lay on the guiding hand. “The whole subject of the domestic relations of husband and wife, parent and child, belongs to the laws of the States and not to the laws of the United States.” In re Burrus, 136 U. S. 586, 593-594 (1890). Federal courts repeatedly have declined to assert jurisdiction over divorces that presented no federal question.

On the rare occasion when state family law has come into conflict with a federal statute, this Court has limited review under the Supremacy Clause to a determination whether Congress has “positively required by direct enactment” that state law be pre-empted. Wetmore v. Markoe, 196 U. S. 68, 77 (1904). A mere conflict in words is not sufficient. State family and family-property law must do “major damage” to “clear and substantial” federal interests before the Supremacy Clause will demand that state law be overridden.

us-ca8-459-f2d-1017.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-459-f2d-1017.citation: Burke v. United States, 459 F.2d 1017 (8th Cir. 1972)
us-ca8-459-f2d-1017.summary: The court applied the federal beneficiary-designation rules governing war risk insurance and held that the insured serviceman’s designation controlled. The federal scheme displaced the appellant’s contrary claim based on state family or community-property principles.
excerpts: Similarly, we find no unjust enrichment or “windfall” to the appellee. A review of the history of war risk insurance discloses that during wartime Congress closely circumscribed the class of permissible beneficiaries to insure that proceeds of such policies would go to persons dependent upon the insured soldier for financial support. Congress in 1946, however, broadened the Act by granting insured servicemen the right to designate their choice of beneficiaries and with the right at all times to change such designations without the consent of the beneficiaries.

Pursuant to such congressional command, the appellee contracted to pay the policy proceeds to Burke’s choice. Unfortunately for the appellant, Burke chose his father and brother. See Wissner v. Wissner, 338 U.S. 655, 658, 70 S.Ct. 398, 94 L.Ed. 424 (1950).

norms.b_justification: Burke interpreted 38 U.S.C. § 717(a) and held that the federal beneficiary-designation scheme controlled over contrary state-law claims to the insurance proceeds. Although the current text contains no verbatim quotation and the provision’s wording cannot be compared directly, Burke applies the same functional federal-preemption principle reflected in the current rule: federal benefits law protects federally established rights from conflicting state family-property law.

us-ca8-453-f2d-925.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-453-f2d-925.citation: Prudential Insurance Co. of America v. King, 453 F.2d 925 (8th Cir. 1971)
us-ca8-453-f2d-925.summary: The court held that Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance is governed by the federal statutory scheme, which preempts contrary state law concerning the insurance and beneficiary designation. It therefore treated the dispute as controlled by the federal acts rather than state community-property or family-law rules.
excerpts: It is the contention of the plaintiff, in part at least, that the state law governs while the defendant contends that the decision rests solely on the federal acts of Congress. Title 38 U.S.C.A. ss. 765 to 776. We think that Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance is a contract between the United States government and approved insurers for the benefit of the insureds, the same being those entering the military service of the United States. The designation of insurers by the federal government under regulations prescribed by the federal act amounts to a preemption of the field of servicemen’s life insurance and it is therefore subject to the rules and regulations provided in the federal acts.

norms.b_justification: Prudential interpreted 38 U.S.C.A. §§ 765–776, including § 770(a), and held that federal Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance law preempted contrary state-law rules. That application is functionally consistent with the current federal-preemption rule protecting federal benefits programs from conflicting state family-property or domestic-relations laws, although the quoted language does not appear verbatim in the current text.

us-scotus-376-306.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-376-306.summary: The Court held that federal savings-bond survivorship regulations preempt Washington community-property rules that would invalidate the beneficiary designation and require the bonds to pass by will or intestacy. The named beneficiary was entitled to at least the deceased spouse’s transferable share, subject to issues of the surviving spouse’s consent, the nature of her community-property interest, and applicable debts.
excerpts: During the husband’s life he was the registered owner of the bonds, and was therefore entitled at any time to convert them into cash upon presentation and surrender “as though no beneficiary had been named in the registration.” 31 CFR § 315.65. Aside from possible consequences of the wife’s consent or ratification, as long as Angel Yiatchos was alive the bonds were community property, and could be used by him— the manager of the community and the registered owner of the bonds — for community purposes just as the assets used to purchase them could have been so used.

The Washington court deemed the transaction void ab initio and required the deceased’s half to pass by his will rather than by virtue of the bonds and the force of the regulation. But the petitioner was entitled to the proceeds only on the death of the husband, and then only if the bonds had not matured or been cashed. During the husband’s life he was the registered owner of the bonds, and was therefore entitled at any time to convert them into cash upon presentation and surrender “as though no beneficiary had been named in the registration.

norms.b_justification: Yiatchos interpreted 31 CFR § 315.65 and held that federal savings-bond registration and beneficiary rules preempted contrary state community-property allocation at the bondholder’s death. That application is consistent in function with the current federal-preemption rule protecting federally established rights from conflicting state family-property law.

us-scotus-369-663.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-369-663.summary: The Court held that Treasury regulations governing United States Savings Bonds created a federally controlling right of survivorship. Under the Supremacy Clause, Texas community-property law could not require the surviving co-owner to reimburse the decedent’s estate in a manner that defeated or impaired that federal survivorship right.
excerpts: The Supreme Court of Texas’ interpretation of the Supremacy Clause is not in accord with controlling doctrine. The relative importance to the State of its own law is not material when there is a conflict with a valid federal law, for the Framers of our Constitution provided that the federal law must prevail. Article VI, Clause 2.

The clear purpose of the regulations is to confer the right of survivorship on the surviving co-owner. Thus, the survivorship provision is a federal law which must prevail if it conflicts with state law. See Wissner v. Wissner, 338 U. S. 655.

We hold, therefore, that the state law which prohibits a married couple from taking advantage of the survivor-ship provisions of United States Savings Bonds merely because the purchase price is paid out of community property must fall under the Supremacy Clause.

norms.b_justification: Free v. Bland interpreted the Supremacy Clause, 31 U.S.C. § 757c(a), and implementing savings-bond regulations to hold that federal survivorship rights prevail over conflicting state community-property law. That holding is consistent in function with the current federal-preemption rule protecting federally created rights from contrary state family-property allocations.

us-ca8-211-f2d-708.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-211-f2d-708.summary: The court applied the federal beneficiary-designation rule governing National Service Life Insurance proceeds, holding that the named beneficiary’s entitlement was not altered by a state divorce decree or property settlement. Federal law therefore preempted any contrary state-law allocation of the insurance proceeds.
excerpts: Neither in the property settlement nor in the divorce proceedings is any reference made to the insurance policies here involved. No act or expression of the insured is even referred to in the evidence indicating that the insured desired or ever intended to change the named beneficiary. Wissner v. Wissner, 338 U.S. 655, 658, 70 S.Ct. 398, 400, 94 L.Ed. 424, is a case in which a soldier named his mother beneficiary in his National Life Insurance policy.
